You may flip any element (change 0 to 1 or 1 to 0) any number of times, and you need to determine the smallest possible number of flips that turns every entry of the array into 1; if no sequence of flips can achieve that, you must report -1. The answer you return is this minimum count (or -1 when it’s impossible).

title: Count the Number of Inversions
explanation_short:
You are given an integer n and a list requirements where each entry is a pair [endi, cnti].  
A permutation of the numbers 0 … n‑1 is considered valid if, for every requirement, the prefix of the permutation ending at index endi contains exactly cnti inversions (a pair (i, j) with i < j and perm[i] > perm[j]).  
Your task is to count how many such permutations exist.  
Return that count modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Find the Minimum Area to Cover All Ones II
explanation_short:
You are given a 2‑D array of 0’s and 1’s.  
Choose three axis‑aligned rectangles (each with positive area) that do not overlap, although they may touch, and make sure every cell containing a 1 lies inside at least one of the rectangles.  
Among all possible ways to place the three rectangles, find the configuration whose combined area is as small as possible.  
Return that minimum total area as an integer.

title: Maximum Height of a Triangle
explanation_short:
You are given two numbers: the amount of red balls and the amount of blue balls.  
You must stack the balls in rows where the first row contains 1 ball, the second row 2 balls, the third row 3 balls, and so on, with every row using only one colour and neighbouring rows using opposite colours.  
Determine the greatest possible number of rows (the triangle’s height) that can be built without exceeding the available balls of either colour.  
Output that maximum height as a single integer.

title: Find the Minimum Area to Cover All Ones I
explanation_short: You receive a rectangular grid of 0s and 1s. Your task is to locate a sub‑rectangle whose sides are parallel to the grid axes and that contains every cell with a 1. Among all such rectangles, you must choose the one with the smallest possible area. Return that minimum area as an integer.

title: Maximize Total Cost of Alternating Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may cut the array into several contiguous pieces, but each piece must have alternating signs (no two adjacent numbers in the same piece share the same sign). The cost of a piece is the sum of the absolute values of its elements, and the total cost is the sum of the costs of all pieces. Return the largest total cost achievable by an appropriate splitting of the array.

title: Maximum Points After Enemy Battles
explanation_short: You receive an array enemyEnergies containing the energy values of each enemy and an integer currentEnergy representing your starting energy. Starting with zero points, you may repeatedly apply the allowed operations-each changes your energy and may mark enemies-to accumulate points. Your task is to choose a sequence of operations that yields the greatest possible total of points. Return that maximum point total as a single integer.

title: Find the Maximum Length of Valid Subsequence I
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums`.  
From this array you may delete any elements (or none) while keeping the original order, forming a subsequence.  
Your task is to find the greatest possible length of a subsequence that satisfies the given validity rule.  
Return that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Find the Maximum Length of Valid Subsequence II
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a parameter `k`. From `nums` you may select elements in their original order to build a subsequence that fulfills the validity rule involving `k` described in the statement. Your task is to find the greatest possible length of any such valid subsequence. Return that length as a single integer.

title: Find Minimum Diameter After Merging Two Trees
explanation_short: You are given two trees: the first described by `edges1` with `n` nodes numbered 0…n‑1, and the second described by `edges2` with `m` nodes numbered 0…m‑1. You may add exactly one new edge that connects any node of the first tree to any node of the second tree. The task is to choose the pair of nodes that makes the longest distance between any two nodes in the combined tree as small as possible. Return that smallest achievable diameter as an integer.

title: Number of Subarrays With AND Value of K
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a target value `k`.  
Consider every possible contiguous segment (subarray) of `nums`.  
Count how many of those subarrays have a bitwise AND of all their elements exactly equal to `k`.  
Return that count as a single integer.

title: Generate Binary Strings Without Adjacent Zeros
explanation_short:
You receive a single positive integer n.  
You must list every binary string of length n in which no two consecutive characters are both 0 (every pair of adjacent bits contains at least one 1).  
Each string should be returned as a separate element of a list, and the order of the strings does not matter.  
If n is 1, the list contains the two strings “0” and “1”.

title: Count Submatrices With Equal Frequency of X and Y
explanation_short:
You are given a rectangular grid where each cell contains either the character ‘X’, ‘Y’, or a dot ‘.’.  
Your task is to count how many rectangular sub‑areas of this grid have the same number of ‘X’ cells as ‘Y’ cells (dots are ignored).  
The answer is a single integer representing that count.

title: Alternating Groups I
explanation_short: You are given an array `colors` where each element is 0 or 1, representing the color of a tile placed around a circle. A group is any three consecutive tiles (including the wrap‑around from the last to the first) where the middle tile’s color differs from both its left and right neighbors. Your task is to count how many such alternating groups exist in the circle. Return that count as an integer.

title: Alternating Groups II
explanation_short: You are given an array `colors` where each element is 0 or 1, representing the colors of tiles placed around a circle, and an integer `k`. An alternating group is any block of `k` consecutive tiles (wrapping from the end back to the start) whose colors strictly alternate from one tile to the next. Your task is to determine how many such `k`‑length blocks exist in the circular arrangement. Return that number as an integer.

title: Find the Encrypted String
explanation_short:
You receive a text `s` and a number `k`.  
Your task is to apply the encryption steps described in the statement to transform the original string.  
After performing those steps, output the resulting encrypted string.

title: Construct String with Minimum Cost
explanation_short: You are given a target string, a list of candidate words, and a matching list of integer costs. Starting from an empty string, you may repeatedly append any of the given words, paying its associated cost each time. Your task is to determine the smallest total cost that makes the built string exactly equal the target, or report -1 if no combination of words can produce the target. The output is a single integer representing that minimum cost (or -1).

title: Minimum Cost for Cutting Cake I
explanation_short: You are given the dimensions m and n of a rectangular cake and two lists of costs: one for each possible horizontal cut and one for each possible vertical cut. Starting with the whole cake, you may repeatedly cut any piece that is larger than 1 × 1, paying the cost associated with the chosen cut line each time. Your task is to choose the order of cuts so that the sum of all paid costs is as small as possible. Output the minimum total cost required to split the cake into individual 1 × 1 squares.

title: Minimum Cost for Cutting Cake II
explanation_short: You receive the dimensions m and n of a rectangular cake and two lists: the costs of possible horizontal cuts and the costs of possible vertical cuts. The cake must be repeatedly cut until every piece is a 1 × 1 square, and each cut adds its given cost to the total. Your task is to pick an ordering of these cuts that yields the smallest possible sum of costs. Return that minimum total cost as a single integer.

title: Lexicographically Smallest String After a Swap
explanation_short: You are given a string `s` that consists only of digit characters. You may perform at most one swap of two neighboring characters, but the two characters can be swapped only if both are odd or both are even. Return the lexicographically smallest string that can be achieved after applying such a swap (or none if no swap improves the order).

title: Delete Nodes From Linked List Present in Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and the head of a singly‑linked list. Every node whose value occurs anywhere in `nums` must be removed from the list. After all such deletions, return the head of the resulting linked list. The output is the sequence of values that remain, preserving their original order.

title: Minimum Length of String After Operations
explanation_short: You are given a single string `s`. By repeatedly applying the allowed operation on the characters of `s`, you may delete or rearrange parts of the string any number of times. Your task is to determine the smallest possible length the string can have after no more operations are possible. Return that minimum length as an integer.

title: Minimum Array Changes to Make Differences Equal
explanation_short: You are given an even‑length integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. In one operation you may replace any element with any value from 0 to `k`. Your goal is to adjust the array so that for every symmetric pair of positions (the i‑th element and the element exactly n/2 places later) the sum of the two numbers is the same constant `X`. Report the smallest possible number of replacements needed to achieve this. The answer is a single integer representing that minimum count.

title: Number of Bit Changes to Make Two Integers Equal
explanation_short: You are given two positive integers n and k. You may only flip bits that are 1 in n to 0, never the other way around. Determine the smallest number of such flips that turns n into exactly k, and output that number; if no sequence of flips can produce k, output -1. The answer is the count of required bit changes.

title: Maximum Number of Operations to Move Ones to the End
explanation_short: You are given a binary string s. You may repeatedly apply the allowed operation, which moves a ‘1’ toward the end of the string. Find the largest possible number of times you can perform this operation before no further moves are possible. Output that maximum count as an integer.

title: Maximum Score From Grid Operations
explanation_short: You are given an n × n grid of integers. You may repeatedly choose a cell (i, j) and turn black every cell in column j from the top down to row i; the score of a final coloring is the sum of the values in all white cells that have a black cell immediately to their left. Compute the greatest possible score achievable by any sequence of such operations and output that maximum value.

title: Find the Winning Player in Coin Game
explanation_short: You receive two positive integers x and y, the counts of 75‑value and 10‑value coins available. Alice moves first, and on each turn a player must take a combination of these coins whose total value equals 115; if a player cannot do that, they lose. Assuming both players choose their moves optimally, you must decide which player will be the eventual winner. Output the winner’s name as the string "Alice" or "Bob".

title: Find the Count of Numbers Which Are Not Special
explanation_short: You receive two positive integers l and r. For each integer x in the inclusive range [l, r], consider its proper divisors (all positive divisors except x itself). A number is “special” if it has exactly two proper divisors; you must count how many numbers in the interval are **not** special. Output that count as a single integer.

title: Vowels Game in a String
explanation_short: You are given a string s containing lowercase letters. Alice and Bob alternately pick a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) that still appears in the current string and delete it; the player who has no vowel to remove on their turn loses. Both players play optimally, and Alice moves first. Return true if Alice can force a win under these rules, otherwise return false.

title: Find if Digit Game Can Be Won
explanation_short: You receive an array `nums` containing only positive integers. Alice may take either every one‑digit number in the array or every two‑digit number, while Bob gets the remaining elements. Alice wins when the total of the numbers she picks is strictly larger than the total of Bob’s numbers. Return **true** if there exists a choice (single‑digit or double‑digit) that lets Alice win; otherwise return **false**.

title: Minimum Number of Flips to Make Binary Grid Palindromic I
explanation_short:
You receive an m × n matrix whose entries are only 0 or 1.  
A row (or column) is palindromic when reading its values from left to right (or top to bottom) yields the same sequence as reading them in reverse.  
You may change any cell’s value, and you must determine the smallest number of cells to flip so that either every row becomes palindromic or every column becomes palindromic.  
Return that minimum flip count as an integer.

title: Check if the Rectangle Corner Is Reachable
explanation_short:
You are given the rectangle’s opposite corners (0, 0) and (xCorner, yCorner) together with a list of circles defined by their centers and radii.  
The task is to decide whether a continuous curve can be drawn from the bottom‑left corner to the top‑right corner while staying completely inside the rectangle, never intersecting or touching any of the circles, and meeting the rectangle’s border only at the two corners.  
If such a curve exists, return true; otherwise return false.

title: Find the Number of Winning Players
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and a list of pairs [xi, yi] where each pair records that player xi picked a ball of color yi. For each player i (0 ≤ i < n) we need to check whether there exists any color that player i has picked more than i times. Count how many players satisfy this condition. The answer is a single integer representing the number of winning players.

title: Time Taken to Mark All Nodes
explanation_short: You are given an undirected tree with n nodes, described by the list edges where each pair [ui, vi] represents a connection between two nodes. For every node i you imagine that it becomes marked at time 0 and the marking spreads through the tree according to the rules of the problem. Your task is to compute, for each starting node i, the moment when the last unmarked node becomes marked. Return an array times of length n, where times[i] holds that finishing time for the scenario that begins at node i.

title: Minimum Number of Flips to Make Binary Grid Palindromic II
explanation_short:
You are given an m × n matrix whose entries are only 0 or 1.  
You may change any cell’s value, and you want every row and every column to read the same forwards and backwards (be palindromic).  
At the same time the total count of 1 s in the final matrix must be a multiple of 4.  
Return the smallest possible number of cells you need to flip to satisfy both conditions.

title: Shortest Distance After Road Addition Queries II
explanation_short: Given an integer n and a list of queries, each query adds a one‑way road from city a to city b. Initially there is only a road from city i to city i + 1 for every i from 0 to n‑2. After processing each query you must determine the length of the shortest directed path from city 0 to city n‑1. The result is an array containing these shortest‑path lengths in the order the queries are applied.

title: Snake in Matrix
explanation_short: You receive an integer n that defines an n × n grid and a list of direction strings such as “UP”, “RIGHT”, “DOWN”, or “LEFT”. Starting from cell 0 (which corresponds to the top‑left corner), the snake follows each command in order, moving one cell at a time while staying inside the grid. After processing all commands, output the index of the cell where the snake ends, calculated as row * n + column.

title: Count the Number of Good Nodes
explanation_short:
You are given an undirected tree with n nodes numbered 0 to n‑1, described by a list of n‑1 edges, and the tree is rooted at node 0.  
For each node, look at the subtrees that start at its children; the node is considered “good” when every one of those child subtrees contains the same number of nodes.  
Your task is to determine how many nodes in the whole tree satisfy this condition.  
Return that count as a single integer.

title: Smallest Missing Integer Greater Than Sequential Prefix Sum
explanation_short: We're given an array of integers as input. Our task is to find the longest sequence of numbers in the array that are in order, calculate their sum, and then determine the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to this sum and missing from the array. The output will be this smallest missing integer. We need to examine the array to identify the sequential prefix and its sum to find the desired output.

title: Design Neighbor Sum Service
explanation_short: You are given an n × n grid filled with unique numbers from 0 to n²‑1. The class is initialized with this grid, then you will be asked repeatedly for a value x that appears somewhere in the grid. For each query you must return either the sum of the numbers that are directly up, down, left, or right of x (“adjacent” sum) or the sum of the numbers that lie on the four diagonal cells around x (“diagonal” sum). The overall output is a list where the first entry is null for the constructor call and each subsequent entry is the integer result of the corresponding query.

title: Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs I
explanation_short:
You are given an array `nums` of `n` positive integers.  
A pair consists of two non‑negative integer arrays `arr1` and `arr2` that satisfy the monotonic condition defined in the statement.  
Your task is to determine how many such pairs exist for the given `nums`.  
Return the total count modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Count the Number of Substrings With Dominant Ones
explanation_short: You are given a binary string s. For every possible contiguous substring of s, check whether the number of ‘1’ characters is at least the square of the number of ‘0’ characters in that substring. Count all substrings that satisfy this condition. Return the total count as an integer.

title: Shortest Distance After Road Addition Queries I
explanation_short: You are given an integer n for cities numbered 0 to n‑1 and a list of queries, each adding a one‑way road from city a to city b. Initially only the roads i → i+1 exist. After each added road you must report the smallest number of roads required to travel from city 0 to city n‑1. Return these shortest‑path lengths in order, one value for each query.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal to Target
explanation_short: You are given two positive integer arrays `nums` and `target` that have the same length. In one move you may pick any contiguous subarray of `nums` and either increase every element in that segment by 1 or decrease every element by 1. The task is to change `nums` so that it becomes identical to `target` using the fewest possible moves. Return that minimum number of operations.

title: Alternating Groups III
explanation_short: You are given an array colors where each element is 0 (red) or 1 (blue) and the tiles form a circle, so the first and last positions are adjacent. A query is either “type 1”: ask how many contiguous groups of exactly k tiles have alternating colors, or “type 2”: change the color of a specific tile to a new value. Process the queries in order, updating the array when a type 2 query occurs and counting groups for each type 1 query. Return an array containing the counts produced by all type 1 queries, in the same order they appear.

title: Maximum Value Sum by Placing Three Rooks II
explanation_short: You are given an m × n grid of integers where each entry represents the value of a board cell. Choose three distinct cells so that no two lie in the same row or the same column (i.e., the rooks don’t attack each other). Compute the sum of the values in the three chosen cells. Return the largest sum achievable.

title: Count Substrings That Satisfy K-Constraint I
explanation_short: You are given a binary string s and an integer k. A substring is any contiguous block of characters from s, and it is considered valid if it satisfies the k‑constraint (the allowed relationship between the numbers of 0’s and 1’s). Your task is to count how many of the possible substrings of s meet this condition. Output the total count as a single integer.

title: Find the Power of K-Size Subarrays I
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
For every consecutive segment of `nums` that contains exactly `k` elements, you must determine its “power” as defined in the statement.  
Collect these values in order, producing a new array whose length is `n - k + 1`.  
The i‑th entry of the result corresponds to the power of the subarray `nums[i … i+k‑1]`.

title: Maximum Value Sum by Placing Three Rooks I
explanation_short:
You receive a rectangular grid where each cell contains an integer value.  
Choose three distinct cells so that no two share the same row or the same column, mimicking the placement of non‑attacking rooks.  
The goal is to make the sum of the three chosen cell values as large as possible.  
Return that maximum achievable sum.

title: Find the Power of K-Size Subarrays II
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`. For every contiguous subarray of length `k` you must evaluate its “power” (the value defined in the statement, which may be `-1` if the subarray has no qualifying element). Produce an array `results` where `results[i]` holds the power of the subarray `nums[i … i+k‑1]`. The length of `results` is `n‑k+1`.

title: Count Substrings That Satisfy K-Constraint II
explanation_short: You are given a binary string s, an integer k, and many queries where each query provides two indices l and r. For each query you must consider the segment s[l…r] and count how many of its contiguous substrings meet the k‑constraint (a substring is valid if it fulfills one of the two specified conditions involving k). The answer for a query is that count, and you should return an array containing the answers in the same order as the queries.

title: Final Array State After K Multiplication Operations I
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`, a count `k`, and a factor `multiplier`. Perform exactly `k` steps; at each step you choose one element of the current array, multiply that element by `multiplier`, and replace it with the new value. After completing all `k` steps, return the entire array as it stands. The output is the final version of `nums` after those `k` multiplications.

title: Maximum Energy Boost From Two Drinks
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays of the same length n, where each element tells how much energy you would gain in that hour from drink A or drink B. Each hour you may drink either A or B, but if you change from one drink to the other you must spend the next hour without drinking and thus gain zero. You can begin with either drink, and you need to decide the sequence of drinks (and possible idle hours) that yields the highest total energy over the n hours. Return that maximum total energy boost.

title: Find the Largest Palindrome Divisible by K
explanation_short: You are given two positive integers n and k. You must find the greatest integer that has exactly n digits (no leading zeros) and satisfies the definition of a k‑palindromic number. The answer should be returned as a string representing that integer. If no such number exists, the output is an empty string.

title: Find the Key of the Numbers
explanation_short: You are given three positive integers num1, num2, and num3. First write each number as a four‑digit string by adding leading zeros if necessary. Then, for each of the four positions, pick the smallest digit that appears among the three strings and concatenate those four minimum digits. Output the resulting number, omitting any leading zeros.

title: Count Almost Equal Pairs I
explanation_short: You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. Two positions `i` and `j` (with `i < j`) form an “almost equal” pair if the two numbers are already the same or can be made the same by changing at most one bit in the binary representation of one of them. Your task is to count how many such index pairs exist in the array. The answer is a single integer representing that count.

title: Count Almost Equal Pairs II
explanation_short: You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. Two numbers are considered “almost equal” if you can apply the allowed operation to each of them no more than twice and make them identical. Your task is to count how many index pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` satisfy this condition. Output that total count as a single integer.

title: Final Array State After K Multiplication Operations II
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`, a count `k`, and a value `multiplier`. Perform exactly `k` multiplication steps, each time updating one element of `nums` according to the operation rule (the element to modify is chosen as specified in the problem). After all `k` steps, replace every entry in `nums` with its remainder modulo \(10^9+7\). Return the resulting array as the answer.

title: Check if Two Chessboard Squares Have the Same Color
explanation_short: You receive two strings like “a1” and “c3”, each describing a square on a standard 8 × 8 chessboard (letter for column, digit for row). The task is to determine whether the two given squares share the same color-both black or both white. Think about how the board’s alternating pattern depends on the parity of the column and row positions. Return “true” if the colors match and “false” otherwise.

title: K-th Nearest Obstacle Queries
explanation_short: You are given an integer k and a sequence of queries, each query adding an obstacle at coordinates (x, y). After each addition you must consider all obstacles placed so far and determine the Manhattan distance |x| + |y| of the kth‑closest obstacle to the origin (the point (0, 0)). Return an array where the i‑th element is that distance after the i‑th query, or –1 if fewer than k obstacles exist.

title: Hash Divided String
explanation_short: You receive a lowercase string s and an integer k such that the length of s is a multiple of k. First split s into consecutive blocks, each containing exactly k characters. For every block, add the alphabetical positions of its letters (a = 0, b = 1, …, z = 25), take the sum modulo 26, and convert that remainder back to a letter. The characters obtained from all blocks, in order, form the output string.

title: Select Cells in Grid With Maximum Score
explanation_short: You are given a rectangular grid of positive integers. From this grid you must pick a non‑empty set of cells that satisfies the stated selection rules, and the score of a choice is the sum of the values in the chosen cells. Your task is to determine the greatest possible score achievable under those rules. The program should output that maximum sum as a single integer.

title: Maximum XOR Score Subarray Queries
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a list of queries, each query given as two indices `li` and `ri`.  
For every query you must consider every contiguous subarray inside `nums[li…ri]` and compute its XOR score, which is the result of XOR‑ing all elements of that subarray together.  
The answer for the query is the largest XOR score among those subarrays.  
Return an array where the i‑th element is the maximum XOR score for the i‑th query.

title: Find the Count of Good Integers
explanation_short: You are given two positive integers n and k. An n‑digit integer is “good” if its digits can be permuted (without creating a leading zero) into a number that is k‑palindromic – i.e., it reads the same when split into blocks of k digits and each block is a palindrome. Your task is to determine how many n‑digit integers satisfy this property. Output that count as a single integer.

title: Maximum Number of Moves to Kill All Pawns
explanation_short: You are given the knight’s starting cell (kx, ky) on a 50 × 50 board and a list of pawn coordinates positions. The players alternate moves: on each turn the current player moves the knight like a chess knight and captures any pawn it lands on. Alice tries to make the game last as long as possible, while Bob tries to end it as quickly as possible. Return the greatest total number of moves that will be played when both sides act optimally.

title: Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs II
explanation_short: We're given an array of positive integers, and we need to find the count of pairs of non-negative integer arrays that are considered monotonic. The input array contains a series of numbers, and we must determine all possible pairs that meet the monotonic condition. Our task is to calculate the total count of these monotonic pairs and return the result modulo 10^9 + 7. The output will be the total count of such pairs.

title: Maximize Score of Numbers in Ranges
explanation_short: You receive an array `start` and an integer `d`; each element defines an interval `[start[i], start[i] + d]`. From each interval you must pick exactly one integer, forming a set of `n` numbers. The score of a selection is the smallest absolute difference between any two chosen numbers. Return the largest score that can be achieved by an appropriate choice of numbers.

title: Convert Date to Binary
explanation_short: You receive a single string `date` written as “yyyy‑mm‑dd”. Convert the year, month, and day numbers individually to binary, drop any leading zeroes, and keep the three parts separated by hyphens. The result is the binary‑formatted date string you must return.

title: Reach End of Array With Max Score
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. Starting from index 0, you may jump only to positions with a larger index, and each jump from i to j adds `(j‑i) × nums[i]` to your total. Find the greatest possible total score you can accumulate by the time you reach the final index `n‑1`. Return that maximum score as a single integer.

title: Find the Maximum Sequence Value of Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`. From the array you must pick any subsequence that contains exactly `2 × k` elements, keep the order they appear, and split it into two consecutive blocks of `k` numbers each. The value of the chosen subsequence is the bitwise OR of the first block XORed with the bitwise OR of the second block. Your task is to output the largest possible value that can be obtained from any such subsequence.

title: The Two Sneaky Numbers of Digitville
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` that should contain each value from 0 to n‑1 exactly once, but two different numbers each appear one extra time, making the array longer than n. Your task is to identify those two numbers that occur twice. Return them as a two‑element array, in any order. The input is the list `nums`; the output is the pair of duplicated values.

title: Length of the Longest Increasing Path
explanation_short: You receive a list of n points, each given as a pair (x, y), and an index k pointing to one of those points. You must form a sequence of points where both the x‑coordinate and the y‑coordinate strictly increase from one point to the next, and the sequence must contain the point at index k. Among all such increasing sequences, determine the maximum possible number of points. Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Find a Safe Walk Through a Grid
explanation_short: You are given a binary matrix grid and an integer health. Starting at cell (0, 0) you may move up, down, left, or right, but every time you step on a cell with value 1 your health drops by 1, and you must always keep health > 0. Determine whether there exists any such walk that reaches the bottom‑right cell (m‑1, n‑1) with health at least 1, and return true if it does and false otherwise.

title: Maximum Multiplication Score
explanation_short:
You are given a length‑4 integer array a and a longer integer array b.  
Pick four positions in b that appear in increasing order (i₀ < i₁ < i₂ < i₃) and form the sum a₀·b[i₀] + a₁·b[i₁] + a₂·b[i₂] + a₃·b[i₃].  
Your task is to find the largest possible value of that sum.  
Print that maximum score as a single integer.

title: Minimum Number of Seconds to Make Mountain Height Zero
explanation_short: You are given a single integer mountainHeight and an array workerTimes where workerTimes[i] is the number of seconds it takes worker i to lower the mountain by one unit of height. All workers act at the same time, each repeatedly reducing the height according to their own speed. Your task is to determine the smallest amount of time after which the combined work of all workers has reduced the mountain’s height to zero. Return that minimum number of seconds as an integer.

title: Minimum Number of Valid Strings to Form Target I
explanation_short:
You receive a list `words` and a single string `target`.  
A piece is allowed only if it matches the beginning of at least one word in `words`, and you may join any number of such pieces end‑to‑end.  
Find the smallest number of allowed pieces whose concatenation equals `target`, and output that number (or ‑1 if no combination can produce `target`).

title: Minimum Number of Valid Strings to Form Target II
explanation_short:
You receive a list of words and a target string.  
A “valid” piece is any prefix of at least one word in the list.  
You must choose the fewest such pieces whose concatenation, in order, exactly matches the target.  
Return that minimum count, or –1 if the target cannot be built from the available prefixes.

title: Report Spam Message
explanation_short: You receive two lists of strings: `message`, the words that were sent, and `bannedWords`, the words that are not allowed. Check how many words from `message` exactly match any entry in `bannedWords`. If two or more matches are found, the result is `true`; otherwise the result is `false`.

title: Minimum Element After Replacement With Digit Sum
explanation_short: You receive an array of integers called nums. For every element you compute the sum of its decimal digits and treat that sum as the element’s new value. After all elements have been replaced, you look for the smallest number among them. The answer you return is that minimum digit‑sum value.

title: Count Substrings That Can Be Rearranged to Contain a String II
explanation_short: You receive two strings, word1 and word2. For every contiguous piece of word1, check whether its letters can be shuffled so that word2 forms the beginning of the rearranged piece. Count how many substrings satisfy this condition. Return that count as an integer.

title: Find the Lexicographically Smallest Valid Sequence
explanation_short: You are given two strings, word1 and word2. You must pick one index from word1 for each character of word2 so that the characters at those positions form a string that can become word2 by changing at most one character. Among all possible index selections that satisfy this condition, you need the lexicographically smallest array of indices. Return that array, or an empty array if no such selection exists.

title: Count Substrings That Can Be Rearranged to Contain a String I
explanation_short:
You are given two strings, word1 and word2.  
Consider every contiguous substring of word1; a substring is “valid” if its letters can be shuffled so that word2 appears at the very beginning of the rearranged version.  
Your task is to count how many substrings of word1 meet this condition.  
Return that count as an integer.

title: Find the Occurrence of First Almost Equal Substring
explanation_short:
You are given two strings `s` and `pattern`.  
A substring of `s` is “almost equal” to `pattern` if you can change at most one character in the substring so that it becomes identical to `pattern`.  
Your task is to locate the earliest position where such a substring starts.  
Return that starting index, or `-1` if no substring of `s` can be made almost equal to `pattern`.

title: Find the K-th Character in String Game I
explanation_short: You are given a positive integer k. Starting with the one‑letter word “a”, the string is repeatedly transformed according to the rule illustrated in the examples, making it longer each step. After enough transformations so that the string’s length reaches at least k, you must determine which character occupies the k‑th position (1‑based). The output is that single lowercase letter.

title: Maximize the Total Height of Unique Towers
explanation_short: You receive an array maximumHeight where each element tells the largest height allowed for the corresponding tower. You must choose a height for every tower, making sure no two towers share the same height and each chosen height does not exceed its tower’s limit. The goal is to make the sum of all chosen heights as large as possible. Return that maximum sum, or -1 if no assignment satisfying the constraints exists.

title: Find the K-th Character in String Game II
explanation_short: You are given a positive integer k and an array operations where each element tells which transformation to apply to the current string (starting from the single character “a”). After applying all the operations in order, you must determine which character ends up in the k‑th position of the final string. The answer is a single lowercase letter, which you return as the output.

title: Count of Substrings Containing Every Vowel and K Consonants I
explanation_short:
You receive a lowercase string `word` and a non‑negative integer `k`.  
A substring is any contiguous segment of `word`.  
You must count how many of those substrings contain each of the five vowels (`a, e, i, o, u`) at least once and contain exactly `k` consonant letters.  
Return that count as an integer.

title: Count of Substrings Containing Every Vowel and K Consonants II
explanation_short:
You receive a lowercase string `word` and a non‑negative integer `k`.  
Consider every contiguous segment (substring) of `word`.  
Count those substrings that include each of the five vowels `a, e, i, o, u` at least once and have exactly `k` consonant letters.  
Return the total number of such substrings as an integer.

title: Remove Methods From Project
explanation_short: You are given the number of methods n, the index k of a buggy method, and a list of pairs where each pair [a, b] means method a calls method b. First, all methods that can be reached from k by following calls (including k itself) are considered suspicious. A set of suspicious methods can be removed only if no method outside that set calls any of them; otherwise nothing is removed. Return the identifiers of the methods that stay in the project (in any order).

title: Construct the Minimum Bitwise Array I
explanation_short:
You are given an array nums containing n prime numbers.  
You must produce another array ans of the same length where, for each index i, the bitwise OR of ans[i] and ans[i] + 1 equals nums[i].  
Choose the smallest non‑negative integer that satisfies this condition for each position; if no such integer exists, put -1 instead.  
The output is the completed ans array.

title: Maximum Possible Number by Binary Concatenation
explanation_short: You receive an array `nums` containing exactly three non‑negative integers. You may reorder the three numbers, write each one in binary (without leading zeros), and then stick those binary strings together to form one longer binary string. Your task is to choose the ordering that yields the largest possible value when that combined binary string is interpreted as a decimal integer, and output that maximum integer.

title: Construct 2D Grid Matching Graph Layout
explanation_short: You receive an integer n and a list of unordered pairs edges, where each pair [ui, vi] means nodes ui and vi are connected by an undirected edge. Your task is to place the n nodes into a rectangular grid (rows × columns) so that two nodes appear next to each other in the grid exactly when there is an edge between them, and no other adjacency exists. The grid may have any dimensions that fit all nodes, and any arrangement that satisfies the adjacency rule is acceptable. Return the grid as a 2‑dimensional array of node indices. If several grids work, any one of them may be output.

title: Construct the Minimum Bitwise Array II
explanation_short: You are given an array `nums` of `n` prime numbers. For each position `i` you must choose the smallest non‑negative integer `ans[i]` such that the bitwise OR of `ans[i]` and `ans[i] + 1` equals `nums[i]`. If no integer satisfies the condition, place `-1` at that index. The output is the array `ans` of length `n` containing those minimal values (or `-1` where impossible).

title: Find X-Sum of All K-Long Subarrays I
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and two parameters `k` and `x`.  
For every consecutive segment of length `k` in `nums` we look at the distinct values inside the segment, rank them by how many times they appear (if several have the same count we prefer the larger value), and keep the top `x` values.  
The required result for that segment is the sum of all occurrences of those kept values (if the segment contains fewer than `x` distinct numbers, we simply sum the whole segment).  
Return an array containing this sum for each possible `k`‑long segment, in order.

title: K-th Largest Perfect Subtree Size in Binary Tree
explanation_short:
You are given the root node of a binary tree and an integer k.  
A perfect binary subtree is one where every internal node has exactly two children and all leaves lie on the same depth.  
Your task is to identify all perfect subtrees, rank their sizes from largest to smallest, and determine the size that appears in the k‑th position.  
Return that size, or ‑1 if fewer than k perfect subtrees exist.

title: Sorted GCD Pair Queries
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` and another integer array `queries`. First, form all unordered pairs of distinct elements from `nums` and compute the greatest common divisor for each pair, collecting these values into a list. After sorting that list in non‑decreasing order, each entry of `queries` tells you which position (0‑based) to read from the sorted list. Return an array containing the retrieved GCD values for all queries, in the same order as the queries appear.

title: Find Maximum Removals From Source String
explanation_short: You receive a string `source`, another string `pattern` that appears as a subsequence of `source`, and a sorted list `targetIndices` of positions that may be deleted. An operation removes the character at one of those positions while leaving the indices of all other characters unchanged. Your task is to choose as many deletions as possible from `targetIndices` so that `pattern` still remains a subsequence of the modified `source`. Return the maximum number of deletions that satisfy this condition.

title: Count The Number of Winning Sequences
explanation_short: You are given a string s of length n containing only the letters ‘F’, ‘W’ and ‘E’, which tells which creature Alice summons in each round. Bob must choose his own length‑n sequence of those three creatures, but he is not allowed to use the same creature in two consecutive rounds. A round’s points are awarded according to a fixed rule (the same for both players), and Bob wins if his total points after all n rounds are strictly larger than Alice’s total. Return the number of Bob’s possible sequences that make him win, taken modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Find X-Sum of All K-Long Subarrays II
explanation_short: You need to slide a window of length k across the given array and, for each position, compute the “x‑sum”: add up the smallest x distinct numbers in that window (or the whole window if it contains fewer than x different values). The answer array should contain one such value for every possible window start. A fast way to do this is to keep track of the frequencies of the numbers inside the current window and, using a coordinate‑compressed Fenwick tree (or similar ordered‑multiset), maintain both the count of distinct values and the sum of those values up to any rank. When the window moves one step, you update the structures by removing the leftmost element and adding the new rightmost one, then query the tree for the sum of the smallest x distinct elements. This yields an O(n log n) solution.

title: Find the Number of Possible Ways for an Event
explanation_short: You are given three integers n, x, and y. There are n performers who each choose one of the x stages, and any stage may end up empty. After all performers are placed, each non‑empty stage (band) receives a score between 1 and y. Compute the total number of distinct ways to assign performers to stages and to pick the scores, and return the result modulo 1,000,000,007.

title: Find the Sequence of Strings Appeared on the Screen
explanation_short:
You are given a single string `target`.  
Starting from an empty screen, Alice presses two special keys to build the text, and you must list every intermediate string that would appear while she produces `target` using the fewest possible key presses.  
The required result is an ordered array containing each of those screen states, from the first character typed up to the final `target` string.  
Return this array exactly as described.

title: Minimum Division Operations to Make Array Non Decreasing
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. In one move you may choose any element and replace it with the result of dividing that element by its greatest proper divisor (the largest divisor smaller than the number itself). Your task is to determine the fewest moves required so that the whole array becomes non‑decreasing (each value is ≤ the next). Output that minimum count, or `-1` if no sequence of moves can achieve a non‑decreasing array.

title: Find the Original Typed String I
explanation_short:
You are given a single string `word` that shows what actually appeared on the screen after Alice typed.  
Alice may have held down one key too long, causing exactly one character in the intended text to be repeated one or more extra times (or she might not have made any mistake).  
Your task is to count how many different original strings could have produced the observed `word` under that condition.  
Output that count as an integer.

title: Count Substrings With K-Frequency Characters I
explanation_short:
You are given a string `s` and an integer `k`.  
Consider every possible contiguous piece of `s` (a substring).  
Count how many of those substrings contain at least one character that shows up `k` or more times within that substring.  
Return that total count as an integer.

title: Check if DFS Strings Are Palindromes
explanation_short: You are given a rooted tree described by the parent array (node 0 is the root) and a string s where s[i] is the label of node i. For each node i you must imagine running the prescribed depth‑first traversal starting at i, appending each visited node’s label to a shared string in the exact order the recursion processes them. After the traversal finishes, you check whether that accumulated string reads the same forward and backward. Return an array of n booleans where the i‑th entry is true if the string produced by the call on node i is a palindrome, and false otherwise.

title: Find the Maximum Factor Score of Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may delete zero or one element from it, then compute the GCD and the LCM of the remaining numbers and multiply these two values to obtain a “factor score”. The task is to find the greatest factor score achievable by such a deletion (the score of an empty array is defined as 0). Return that maximum score as an integer.

title: Find the Number of Subsequences With Equal GCD
explanation_short:
You are given an array of integers `nums`.  
Consider all possible non‑empty subsequences of this array; for each pair of subsequences, compute the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the numbers inside each subsequence.  
Count how many pairs have the same GCD value, and return that count modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Find Subtree Sizes After Changes
explanation_short: You receive a tree of n nodes described by a parent array (‑1 for the root) and a string s where s[i] is the label of node i. For every non‑root node a single simultaneous re‑parenting is performed according to the given rule that depends on the labels. After all those changes, you must determine how many nodes belong to the subtree of each node, including the node itself. Return an array answer where answer[i] holds the final subtree size of node i.

title: Find the Original Typed String II
explanation_short:
You are given a string `word` that shows the characters actually printed on the screen and a positive integer `k`.  
You must count how many different original strings of length at least `k` could have produced `word` if each intended character might have been repeated one or more times because the key was held down too long.  
Return that count modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Maximum Points Tourist Can Earn
explanation_short: You are given the number of cities n, the total number of days k, a matrix stayScore where stayScore[d][c] is the points earned if the tourist stays in city c on day d, and a matrix travelScore where travelScore[i][j] is the points earned when moving from city i to city j on a day. The tourist may start in any city and on each day either stay in the current city or travel to a different city, collecting the corresponding points. Your task is to choose the starting city and the sequence of stay/travel actions that yields the highest possible total score after exactly k days. Output that maximum total score as a single integer.

title: Total Characters in String After Transformations I
explanation_short: You are given a string s and an integer t that tells how many times a transformation is applied, where each character in the current string is replaced by a fixed new sequence of characters. After performing exactly t transformations, you must determine how many characters the resulting string contains. The answer should be printed modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Check Balanced String
explanation_short: You are given a string that contains only digit characters. Compute the sum of the digits that appear at even positions (0‑based) and the sum of the digits at odd positions. Return true if the two sums are equal; otherwise return false.

title: Total Characters in String After Transformations II
explanation_short: You receive a lowercase string s, an integer t, and an array nums of 26 integers. One transformation replaces each character in s with a new substring determined by its alphabet index and the corresponding value in nums. After applying exactly t transformations, output the length of the final string modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Find Minimum Time to Reach Last Room II
explanation_short: You are given an n × m grid where each cell (i, j) contains a value moveTime[i][j] that indicates the earliest second you are allowed to start moving into that room. Starting from the top‑left cell at time 0, you may travel to any orthogonal neighbor, but the travel time for successive steps alternates between 1 second and 2 seconds. Your task is to determine the smallest possible arrival time at the bottom‑right cell while respecting both the alternating step durations and the per‑room start‑time constraints. Output that minimum arrival time as a single integer.

title: Find Minimum Time to Reach Last Room I
explanation_short: You are given an n × m grid `moveTime` where `moveTime[i][j]` is the earliest second at which the room (i, j) becomes traversable. Starting from the top‑left corner at time 0, you may move to any horizontally or vertically adjacent room, each move consuming exactly one second, but you cannot step into a room before its opening time. Compute and return the smallest possible arrival time at the bottom‑right corner (n‑1, m‑1).

title: Smallest Divisible Digit Product I
explanation_short: You receive two integers n and t. Your task is to locate the smallest integer that is at least n and whose digits, when multiplied together, give a product that is a multiple of t. Output that integer.

title: Count Number of Balanced Permutations
explanation_short: You receive a string `num` consisting only of digit characters. A permutation of the string is any rearrangement of all its characters, and it is called balanced when the sum of the digits placed at even positions equals the sum of the digits placed at odd positions. Your task is to count how many distinct balanced permutations exist for the given `num`. Return that count modulo 1,000,000,007.

title: Adjacent Increasing Subarrays Detection I
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
You must determine whether there are two consecutive blocks of exactly `k` elements-one starting at position `a` and the next starting at `a + k`-such that each block’s elements increase strictly from left to right.  
If such a pair of adjacent increasing subarrays exists, the answer is `true`; otherwise it is `false`.

title: Maximum Frequency of an Element After Performing Operations I
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` together with two parameters `k` and `numOperations`. In each of the `numOperations` steps you may increase any single element of the array by at most `k` (you can choose which element to modify each time). After applying all operations, you need to determine the greatest possible number of array entries that are exactly the same. The answer is that maximum frequency, returned as a single integer.

title: Maximum Frequency of an Element After Performing Operations II
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`, a limit `k`, and a count `numOperations`. In each of the `numOperations` steps you may change a single element of the array by at most `k` (in either direction). After performing all the steps, you need to determine the largest number of array entries that can be made equal to the same value. The answer you output is that maximum achievable frequency.

title: Adjacent Increasing Subarrays Detection II
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums`.  
Your task is to determine the largest possible length `k` for which you can locate two back‑to‑back subarrays, each of length `k`, where every element in each subarray is strictly larger than the one before it.  
The two subarrays must be adjacent, meaning the second one starts immediately after the first ends.  
Return that maximum `k` (or 0 if no such pair exists).

title: Make Array Elements Equal to Zero
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. First you must pick an index whose value is 0 and decide whether you will move leftward or rightward from that index. Following the prescribed moving‑and‑zeroing process, a selection is considered valid only if it can turn every element of the array into 0. Return the total number of such valid (starting index, direction) pairs.

title: Smallest Divisible Digit Product II
explanation_short:
You are given a decimal string `num` that represents a positive integer and an integer `t`.  
Find the smallest integer that is at least `num`, contains no digit 0, and whose digits’ product is a multiple of `t`.  
Return that integer as a string, or “-1” if no such zero‑free number exists.

title: Sum of Good Subsequences
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. A good subsequence is any subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) where each pair of consecutive elements differs by exactly 1, and a single element counts as good. For every such subsequence you add up the values of its elements, then sum these totals over all possible good subsequences. Return that overall sum modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Count K-Reducible Numbers Less Than N
explanation_short:
You are given a binary string `s` that encodes a positive integer `n` and an integer `k`.  
An integer `x` is *k‑reducible* if, by repeatedly replacing it with the number of 1‑bits in its binary form at most `k` times, the value becomes 1.  
Count how many positive integers `x` are strictly less than `n` and are k‑reducible.  
Return that count modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Stone Removal Game
explanation_short: You are given a single positive integer n representing the number of stones in a pile. Alice moves first, and on each turn a player must remove a legal number of stones; the player who cannot make a move loses. Your task is to decide whether Alice can force a win assuming both players play optimally. Return true if Alice has a winning strategy for the given n, otherwise return false. The output is a single Boolean value.

title: Zero Array Transformation I
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` and a list of queries, each query given as a pair `[l, r]`. The queries are applied one after another, and after each one you may perform the allowed operation on the segment `nums[l…r]`. Your task is to decide whether, after all queries have been processed, the entire array can become all zeros. Return **true** if it is possible and **false** otherwise.

title: Shift Distance Between Two Strings
explanation_short: You are given two strings `s` and `t` that have the same length, plus two arrays `nextCost` and `previousCost` (each of size 26) describing the cost of moving a letter one step forward or backward in the alphabet. At any index you may repeatedly shift the current character forward or backward, paying the corresponding cost each time, until it matches the target character at that position. Your task is to compute the smallest possible total cost required to transform the whole string `s` into `t`. Return that minimum cost as a single integer.

title: Minimize the Maximum Adjacent Element Difference
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` where some positions are marked `-1` to indicate missing values. You may pick two positive integers `x` and `y` exactly once, and replace every `-1` in the array with either `x` or `y` (you decide which one for each position). After the replacements, look at the absolute differences between every pair of neighboring elements and take the largest of those differences. Return the smallest possible value of this largest difference that can be achieved by an optimal choice of `x` and `y`.

title: Zero Array Transformation II
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a list of queries, where each query is a triple `[l, r, val]`.  
Processing a query means applying its operation to every element of `nums` whose index lies between `l` and `r` (inclusive).  
You must find the smallest non‑negative integer `k` such that after applying the first `k` queries in order, the entire array becomes all zeros; if no prefix of queries can achieve this, output `-1`.  
The answer is a single integer `k` (or `-1` when impossible).

title: Find the Maximum Number of Fruits Collected
explanation_short: You are given an n × n grid where each cell contains a number of fruits. Three children start at the three corner cells (0,0), (0,n‑1) and (n‑1,0) and each must make exactly n‑1 moves to end at the bottom‑right corner (n‑1,n‑1), collecting the fruits in every room they enter. If two or more children pass through the same room, only one of them can take the fruits, and the room becomes empty afterward. Return the greatest total number of fruits that can be collected by the three children together.

title: Rearrange K Substrings to Form Target String
explanation_short: You receive two strings `s` and `t` that contain the same multiset of characters, and an integer `k`. The question is whether you can cut `s` into exactly `k` contiguous pieces of equal length, permute those pieces, and join them to obtain `t`. Return **true** if such a rearrangement exists; otherwise return **false**.

title: Minimum Array Sum
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and three integers `k`, `op1` and `op2`. For each position in the array you may apply the first operation at most once, the second operation at most once, and you may use both on the same element if you wish. After applying any combination of these operations (including none), you need to make the total sum of the array as small as possible. The required output is that minimum achievable sum.

title: Minimum Positive Sum Subarray
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` and two bounds `l` and `r`. Among all contiguous subarrays whose length is at least `l` and at most `r`, you must look for those whose total sum is greater than zero and pick the smallest such sum. Return that minimum positive sum, or `-1` if no subarray in the given length range has a positive sum.

title: Zero Array Transformation III
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a list of interval queries, each query specifying a sub‑range `[l, r]` of the array.  
Using a query you may apply some operation (unspecified here) that helps turn the elements in its range toward zero.  
Your task is to discard as many queries as possible while still being able to make every entry of `nums` equal to 0 with the remaining queries.  
Return the largest number of removable queries, or `-1` if no selection of queries can achieve a completely zero array.

title: Identify the Largest Outlier in an Array
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. Exactly two elements of the array are not part of the original set of “special” numbers: one of them equals the sum of all special numbers, and the other is an outlier that is neither a special number nor the sum element. Your task is to determine which value could serve as the outlier and return the greatest such value that satisfies the conditions. The output is a single integer representing that largest possible outlier.

title: Maximize Sum of Weights after Edge Removals
explanation_short: You are given a list of n‑1 triples [ui, vi, wi] describing an undirected tree (ui and vi are the connected nodes, wi is the edge weight) and an integer k. You may delete at most k edges from the tree, leaving a forest of components. Your goal is to choose which edges to remove so that the sum of the weights of all edges that remain is as large as possible. Output that maximum achievable total weight.

title: Maximize the Number of Target Nodes After Connecting Trees I
explanation_short: You are given two separate undirected trees, each described by a list of edges, and an integer k. For every node i in the first tree you may add one extra edge that links i to any node of the second tree, then consider all nodes (in both trees) whose shortest‑path distance from i is at most k. The task is to compute, for each i, the largest possible number of such “target” nodes achievable by choosing the best connection. Return an array where the i‑th entry is this maximum count.

title: Smallest Number With All Set Bits
explanation_short:
You receive a single positive integer n.  
Your task is to locate the smallest integer x that is not less than n and whose binary form is made up entirely of 1‑bits (for example, 111 or 1111).  
In other words, x must be the next “all‑ones” number that is at least n.  
Return that value x as the answer.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Values Equal to K
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a target value `k`.  
An operation lets you pick a number `h` such that every element larger than `h` is the same, and then change all those larger elements to any smaller value (including `k`).  
Your task is to determine the smallest possible number of such operations that turns every entry of `nums` into `k`, or report `-1` if it cannot be done.  
The answer is a single integer representing that minimum count (or `-1`).

title: Digit Operations to Make Two Integers Equal
explanation_short: You are given two integers n and m that have the same number of digits. By applying a series of allowed digit‑wise operations you must change n into m, while n is never allowed to become a prime number at any step (including the initial value). The cost of a sequence is the sum of every value that n takes during the transformation, and you need the smallest possible total cost. Return that minimum cost, or ‑1 if no sequence can satisfy the non‑prime condition.

title: Count Connected Components in LCM Graph
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `threshold`. Treat each index as a node whose value is the corresponding element of `nums`; draw an undirected edge between two nodes `i` and `j` exactly when the least common multiple of `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` does not exceed `threshold`. Your task is to determine how many separate groups of nodes exist when all such edges are considered. Output a single integer representing the number of connected components in that graph.

title: Transformed Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` that should be considered circular, so moving past the end wraps around to the start. From this circular view you must create a new array `result` of the same length, filling each position according to the transformation rules described in the statement. Return the completed `result` array.

title: Maximize the Number of Target Nodes After Connecting Trees II
explanation_short: You are given two undirected trees: the first with n nodes and edges edges1, the second with m nodes and edges edges2. For each node i in the first tree you may add exactly one new edge that links i to any node of the second tree, then consider the whole combined graph. A node u is “target” to i if the length of the shortest path between u and i has even parity (a node is always target to itself). Return an array answer where answer[i] is the largest possible number of target nodes for i after choosing the best connection; each query is independent, so the added edge is removed before evaluating the next i.

title: Minimum Time to Break Locks I
explanation_short: You are given an array strength where strength[i] is the energy needed to open the i‑th lock, and an integer k that describes how the sword’s power can be distributed among the locks each minute. Each minute you may choose a subset of locks and allocate the sword’s power according to the given rules, reducing their remaining energy accordingly. Your task is to determine the smallest number of minutes required to reduce the energy of every lock to zero. Return that minimum time as an integer.

title: Maximum Subarray Sum With Length Divisible by K
explanation_short:
You are given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `k`.  
Consider every contiguous subarray whose length is a multiple of `k`.  
Among those subarrays, identify the one that yields the greatest total sum.  
Return that maximum sum (the answer may be negative if all numbers are negative).

title: Maximum Area Rectangle With Point Constraints I
explanation_short: You receive a list of points (xᵢ, yᵢ) on an infinite plane. From these points you must choose four that form the vertices of an axis‑aligned rectangle, with the condition that no other given point lies inside the rectangle or on its edges. Return the largest possible rectangle area, or -1 if no rectangle satisfies the constraint.

title: Maximum Area Rectangle With Point Constraints II
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays that together list the (x, y) coordinates of n points on the plane. From these points you must choose four that form the vertices of an axis‑aligned rectangle, and the rectangle must contain no other given point either inside it or on its edges. Among all such rectangles, determine the one with the largest possible area. Output that maximum area, or -1 if no rectangle satisfies the condition.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Character Frequencies Equal
explanation_short: You are given a single string `s`. A string is “good” when every distinct character that appears in it does so the same number of times. You may apply any allowed operations (adding, removing, or changing characters) any number of times, and you must determine the smallest possible total number of such operations that will turn `s` into a good string. The answer to return is that minimum operation count.

title: Button with Longest Push Time
explanation_short: You receive a list of pairs [index, time] that records when each button was pressed. For every button you must determine how long it was held down, based on the timestamps given. Then pick the button whose holding time is the greatest; if several buttons share the same longest duration, choose the one with the smallest index. Output that button’s index as a single integer.

title: Maximize Amount After Two Days of Conversions
explanation_short: You are given the name of a starting currency and two independent sets of exchange pairs with their rates – one for day 1 and one for day 2. Beginning with 1.0 unit of the starting currency, you may apply any sequence of conversions using the day 1 rates, then after that apply any sequence using the day 2 rates. Your task is to determine the largest amount of the original currency that can be obtained after the two‑day conversion process. Return that maximum amount as a floating‑point number.

title: Count Beautiful Splits in an Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. A split means choosing an index that separates the array into a left part and a right part, and the split is called beautiful if it meets the specific condition described in the statement. Your task is to count how many indices produce a beautiful split. Return that count as an integer.

title: Check if Grid can be Cut into Sections
explanation_short: You receive an integer n defining an n × n grid and a list of non‑overlapping rectangles given by their bottom‑left and top‑right coordinates. You must decide whether there exist either two horizontal lines or two vertical lines that cut the whole grid into three strips, each strip being completely filled by the given rectangles without any rectangle crossing a cut. The cuts may be placed at any integer coordinate between 0 and n. Return true if such a pair of parallel cuts exists; otherwise return false.

title: Count Subarrays of Length Three With a Condition
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums`.  
Examine every consecutive group of three elements in the array.  
A group counts if the sum of its first and third numbers is exactly half of the middle number.  
Return the total number of such groups as an integer.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make Elements in Array Distinct
explanation_short: You are given an integer array nums. You may apply the permitted operation any number of times to modify elements so that each value appears only once. Your goal is to determine the smallest number of operations needed to achieve a completely distinct array. Return that minimum count as an integer.

title: Subsequences with a Unique Middle Mode I
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. From it you must consider every possible subsequence of exactly five elements (keeping the original order) and count those where the element that ends up in the third position is the only value that appears most often in that five‑element group. The answer should be returned modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Count Paths With the Given XOR Value
explanation_short:
You receive a rectangular grid of integers and a target value k.  
A path starts at the cell (0, 0) and moves only right or down until it reaches the cell (m‑1, n‑1).  
For each possible path you compute the XOR of all numbers visited along the way, and you need to count how many paths produce exactly k.  
Return that count modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Smallest Substring With Identical Characters I
explanation_short: You are given a binary string `s` and an integer `numOps`. You may change at most `numOps` characters of `s` to the opposite bit. After performing those changes, look at every contiguous block where all characters are the same and note the length of the longest such block. Return the smallest possible length of that longest block.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Columns Strictly Increasing
explanation_short: You receive an m × n grid of non‑negative integers. In each move you may add 1 to any single cell. Your task is to determine the smallest total number of such increments required so that, in every column, the numbers strictly increase from top to bottom. The answer is a single integer representing that minimum count.

title: Maximum Number of Distinct Elements After Operations
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. For each element you may add `k`, subtract `k`, or leave it unchanged, but you can apply at most one of these choices to each position. Your task is to adjust the values so that the array contains as many different numbers as possible. The answer is the largest count of distinct values achievable after the operations. Output that maximum count as a single integer.

title: Smallest Substring With Identical Characters II
explanation_short: You receive a binary string `s` and an integer `numOps`. You may flip at most `numOps` characters in the string, and after doing so you want the longest consecutive block of equal bits to be as short as possible. Return the smallest length that this longest block can achieve.

title: Find the Lexicographically Largest String From the Box I
explanation_short: You are given a string `word` and an integer `numFriends`. The task is to cut the string into exactly `numFriends` non‑empty consecutive parts (preserving the original order). Among the parts of a particular cut, look at the lexicographically largest piece, and you want the maximum possible such piece over all valid cuts. Output that string.

title: Count Special Subsequences
explanation_short:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers.  
We need to count how many index quadruples `(p, q, r, s)` exist with `p < q < r < s` such that the element at `p` equals the element at `r` and the element at `q` equals the element at `s`.  
The answer is a single integer representing the total number of such special subsequences.

title: Substring Matching Pattern
explanation_short: You receive two strings: `s`, the text to search, and `p`, a pattern that includes exactly one ‘*’ character. The ‘*’ may stand for any sequence of characters, even an empty one. Your task is to decide whether you can replace the ‘*’ so that the resulting pattern occurs somewhere inside `s` as a contiguous substring. Return `true` if such a replacement exists, otherwise return `false`.

title: Count the Number of Arrays with K Matching Adjacent Elements
explanation_short: You are given three integers n, m, and k. A good array is a sequence of n numbers, each chosen from 1 to m, that contains exactly k adjacent pairs where the two neighboring values are equal. Compute how many such arrays can be formed and output the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

title: Design Task Manager
explanation_short: The input is a list of operations applied to a task manager, starting with an initialization that receives a set of tasks where each task is defined by a user ID, a task ID, and a priority value. Subsequent operations may add a new task, change the priority of an existing task, remove a task, or request the execution of the current highest‑priority task, which should return that task’s ID. For every operation that produces a result (the execution request) the output contains the returned task ID; all other operations contribute a placeholder (e.g., `null`) to keep the output sequence aligned with the input sequence.

title: Maximize Subarray Sum After Removing All Occurrences of One Element
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may optionally choose a single value and delete every occurrence of that value from the array, but you can do this at most once. After performing (or skipping) this operation, you need to determine the largest possible sum of any contiguous subarray in the resulting array. Output that maximum subarray sum as a single integer.

title: Maximum Coins From K Consecutive Bags
explanation_short: You receive a list of non‑overlapping intervals `[li, ri, ci]`, each meaning that every bag at positions `li` through `ri` holds `ci` coins, plus an integer `k`. You must pick any block of exactly `k` consecutive bag positions on the number line and compute the total coins contained in those positions. Return the largest possible total coin amount achievable by such a choice.

title: Maximum Subarray With Equal Products
explanation_short:
You receive an array `nums` of positive integers.  
A subarray is “product equivalent” when the product of all its elements equals the product of its greatest common divisor and its least common multiple.  
Your task is to determine the maximum length among all contiguous subarrays that satisfy this condition.  
Return that length as a single integer.

title: Longest Subsequence With Decreasing Adjacent Difference
explanation_short: You are given an array of integers `nums`. Choose a subsequence (keeping the original order) so that the absolute differences between each pair of consecutive elements never increase-they must form a non‑increasing sequence. Among all subsequences that satisfy this condition, find the one with the greatest possible length. Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Find Mirror Score of a String
explanation_short:
You are given a single string `s`.  
Each lowercase letter has a “mirror” letter defined by reversing the alphabet (e.g., ‘a’ ↔ ‘z’, ‘b’ ↔ ‘y’, etc.).  
Following the described marking procedure, you must calculate the total score accumulated by the end of the process.  
Print that final score as an integer.

title: Maximum Score of Non-overlapping Intervals
explanation_short: You are given a list where each element describes an interval by its left endpoint, right endpoint, and a weight. From these intervals you may select at most four that do not share any points, even at their boundaries. The task is to maximize the total weight of the selected intervals, and if several selections achieve the same maximum, return the one whose index list is lexicographically smallest. The answer is the array of the chosen interval indices.

title: Minimize the Maximum Edge Weight of Graph
explanation_short:
You are given the number of nodes n, a list of directed edges where each entry contains a start node, an end node, and its weight, and an integer threshold.
