Your task is to delete any subset of edges (possibly none) so that the remaining graph meets the required conditions involving the threshold.  
Among all feasible ways to delete edges, you must report the smallest possible value of the largest edge weight that stays in the graph; if no deletion can satisfy the conditions, output ‑1.

title: Zigzag Grid Traversal With Skip
explanation_short: You receive an m × n grid of positive integers. Starting from the top‑left corner, you must move through the grid in a zigzag fashion-alternating direction each row or column-and you are required to ignore (skip) every second cell you encounter. Collect the values of the cells you actually visit, and return them as an array in the order they were visited.

title: Count Non-Decreasing Subarrays After K Operations
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` and a limit `k`. For every possible contiguous subarray you may add 1 to any of its elements, using at most `k` total additions, and you must decide whether the subarray can be turned into a non‑decreasing sequence. Return the total number of subarrays for which this is achievable.

title: Minimum Cost to Make Arrays Identical
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays arr and brr of equal length n and an integer k. You may apply the permitted operation on arr any number of times, each time incurring a cost that depends on k and the values being changed. The task is to change arr so that it matches brr exactly while minimizing the total cost spent. Return that minimum total cost (which is 0 when the arrays are already identical).

title: Maximum Amount of Money Robot Can Earn
explanation_short: You are given an m × n grid of integers where each cell holds the amount of coins the robot would collect (or lose) if it passes through that cell. The robot starts at the top‑left corner, moves only right or down, and may choose up to two cells on its route where it neutralizes the robber, effectively ignoring the cell’s value. Your task is to determine the greatest possible total of coins the robot can accumulate when it reaches the bottom‑right corner. The answer is a single integer representing that maximum profit (which may be negative).

title: Maximum Difference Between Adjacent Elements in a Circular Array
explanation_short: You are given an array of integers that should be treated as circular, meaning the first and last elements are also neighbors. Your task is to determine the greatest absolute difference between any two adjacent elements in this circular arrangement. Return that maximum difference as a single integer.

title: Maximum and Minimum Sums of at Most Size K Subsequences
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
Consider every subsequence of `nums` whose length is at most `k`.  
For each such subsequence add its largest element and its smallest element, and accumulate these sums over all subsequences.  
Return the total sum modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Longest Special Path
explanation_short:
You are given an undirected tree rooted at node 0, described by a list of edges where each edge includes its two endpoints and its length, and an array nums that assigns a value to every node.  
A “special” path is any downward sequence from an ancestor to a descendant (including a single node) in which all node values are distinct.  
Your task is to determine the greatest total length among all such special paths and, among those with that maximum length, the smallest possible number of nodes they contain.  
Return these two numbers as a two‑element array: the first element is the maximum length, and the second is the minimal node count for paths achieving that length.

title: Manhattan Distances of All Arrangements of Pieces
explanation_short: You receive three integers m, n, and k that define an m × n grid and k identical pieces. A valid arrangement places each piece on a different cell of the grid. For every possible arrangement, compute the Manhattan distance for each pair of pieces, add those distances together, and then sum this total over all arrangements. Output the resulting sum modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Count Partitions with Even Sum Difference
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. A partition is any index `i` (0 ≤ i < n‑1) that splits the array into a left part `nums[0…i]` and a right part `nums[i+1…n‑1]`. You must count how many such splits make the difference between the sum of the left part and the sum of the right part an even number. The answer is a single integer representing that count.

title: Sum of Variable Length Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given an array and need to add up the smallest value from every possible contiguous subarray of that array. In other words, for each possible start index you extend the subarray to the right, keep track of the minimum element seen so far, and add that minimum to a running total. A straightforward way is to loop over all start positions, update the current minimum as you move the end index, and accumulate the sums. This double‑loop approach runs in O(n²) time, which is fine for the given size limits.

title: Paint House IV
explanation_short: You receive an even number n and a matrix cost where cost[i][j] is the price of painting house i with color j (1‑indexed). You must choose a color for each house so that the whole row of houses satisfies the “beautiful” painting rules given in the statement. The task is to compute the smallest possible total expense of such a coloring. The answer you return is this minimum sum.

title: Maximum and Minimum Sums of at Most Size K Subarrays
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
Consider every contiguous subarray whose length is at most `k`.  
For each such subarray, take the largest value and the smallest value, add them together, and then add this result to a running total.  
Return the final total sum of all those maximum‑plus‑minimum values.

title: Reschedule Meetings for Maximum Free Time I
explanation_short: You are given the total event duration `eventTime`, a limit `k` on how many meetings you may move, and two equal‑length arrays `startTime` and `endTime` that list the original, non‑overlapping meetings inside the interval [0, eventTime]. You may shift the start of at most `k` meetings (keeping each meeting’s length the same) while preserving their relative order, staying within the event, and remaining non‑overlapping. The task is to arrange the meetings so that the longest continuous gap with no meetings inside the event becomes as large as possible. Output that maximum possible length of free time.

title: Count Mentions Per User
explanation_short:
You receive an integer `numberOfUsers` and a chronological list `events`, where each entry describes either a status change (a user goes offline or comes back online) or a message that may mention specific users or the keyword “ALL”.  
All users start online, and any status change that shares a timestamp with a message is applied first.  
Your task is to tally, for every user id from 0 to `numberOfUsers‑1`, how many times that user is mentioned across all message events, counting multiple mentions in the same message separately and treating “ALL” as a mention of every user regardless of their online state.  
Return the result as an array `mentions` where `mentions[i]` holds the total count for user i.

title: Maximum Frequency After Subarray Operation
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a target value `k`. You may choose a single contiguous subarray and add the same integer to every element of that subarray exactly once. After performing this operation, count how many positions in the whole array contain the value `k`. Output the largest possible count you can achieve.

title: Frequencies of Shortest Supersequences
explanation_short:
You receive an array of lowercase strings `words`.  
Your task is to consider every shortest common supersequence that contains each string in `words` as a subsequence, but treat two supersequences that are merely permutations of the same letters as a single case.  
For each distinct supersequence you must count how many times each of the 26 letters appears.  
Return a list of these 26‑element frequency arrays, in any order.

title: Minimum Cost Good Caption
explanation_short: You are given a single string `caption`. You may change individual characters (each change counts as one operation) until the string becomes “good”, meaning every character that appears does so in blocks of at least three identical letters in a row. Among all good strings that can be reached with the smallest possible number of operations, you must return the lexicographically smallest one. The output is that resulting string.

title: Maximum Difference Between Even and Odd Frequency I
explanation_short: You receive a single string `s` made of lowercase English letters. Count how many times each distinct character appears, then choose two characters `a1` and `a2` so that the difference `freq(a1) − freq(a2)` is as large as possible. Output that largest difference as an integer.

title: Find Valid Pair of Adjacent Digits in String
explanation_short: You are given a string `s` that contains only digit characters. A valid pair consists of two neighboring digits whose overall frequencies in the entire string match their numeric values (e.g., the digit ‘2’ must appear exactly twice). Scan the string from left to right and return the first such two‑character substring you encounter. If no adjacent digits satisfy the condition, output an empty string.

title: Maximum Manhattan Distance After K Changes
explanation_short: You receive a string s made of the letters N, S, E, W that describes moves on an infinite grid, starting from (0, 0), and an integer k. You may change at most k of the characters to any of the four directions before following the sequence. While walking according to the (possibly modified) string, you need to determine the greatest Manhattan distance (|x| + |y|) from the origin that can ever be reached at any step. Output that maximum distance as a single integer.

title: Minimum Increments for Target Multiples in an Array
explanation_short: You receive two integer arrays, nums and target. You may repeatedly add 1 to any element of nums, counting each addition as one operation. The task is to make sure that for every value in target there is at least one element in nums that is a multiple of that value, and you must output the smallest total number of additions required.

title: Reschedule Meetings for Maximum Free Time II
explanation_short: You are given the total event duration `eventTime` and two equal‑length arrays `startTime` and `endTime` that list the start and end of each non‑overlapping meeting inside the interval [0, eventTime]. You may shift the start of at most one meeting (keeping its length) to any position within the event, as long as all meetings still do not overlap, and the relative order of meetings may change. Return the length of the longest continuous free period that can be achieved after this optional rescheduling.

title: Sort Matrix by Diagonals
explanation_short: You receive an n × n integer matrix called grid. For every diagonal that runs from the bottom‑left toward the top‑right you must rearrange the numbers on that diagonal so they appear in non‑increasing order, while each diagonal that runs from the top‑left toward the bottom‑right must end up in non‑decreasing order. Return the matrix after all such diagonal reorderings have been applied.

title: Assign Elements to Groups with Constraints
explanation_short: You receive two integer arrays: `groups`, where each entry is the size of a group, and `elements`, which holds candidate numbers. For every group you must choose an element whose value divides the group’s size without remainder; an element may be reused for different groups. Return an array `assigned` of the same length as `groups` where `assigned[i]` is the index of a suitable element for group `i`, or `-1` if no element satisfies the condition.

title: Maximum Difference Between Even and Odd Frequency II
explanation_short: You’re given a string s and an integer k. Consider every contiguous substring of s that has length k, count how many times each character appears in that substring, and for any two characters a and b compute freq[a] − freq[b]. Among all such substrings, keep the largest difference you can obtain. The output is that maximum value (or ‑1 if no substring yields a positive difference).

title: Maximize the Minimum Game Score
explanation_short: You are given an array points of length n and an integer m. Starting with a second array gameScore filled with zeros, you may perform at most m allowed moves that change the values in gameScore according to the rules (the index starts at -1 and must stay inside the array after the first move). Your task is to arrange those moves so that the smallest entry in gameScore becomes as large as possible. Return that largest achievable minimum value.

title: Count Substrings Divisible By Last Digit
explanation_short:
You receive a string `s` that contains only decimal digits.  
For every possible contiguous substring of `s` (including those that start with 0), check whether the integer represented by the substring is divisible by its last digit, provided that last digit is not zero.  
Count all substrings that satisfy this condition.  
Return that count as an integer.

title: Sum of Good Numbers
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a distance `k`. An element is “good” if it is strictly larger than the element `k` positions to its left and also larger than the element `k` positions to its right, whenever those positions exist. Compute the sum of all good elements and return that sum as the answer.

title: Separate Squares I
explanation_short:
You receive a list of squares, each described by the x‑ and y‑coordinates of its bottom‑left corner and its side length.  
Your task is to choose a horizontal line (a y‑value) so that the sum of the areas of all squares lying above the line equals the sum of the areas lying below it, counting overlapping parts each time they appear.  
Among all possible balancing lines, you must return the smallest y‑coordinate that achieves this equality.  
Print that y‑value as a real number; an answer accurate to within 10⁻⁵ is accepted.

title: Find Special Substring of Length K
explanation_short:
You receive a string `s` and an integer `k`.  
Your task is to examine every contiguous piece of `s` that is exactly `k` characters long and see whether any of those pieces meet the required condition.  
If at least one such substring satisfies the condition, you should report “true”; otherwise you report “false”.  
The answer is a single boolean value indicating whether such a substring exists.

title: Shortest Matching Substring
explanation_short: You are given a text string `s` and a pattern string `p` that contains exactly two ‘*’ wildcards, each of which can stand for any (possibly empty) sequence of characters. Your task is to locate a contiguous segment of `s` that fits the pattern, allowing the two wildcards to match arbitrary substrings, and determine the smallest possible length of such a segment. If no segment of `s` can be matched to `p`, you must output `-1`; otherwise you output the length of the shortest matching substring.

title: Separate Squares II
explanation_short: You receive a list of triples, each giving the x‑ and y‑coordinates of a square’s bottom‑left corner and its side length, all squares being axis‑parallel. Consider the union of these squares on the plane, counting any overlapping region only once. Find the smallest y‑coordinate of a horizontal line that splits the total covered area into two equal parts-area above the line must equal area below it. Output that y‑value as a floating‑point number, accurate within 1e‑5.

title: Maximum Sum With at Most K Elements
explanation_short: You are given an n × m integer matrix grid, an array limits of length n where limits[i] specifies how many elements may be taken from row i, and an integer k that limits the total number of chosen entries. Select at most k elements from the matrix, never exceeding the per‑row limit for any row, to make the sum of the selected numbers as large as possible. Output the maximum achievable sum.

title: Eat Pizzas!
explanation_short: The task gives an array of pizza weights and requires you to eat exactly four pizzas each day, gaining weight equal to the sum of the lightest and the heaviest pizza in that day's group. You must partition the entire list into groups of four so that the total weight gained after all days is as large as possible. The key insight is that after sorting the weights, the optimal strategy is to pair the smallest remaining pizza with the largest remaining one and ignore the two middle ones in each group, which lets you compute the answer by scanning the sorted array from both ends.

title: Select K Disjoint Special Substrings
explanation_short: You are given a string s and an integer k. A special substring is any contiguous piece of s that satisfies the condition described in the statement. Your task is to decide whether you can choose k such substrings that do not overlap each other. Output “true” if it is possible, otherwise output “false”.

title: Length of Longest V-Shaped Diagonal Segment
explanation_short:
You receive an n × m grid whose entries are only 0, 1, or 2.  
A V‑shaped diagonal segment is a sequence of cells that first moves along one diagonal direction, makes a single 90‑degree turn at a pivot cell, and then continues along the opposite diagonal direction, with every visited cell containing the same non‑zero value.  
Your task is to determine the maximum number of cells that can be included in any such V‑shaped segment.  
Print that maximum length, or 0 if no valid segment exists.

title: Check If Digits Are Equal in String After Operations I
explanation_short: You receive a string `s` that contains only digit characters. By repeatedly applying the given operation, the string is reduced until exactly two digits are left. Your task is to determine whether those final two digits are identical. Return `true` if they match, otherwise return `false`.

title: Maximize the Distance Between Points on a Square
explanation_short: You are given the side length of a square, an integer k, and a list of points that lie on the square’s perimeter. From these points you must pick exactly k of them so that the smallest Manhattan distance between any two chosen points is as large as possible. Return that largest achievable minimum distance.

title: Transform Array by Parity
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. First, change every element to `0` if it is even and to `1` if it is odd. Then reorder the resulting values so that all `0`s appear before any `1`s, keeping the array length unchanged. The output is this transformed array of 0s and 1s.

title: Find the Number of Copy Arrays
explanation_short: You receive an integer array original of length n and a matrix bounds of size n × 2, where bounds[i] = [ui, vi] defines the allowed range for the i‑th element. A copy array of length n is considered valid if each of its entries lies inside the corresponding interval [ui, vi] while also respecting the conditions imposed by the original array. Your task is to determine how many distinct valid copy arrays can be formed. Output this count as a single integer.

title: Check If Digits Are Equal in String After Operations II
explanation_short: You receive a string `s` made up only of decimal digits. A specific operation (as defined in the statement) is applied over and over until only two characters remain in the string. Your task is to determine whether those final two digits are identical. Return `true` if they match and `false` otherwise.

title: Lexicographically Smallest Generated String
explanation_short: You are given two strings `str1` (length n) and `str2` (length m). A “generated” string must have length n + m − 1 and satisfy the positional constraints that relate characters of the generated string to the characters of `str1` and `str2` as described in the statement. Your task is to decide whether any string fulfills those constraints; if several do, return the one that comes first in lexicographic order, and if none do, return an empty string.

title: Find Minimum Cost to Remove Array Elements
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. At each step you may apply one of the allowed removal operations, each incurring a specific cost, until the array becomes empty. Your task is to pick a sequence of operations that makes the total cost as low as possible. Output the minimum total cost required to remove all elements.

title: Permutations IV
explanation_short: You are given two integers n and k. First list every permutation of the numbers 1 through n that never places two odds or two evens next to each other, then order those valid permutations lexicographically. Return the k‑th permutation in that order as an array, or return an empty array if fewer than k such permutations exist.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence After at Most K Operations
explanation_short: You are given a string s and an integer k. You may change any character up to k times, each change moving the letter one step forward or backward in the alphabet (with wrap‑around). Your task is to determine the greatest possible length of a subsequence of the resulting string that reads the same forward and backward. Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Sum of K Subarrays With Length at Least M
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and two integers `k` and `m`.  
Your task is to pick exactly `k` subarrays that do not overlap, and each chosen subarray must contain at least `m` elements.  
Among all possible selections, you must determine the greatest total sum of the elements in those `k` subarrays.  
Return that maximum sum as a single integer.

title: Find the Largest Almost Missing Integer
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
Consider every contiguous subarray of `nums` that has length `k`; an integer is “almost missing” if it occurs in exactly one of those subarrays.  
Your task is to find the greatest value among all almost‑missing integers.  
If no integer satisfies the condition, output `-1`.

title: Fruits Into Baskets II
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays of equal length: `fruits[i]` tells how many items of the i‑th fruit type you have, and `baskets[j]` tells the capacity of the j‑th basket. Starting from the first fruit type and moving right, you try to put each fruit type into any basket that still has enough remaining space, using the baskets in order as you go. After you cannot place a fruit type any more, you move on to the next type. The answer is the number of fruit types that end up unplaced after this process.

title: Fruits Into Baskets III
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays of equal length n: `fruits[i]` tells how many items of the i‑th fruit type you have, and `baskets[j]` tells the capacity of the j‑th basket. Starting from the leftmost fruit type, you try to put its items into the baskets in order, respecting each basket’s remaining capacity. After you cannot place any more fruit types, you need to count how many fruit types are still left unplaced. The answer is this count, returned as a single integer.

title: Choose K Elements With Maximum Sum
explanation_short: You receive two integer arrays of the same length, nums1 and nums2, and a positive integer k. For each position i, consider every index j where the value in nums1 is strictly smaller than nums1[i]. From those qualifying indices pick up to k of them that have the largest corresponding nums2 values and add those values together. The result for each i is placed in an output array of the same size, which you return.

title: Maximize Subarrays After Removing One Conflicting Pair
explanation_short: You are given an integer n, which defines the array [1, 2, …, n], and a list of conflicting pairs, each pair [a, b] meaning that a subarray containing both a and b is forbidden. You must choose exactly one of those pairs to delete, then count all non‑empty subarrays of the original array that avoid containing both elements of every remaining pair. The task is to determine the largest possible count of such sub‑arrays after the optimal deletion. Return that maximum count as a single integer.

title: Longest Special Path II
explanation_short:
You are given an undirected tree rooted at node 0, described by a list of edges where each edge contains its two endpoints and its length, together with an array nums that assigns a value to every node.  
A “special” path is any downward path from an ancestor to a descendant in which all node values are different, except that one value may appear twice at most.  
Your task is to determine the greatest total length of such a path and, among all paths that achieve this length, the smallest possible number of nodes they contain.  
Return these two numbers as a two‑element array: the first element is the maximum length, and the second is the minimal node count for the longest special paths.

title: Unique 3-Digit Even Numbers
explanation_short: You receive an array containing single‑digit numbers, possibly with repeats. From these digits you must form three‑digit numbers that are even, using each copy of a digit at most once in a single number and never placing a zero in the hundreds place. Count how many different numbers satisfy those rules. The answer you return is this count as an integer.

title: Design Spreadsheet
explanation_short: You are given a series of operations on a spreadsheet that has columns A‑Z and a specified number of rows, where each cell can store an integer. The operations include setting a cell to a value, resetting a cell (which makes its value default to 0), and querying a cell’s value; queries may be plain numbers or formulas that start with ‘=’ and can add values from other cells. For each operation you must return the result of the call-`null` for the mutating methods and the computed integer for the queries. The overall output is the list of these return values in the order the operations are performed.

title: Closest Equal Element Queries
explanation_short: You are given a circular array `nums` and another array `queries` that contains indices into `nums`. For each index in `queries` you must locate the closest different position in the circle whose element equals the element at the queried index. If such a position exists, record the number of steps needed to reach it (moving either direction around the circle); otherwise record `-1`. The result is an array of these values, one for each query, in the same order as the queries appear.

title: Zero Array Transformation IV
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a list of queries, each query described by three numbers `[l, r, val]`. Processing a query means applying its operation to every element of `nums` whose index lies between `l` and `r` (inclusive). Your task is to find the smallest non‑negative integer `k` such that after performing the first `k` queries in order, the entire array becomes all zeros; if no prefix of the queries can achieve this, return `-1`.

title: Longest Common Prefix of K Strings After Removal
explanation_short: You are given a list of strings `words` and an integer `k`. For each position `i` in the list, imagine removing the string at that index; from the remaining strings you must consider any `k` distinct elements and determine the longest prefix that all `k` of them share, then record its length. If fewer than `k` strings remain after the removal, the answer for that index is 0. Return an array where the `i`‑th entry holds the length computed for the removal of the `i`‑th string.

title: Count Beautiful Numbers
explanation_short: You receive two positive integers l and r. For every integer between l and r (including the endpoints) you look at its decimal digits, compute their sum and their product, and check whether the product is a multiple of the sum. The task is to count how many numbers in this interval satisfy that condition. The answer you return is this count.

title: Find the Minimum Amount of Time to Brew Potions
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays: skill, where skill[i] is the processing speed of the i‑th wizard, and mana, where mana[j] is the size of the j‑th potion. Each potion must pass through all wizards in order, and the time wizard i spends on potion j is skill[i] × mana[j]; a wizard can only start a potion exactly when it arrives from the previous wizard. The task is to schedule the flow so that all m potions are brewed without idle gaps and the overall completion time is as small as possible. Return that minimum total time as a single integer.

title: Maximum Unique Subarray Sum After Deletion
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. You may remove any subset of its elements (leaving at least one element) and then choose a contiguous segment from the remaining numbers. The task is to report the largest possible sum of such a chosen subarray.

title: Reverse Degree of a String
explanation_short: You are given a string s of lowercase English letters. For each character, determine its position in the reversed alphabet (a → 26, b → 25, …, z → 1) and multiply that value by the character’s 1‑based index in the string. Add up all of these products. Output the total sum as an integer.

title: Maximum Containers on a Ship
explanation_short: You receive three integers - the side length n of a square cargo deck, the weight w of each container, and the ship’s weight limit maxWeight. The deck has n × n cells, each able to hold one container, but the total weight of the loaded containers must stay at or below maxWeight. Your task is to compute and return the greatest possible number of containers that can be placed on the deck under this restriction.

title: Properties Graph
explanation_short: You receive an array `properties` containing `n` rows, each row being a list of integers, and an integer `k`. For any two different rows, count how many distinct numbers appear in both rows; if that count is at least `k`, imagine an undirected edge connecting the corresponding nodes. The task is to determine how many separate groups of nodes (connected components) exist when all such edges are added. Return that number as a single integer.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Elements Zero
explanation_short: The input is a list named queries, each entry being a pair [l, r] that defines a consecutive range of integers. For every query you consider an array that contains every integer from l to r inclusive. You may apply the given operation repeatedly until all numbers in that array become zero, and you need to find the smallest possible number of operations for each query. Finally, return the sum of those minimal operation counts over all queries.

title: Maximize Active Section with Trade II
explanation_short: You are given a binary string s of length n and a list of queries, each query defined by two indices li and ri that specify a substring s[li…ri]. For each query you may apply at most one “trade” operation inside that substring, which can change some characters according to the rules of the trade. After performing the best possible trade (or none at all), you must determine the greatest number of contiguous blocks of ‘1’s-called active sections-that can appear in the whole string s. Return an array where the i‑th element is the maximum number of active sections achievable for the i‑th query.

title: Longest Palindrome After Substring Concatenation I
explanation_short:
You are given two strings `s` and `t`.  
You may pick any contiguous piece (or nothing) from `s` and any contiguous piece (or nothing) from `t`, place the piece from `s` first and the piece from `t` after it, and look at the resulting string.  
Your task is to determine the maximum possible length of a palindrome that can appear among all such concatenations.  
Return that length as an integer.

title: Minimum Cost to Reach Every Position
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `cost` of length `n`, where `cost[i]` is the price to swap places with the person standing at position `i`. Starting from the back of the line (position `n`), you may perform any sequence of swaps, paying the corresponding costs, to move forward toward the front. For each position `i` from 0 to `n‑1`, you must determine the smallest total amount of money required to end up exactly at that position. Return an array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` holds this minimum cost for position `i`.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Elements Within K Subarrays Equal
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` together with two parameters `x` (the exact length of each subarray) and `k` (the required count of such subarrays). You may change individual elements of the array any number of times, and each change counts as one operation. The goal is to perform as few operations as possible so that the final array contains at least `k` non‑overlapping subarrays of length `x` whose elements are all identical. The answer you must output is that minimum number of operations.

title: Maximize Active Section with Trade I
explanation_short:
You are given a binary string `s` of length `n`.  
Imagine the string padded with a leading and trailing `1`, forming `t = "1" + s + "1"` (the extra `1`s are only for counting purposes).  
You may apply at most one trade-an operation defined in the statement-to change `s` and try to increase the number of “active sections” (contiguous groups of `1`s) that appear in `t`.  
Return the greatest possible number of active sections after the optimal trade (or none, if a trade would not improve the count).

title: Minimum Cost to Divide Array Into Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given two integer arrays `nums` and `cost` of the same length, plus an integer `k`. You may split the sequence of `nums` into consecutive subarrays, and the cost of each subarray depends on the elements in that segment, the matching entries from `cost`, and the subarray’s position in the division (first, second, …). Your task is to pick a partition that makes the sum of all subarray costs as small as possible. Output the minimum total cost as a single integer.

title: Maximum Product of Subsequences With an Alternating Sum Equal to K
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` together with two numbers `k` and `limit`. You must pick a non‑empty subsequence of `nums` whose alternating sum (even‑positioned elements minus odd‑positioned elements, in the subsequence order) is exactly `k`, and among all such subsequences choose the one whose product of elements is as large as possible without exceeding `limit`. Output that maximum product, or `-1` if no subsequence meets the alternating‑sum requirement.

title: Minimum Pair Removal to Sort Array II
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may apply a certain operation any number of times (the operation removes a pair of elements according to the rules of the problem). Your task is to determine the smallest possible number of such operations that will transform `nums` into a non‑decreasing sequence, where each element is at least as large as the one before it. The answer you return is that minimum count; if the array is already sorted, the answer is 0.

title: Longest Palindrome After Substring Concatenation II
explanation_short: You are given two strings `s` and `t`. From each string you may pick any contiguous segment (or choose none) and place the segment from `s` in front of the segment from `t` to form a new string. Among all such concatenations, determine the greatest possible length of a palindrome that can appear. Return that maximum length as an integer.

title: Minimum Pair Removal to Sort Array I
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may apply a certain operation repeatedly (the exact operation is defined in the statement) to change the array. Your task is to figure out the smallest number of times you must apply that operation so that the final array is non‑decreasing, meaning each element is at least as large as the one before it. Return that minimum count as an integer.

title: Number of Unique XOR Triplets I
explanation_short:
You receive an array `nums` that contains each integer from 1 to `n` exactly once.  
For every possible choice of three distinct positions `i, j, k` (order irrelevant), compute the value `nums[i] XOR nums[j] XOR nums[k]`.  
Collect all the results and determine how many different XOR values appear.  
Return that count as the answer.

title: Implement Router
explanation_short: You are given a series of commands that construct a Router object, insert packets, retrieve the next packet in FIFO order, and count packets for a specific destination within a time window. Each addPacket call supplies a source, destination, and timestamp and returns whether the packet could be stored without exceeding the router’s memory limit. forwardPacket removes and returns the earliest‑added packet (or an empty result if none exist). getCount asks for the number of stored packets whose destination matches the query and whose timestamps fall between startTime and endTime (inclusive).

title: Number of Unique XOR Triplets II
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. For every possible choice of three (not necessarily distinct) elements from the array, compute the value of their bitwise XOR. Among all those XOR results, determine how many different values appear. The answer you return is this count of unique XOR results.

title: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement I
explanation_short:
You receive a single string `s` that is known to be a palindrome.  
Your task is to reorder the characters of `s` so that the resulting string is still a palindrome and is the smallest possible in lexicographic order.  
Return that reordered palindrome as the answer.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Sum Divisible by K
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
First compute the total sum of all elements in `nums`.  
You may add any non‑negative integer to the sum as many times as you like, and each addition counts as one operation.  
Report the smallest number of such operations needed so that the final sum is a multiple of `k`.

title: Find Closest Person
explanation_short: You receive three integers x, y, and z that represent the positions of Person 1, Person 2, and Person 3 on a straight line. Both Person 1 and Person 2 travel toward Person 3 at the same constant speed. You must decide which of the two will meet Person 3 first based solely on their starting distances. Output 1 if Person 1 arrives first, otherwise output 2.

title: Shortest Path in a Weighted Tree
explanation_short: You are given the number of nodes n, a list of n‑1 weighted edges that form a tree rooted at node 1, and a sequence of queries. Each query is either of the form [1, u, v, w] to change the weight of the edge between u and v to w, or of the form [2, x] asking for the total weight along the unique path from the root (node 1) to node x. Process the queries in order, updating the tree when required and answering every type‑2 query. Return an array containing the answers for all type‑2 queries, in the same order they appear.

title: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement II
explanation_short: You are given a string s that is already a palindrome and an integer k. From all distinct palindromes that can be formed by rearranging the characters of s, you must identify the k‑th one in lexicographic order. Return that palindrome, or an empty string if fewer than k different palindromic permutations exist.

title: Make Array Non-decreasing
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. You may repeatedly pick any contiguous segment of the array and replace that whole segment by a single element equal to the segment’s maximum value. After performing zero or more such replacements, the resulting array must be non‑decreasing. Your task is to determine the greatest possible length of an array that can be obtained under these rules. Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Find X Value of Array II
explanation_short: You are given a positive‑integer array `nums`, a modulus `k`, and a list of queries where each query supplies four numbers `[index, value, start, x]`. For every query you first change `nums[index]` to `value`, then consider all possible ways to cut off a suffix (the cut may be empty but the remaining prefix must stay non‑empty) that begins at or after position `start`. The task is to count how many of those suffix‑removal choices make the product of the remaining elements leave remainder `x` when divided by `k`. Return an array whose i‑th entry is the count for the i‑th query.

title: Count Numbers with Non-Decreasing Digits
explanation_short:
You receive three values: the lower bound `l` and upper bound `r` given as decimal strings, and an integer base `b`.  
Consider every integer `x` with `l ≤ x ≤ r`; write `x` in base `b` and check whether each digit is at least as large as the digit before it when read from most to least significant.  
Count how many numbers satisfy this non‑decreasing‑digit condition.  
Return the count modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Count Cells in Overlapping Horizontal and Vertical Substrings
explanation_short: You receive an m × n grid of letters and a pattern string. A horizontal occurrence reads the pattern left‑to‑right, wrapping to the next row when the row ends; a vertical occurrence reads top‑to‑bottom, wrapping to the next column when the column ends. A cell is counted if it lies inside at least one matching horizontal substring **and** at least one matching vertical substring. The answer is the total number of such cells.

title: Calculate Score After Performing Instructions
explanation_short: You are given two equal‑length arrays: `instructions`, where each element is either “add” or “jump”, and `values`, which provides an integer for each position. Starting at index 0, follow the instructions one by one-“add” changes a running score by its associated value and then moves to the next index, while “jump” moves the current index forward or backward by its associated value without changing the score. The simulation stops as soon as the index moves outside the array bounds. After the process ends, output the final score you have accumulated.

title: Find X Value of Array I
explanation_short: You receive a list of positive integers `nums` and a positive integer `k`. For every possible way to cut off a (possibly empty) prefix and a (possibly empty) suffix while leaving at least one element, you look at the product of the remaining numbers and record its remainder when divided by `k`. For each remainder `x` from 0 to `k‑1`, you must count how many such cuts produce that remainder, and return those counts in an array of length `k`.

title: Path Existence Queries in a Graph I
explanation_short: You receive the number of vertices n, a non‑decreasing array nums of length n, an integer maxDiff, and a list of queries where each query is a pair [u, v]. An undirected edge connects two vertices i and j whenever the absolute difference between nums[i] and nums[j] does not exceed maxDiff, and you must decide for every query whether a path exists between the two specified vertices using those edges. Return a Boolean array indicating “true” for queries that are connected and “false” for those that are not.

title: Find the Most Common Response
explanation_short: You receive a two‑dimensional array where each inner array contains the strings people answered on a particular day. For each day you count every distinct answer only once, ignoring repeats inside that day. Find the answer that shows up in the greatest number of days; if several answers are tied, pick the one that is alphabetically earliest. Output that answer as a single string.

title: Concatenated Divisibility
explanation_short:
You receive an array `nums` of positive integers and a positive integer `k`.  
Consider any ordering of the elements; write each number in decimal and glue them together to form one large integer.  
Your task is to pick the ordering that makes this concatenated integer divisible by `k` and is lexicographically smallest among all such orderings.  
Return that ordering as a list, or an empty list if no ordering satisfies the divisibility condition.

title: Unit Conversion I
explanation_short: You are given n different unit types numbered 0 to n‑1 and a list of conversion triples [source, target, factor] where one unit of source equals factor units of target. Starting from a single unit of type 0, you must determine how many units of each type are equivalent to that one base unit. The result is an array of length n where the i‑th entry holds the equivalent count for type i, taken modulo 10⁹ + 7. Return this array as the final answer.

title: Maximum Profit from Valid Topological Order in DAG
explanation_short:
You are given n nodes, a list of directed edges that form a DAG, and an array score where score[i] is the value of node i.  
You must place the nodes in a linear sequence that respects every edge (a topological order), assigning positions 1…n to the nodes.  
The profit of an ordering is the sum of each node’s score multiplied by its position in the sequence.  
Return the maximum profit achievable among all valid topological orders.

title: Fill a Special Grid
explanation_short: You receive a single non‑negative integer n, which defines a square grid of size 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ. The task is to place every integer from 0 up to 2^(2n) − 1 exactly once into the cells so that the resulting grid satisfies the given “special” ordering rules (the rules guarantee a unique relative ordering among the four quadrants). The program must return the completed grid as a two‑dimensional array. A grid of size 1 × 1 is automatically special, so for n = 0 the answer is [[0]].

title: Count Covered Buildings
explanation_short: You receive an integer n describing an n × n grid and a list of distinct coordinates, each marking a building’s location. A building is considered “covered” when there is at least one other building somewhere to its left, one to its right, one above, and one below it. Your task is to count how many buildings satisfy this condition. Return that count as a single integer.

title: Merge Operations for Minimum Travel Time
explanation_short: You are given the road length l, the number of signs n, the required number of merges k, and two arrays: position (the increasing locations of the signs, with the first at 0 and the last at l) and time (the minutes per kilometre for each segment between consecutive signs). A merge removes one sign that is not the first, combines its segment with the next, and adds the two corresponding travel‑time values together for the new longer segment. After performing exactly k such merges, compute the total travel time as the sum of (segment length × its per‑kilometre time) over all remaining segments. Output the smallest possible total travel time achievable.

title: Path Existence Queries in a Graph II
explanation_short: You are given the number of vertices n, an array nums of length n, a threshold maxDiff, and many pairs of vertices in queries. An undirected edge joins i and j whenever the absolute difference between nums[i] and nums[j] does not exceed maxDiff. For each query you must report the smallest number of edges required to travel from the first vertex to the second, or -1 if no such route exists. Return the answers in the same order as the queries.

title: Maximum Product of Two Digits
explanation_short:
You receive a single positive integer n.  
Look at each digit that appears in n, and consider every possible pair of digits (a digit can be paired with itself only if it occurs at least twice).  
Find the largest product you can obtain from any such pair.  
Return that maximum product as an integer.

title: Minimum Operations to Convert All Elements to Zero
explanation_short: You are given an array `nums` of non‑negative integers. In one move you may pick any contiguous segment of the array and decrease every element in that segment by 1. The task is to determine the smallest possible number of such moves that will turn every entry of the array into 0. Return that minimum count as a single integer.

title: Minimum Deletions for At Most K Distinct Characters
explanation_short: You are given a lowercase string s and an integer k. You may delete any characters from the string, and after deletions the remaining characters must contain at most k different letters. Output the minimum number of deletions needed to achieve this condition.

title: Subtree Inversion Sum
explanation_short: You are given an undirected tree rooted at node 0, described by the list edges, and an array nums where nums[i] is the value attached to node i. A parameter k limits how many nodes you may apply an inversion operation to (each chosen node changes the sign of its own value and possibly its descendants, according to the rules). Your task is to decide which nodes to invert so that the total sum of all node values after the operations is as large as possible. The program should output that maximum achievable sum.

title: Find Sum of Array Product of Magical Sequences
explanation_short: You are given two integers m and k and an array nums. A magical sequence is any length‑m list of indices from nums that satisfies the condition involving exactly k set bits (as defined by the problem). For each magical sequence you multiply the nums values at those indices, then add up all those products. Return the total sum modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Find Most Frequent Vowel and Consonant
explanation_short:
You receive a single lowercase string `s`.  
Count how many times each vowel (a, e, i, o, u) appears and how many times each consonant appears.  
Identify the vowel with the highest count and the consonant with the highest count (if a group is absent, its count is 0).  
Return the sum of those two maximum frequencies as an integer.

title: Smallest Index With Digit Sum Equal to Index
explanation_short:
You receive an array of integers called `nums`.  
For each position `i` (starting from 0), look at the number `nums[i]` and add up its decimal digits.  
Find the first index where that digit sum exactly matches the index `i`.  
If such an index exists, output it; otherwise output `-1`.

title: Maximum Weighted K-Edge Path
explanation_short:
You are given the number of vertices n, a list of directed edges (each with a start node, end node, and weight), and two integers k and t.  
Among all directed paths that use exactly k edges and whose total weight does not exceed t, you must find the greatest possible sum of the edge weights.  
If such a path exists, output that maximum sum; otherwise output -1.

title: Equal Sum Grid Partition I
explanation_short: You receive an m × n grid of positive integers. You must decide whether a single straight cut-either between two rows (horizontal) or between two columns (vertical)-can divide the grid into two non‑empty sections whose sums of elements are exactly the same. Return true if such a cut exists; otherwise return false.

title: Minimum Weighted Subgraph With the Required Paths II
explanation_short: You are given a weighted tree described by a list of edges, and a list of queries where each query contains two source nodes and one destination node. For every query you must pick a connected subset of edges (a subtree) that lets both sources reach the destination using only those edges. Among all possible subtrees that satisfy this condition, you need the one with the smallest total edge weight. Return an array whose j‑th element is that minimum weight for the j‑th query.

title: Maximum Sum of Edge Values in a Graph
explanation_short: You receive an integer n and a list of m undirected edges connecting nodes numbered 0 to n‑1, where each node has degree at most 2. Assign each node a distinct value from 1 to n; the value of an edge is the product of the two node values it joins. Your task is to choose the assignment that makes the total sum of all edge values as large as possible. Return that maximum sum.

title: Equal Sum Grid Partition II
explanation_short: You are given an m × n grid of positive integers. You must decide whether a single straight cut-either along a row line (horizontal) or a column line (vertical)-can split the grid into exactly two connected pieces whose sums of values are the same. The cut may not intersect any cell; it separates whole rows or whole columns. Return true if such a partition exists, otherwise return false.

title: Sum of Largest Prime Substrings
explanation_short: You are given a string `s` that consists of decimal digits. From any contiguous segment of the string you can form an integer (ignoring any leading zeros) and check whether it is a prime number. Collect all distinct prime values that can be obtained, then identify the three largest of them (or fewer if less than three exist). Return the sum of those selected primes; if none are found, the answer is 0.

title: Find Maximum Number of Non Intersecting Substrings
explanation_short:
You are given a single string `word`.  
Choose a collection of substrings that (1) are at least four characters long, (2) start and end with the same letter, and (3) do not overlap each other.  
Each character of `word` may belong to at most one chosen substring.  
Return the largest possible number of substrings that satisfy these conditions.

title: Minimum Swaps to Sort by Digit Sum
explanation_short:
You are given an array of distinct positive integers.  
The goal is to rearrange the array so that the numbers appear in non‑decreasing order of the sum of their digits, and when two numbers have the same digit sum the smaller number comes first.  
You must compute the smallest possible number of swaps of two positions that will transform the original array into this sorted order.  
Return that minimum swap count as an integer.

title: Resulting String After Adjacent Removals
explanation_short: You are given a lowercase string s. Whenever two neighboring characters are consecutive letters in the alphabet (with ‘a’ and ‘z’ considered neighbors), that pair is removed from the string. This removal is repeated until no such adjacent pair exists. The required output is the string that remains after all possible deletions, which may be empty. Return that final string.

title: Grid Teleportation Traversal
explanation_short: You are given an m × n grid of characters, where each cell is either empty, an obstacle ‘#’, or a portal labeled with a capital letter. Starting from the top‑left cell (0,0), you may walk to any orthogonal neighbor that is inside the grid and not an obstacle, and you may also teleport once per letter from a portal cell to any other cell bearing the same letter. Your task is to determine the smallest number of walking steps needed to reach the bottom‑right cell (m‑1, n‑1). Return that minimum step count, or -1 if the destination cannot be reached.

title: Number of Ways to Assign Edge Weights I
explanation_short: You are given an undirected tree with n nodes (1 to n) and a list of n − 1 edges; node 1 is the root. Each edge on the tree can be assigned a weight of 1 or 2, and you only consider the unique path from the root to a deepest node x (any node with maximum depth). Your task is to count how many weight assignments on that path make the total sum of the weights odd. Return the count modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Number of Ways to Assign Edge Weights II
explanation_short: You are given an undirected tree described by a list of n‑1 edges and a list of queries, each query containing two nodes u and v. For every query you must consider only the edges on the unique path between u and v, assign each of those edges a weight of 1 or 2, and count how many assignments make the total weight along the path odd. The answer for each query is the number of such assignments, taken modulo 10⁹ + 7. Return the answers in the same order as the queries.

title: Find Minimum Log Transportation Cost
explanation_short: You receive three integers n, m, and k, representing the lengths of two logs and the maximum length a truck can carry. Each of three trucks may hold at most one piece of log whose length does not exceed k, and you may cut a log of length x into two parts len1 and len2 (at a cost of len1 × len2). Your task is to decide how, if at all, to cut the logs so that all resulting pieces can be placed on the three trucks while minimizing the total cutting cost. Output the smallest possible total cost; if the original logs already fit, the answer is 0.

title: Minimum Absolute Difference in Sliding Submatrix
explanation_short: You receive an m × n integer matrix grid and an integer k. For every contiguous k × k submatrix, you must find the smallest absolute difference between any two distinct values inside it (zero if all values are identical). The result is a new matrix of size (m − k + 1) × (n − k + 1), where each entry holds the minimum difference for the submatrix whose top‑left corner is at that position.

title: Maximum Profit from Trading Stocks with Discounts
explanation_short: You are given the number of employees n, two arrays present and future (each of length n) describing the purchase price and future selling price of each employee’s stock, a list of boss‑subordinate pairs defining the company hierarchy, and a total budget. You may choose any subset of employees to buy stock, but if an employee’s direct boss is also bought, that employee’s purchase price is reduced to half (rounded down). The task is to select purchases so that the sum of the chosen purchase prices does not exceed the budget while the total profit (future price minus purchase price for each bought employee) is as large as possible. Return that maximum achievable profit as an integer.

title: Lexicographically Smallest String After Adjacent Removals
explanation_short: You are given a single string `s` made of lowercase English letters. You may repeatedly delete any pair of neighboring characters that are consecutive in the circular alphabet (e.g., ‘a’ next to ‘z’ or ‘c’ next to ‘d’). After performing any number of such deletions, you must produce the lexicographically smallest string that can remain. The output is that final string, which may be empty if all characters can be removed.

title: Partition Array into Two Equal Product Subsets
explanation_short:
You are given a list of distinct positive integers `nums` and an integer `target`.  
You must decide whether the elements can be divided into two non‑empty, disjoint groups that together use every number exactly once, and where the product of the numbers in each group equals `target`.  
Return `true` if such a partition exists; otherwise return `false`.

title: Minimum Moves to Clean the Classroom
explanation_short: The input gives a rectangular grid of characters, where ‘S’ marks the student’s start, ‘L’ cells contain litter to be collected, ‘R’ cells are energy‑reset stations, and ‘.’ are empty spaces; an integer energy specifies the maximum energy the student can have at any time. From the start the student may move up, down, left, or right, spending one unit of energy per step, and when the energy reaches zero the student can only continue if standing on a reset cell, which restores the energy to the full amount. The task is to determine the smallest number of moves needed to visit every litter cell at least once, respecting the energy‑reset rule. Return that minimum move count, or –1 if no sequence of moves can collect all litter.

title: Maximum Good Subtree Score
explanation_short:
You are given a rooted tree (node 0 is the root) with n nodes; each node i has an integer value vals[i] and its parent is specified by par[i] (‑1 for the root).  
For every node u, consider any subset of nodes that lies completely inside the subtree of u (including u itself) and that never repeats any decimal digit among the values of the chosen nodes; such a subset is called “good”.  
The task is to find, for each u, the largest possible sum of values of a good subset inside its subtree, then add up all these maximum sums.  
Return this total sum modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Maximize Count of Distinct Primes After Split
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a list of queries, each query being a pair `[idx, val]` that replaces `nums[idx]` with `val` (the change stays for later queries). After each update you may break every element of the current array into any collection of prime numbers whose sum equals that element. From all possible ways of breaking the numbers, you must determine the greatest number of different prime values that can appear simultaneously. Return the sequence of these maximum counts, one for each query, in the order the queries are processed.

title: Maximize Subarray GCD Score
explanation_short: You are given an array of positive integers `nums` and an integer `k`. You may double the value of at most `k` different elements, and each element can be doubled only once. After the modifications, pick any contiguous subarray; its score is the subarray’s length multiplied by the greatest common divisor of all its elements. Your task is to decide which elements to double and which subarray to choose so that this score becomes as large as possible. Output the maximum achievable score as a single integer.

title: Transform Array to All Equal Elements
explanation_short: You are given an array `nums` that contains only the values 1 and -1, together with an integer `k`. In one operation you may change the sign of any element (you may pick the same position multiple times). You need to decide whether it is possible to make every entry of the array identical using at most `k` such operations. Return **true** if it can be done, otherwise return **false**.

title: Maximize Y‑Sum by Picking a Triplet of Distinct X‑Values
explanation_short: You receive two integer arrays x and y of equal length n. Choose three different indices i, j, k so that the three values x[i], x[j], x[k] are all distinct, and compute the sum y[i] + y[j] + y[k]. The task is to output the largest possible sum that satisfies the distinct‑x condition, or -1 if no such triple exists.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock V
explanation_short: You receive an array prices where prices[i] gives the stock price on day i, and an integer k that limits how many transactions you may perform. A transaction consists of buying on one day and later selling on a different day, and you must finish one transaction before beginning the next. Choose up to k such buy‑sell pairs so that the sum of their profits is as large as possible. Return that maximum total profit as a single integer.

title: Count Partitions With Max-Min Difference at Most K
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. You need to divide the array into one or more non‑empty contiguous segments so that, for every segment, the difference between its maximum and minimum elements does not exceed `k`. Count all possible partitions that satisfy this condition and output the total modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Generate Tag for Video Caption
explanation_short:
You receive a single line of text `caption`.  
You must turn it into a video tag by prefixing a ‘#’, keeping the first word exactly as it appears, and capitalizing the first letter of every following word while removing all spaces.  
The result is the transformed string that should be printed.

title: Count the Number of Computer Unlocking Permutations
explanation_short: You are given an array `complexity` of size `n`, where `complexity[i]` is the password difficulty of computer `i`. Computer 0 is already unlocked, and each subsequent computer can be unlocked only after at least one already‑unlocked computer has a password whose complexity meets the required condition (as described in the statement). Your task is to count how many permutations of the indices `[0,1,…,n‑1]` can serve as a valid unlocking sequence that starts with computer 0. Return that count modulo `1 000 000 007`.

title: Minimum Steps to Convert String with Operations
explanation_short: You are given two strings of the same length, word1 and word2. You may cut word1 into one or more contiguous pieces, and on each piece you can apply a replace, a swap, or a reverse, with the restriction that any character position can participate in at most one of each operation type. Your task is to choose a partition and a set of operations that turn word1 into word2 using as few operations as possible. Return that minimum number of operations.

title: Find Weighted Median Node in Tree
explanation_short: You are given the number of nodes n, a list of n − 1 edges where each edge specifies its two endpoints and a weight, and a list of queries each containing two nodes u and v. For every query you must look at the unique path connecting u to v and locate the first node on that path where the accumulated edge weight from u reaches at least half of the total weight of the whole path. The answer for a query is the index of that node. Return an array containing the answers for all queries in order.

title: Count Special Triplets
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums`. A *special triplet* is any three indices `i < j < k` that satisfy the condition described in the statement (the ends of the triplet must relate to the middle element in the required way). Your task is to count how many such index triples exist in the given array. Return that count modulo \(10^9+7\).

title: Minimum Adjacent Swaps to Alternate Parity
explanation_short: You receive an array `nums` containing distinct integers. You may repeatedly swap any two neighboring elements. The task is to rearrange the array so that every adjacent pair consists of one even and one odd number, using the fewest possible adjacent swaps, and report -1 if such an alternating parity ordering cannot be achieved. Return that minimum swap count (or -1).

title: Find Maximum Area of a Triangle
explanation_short: You receive a list of n points, each given as an [x, y] pair. From these points you must choose any three that form a non‑degenerate triangle whose at least one side runs horizontally or vertically. Among all such triangles, determine the one with the largest area and output twice that area (so the result is an integer). If no three points satisfy the axis‑parallel side condition, return ‑1.

title: Maximum Product of First and Last Elements of a Subsequence
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `m`.  
Pick any subsequence of exactly `m` elements, keeping their original order.  
For each chosen subsequence compute the product of its first and last elements, and find the largest such product among all possible subsequences.  
Output that maximum product as a single integer.

title: Kth Smallest Path XOR Sum
explanation_short: You are given a rooted tree where each node has an integer value, and for every node you can compute the XOR of all values on the path from the root to that node. Each query provides a node u and an integer k; you must look at all nodes in the subtree of u, collect the distinct path‑XOR values that appear, sort them, and report the k‑th smallest one. If the subtree contains fewer than k different XOR sums, the answer for that query is -1. Return an array containing the answer for each query in the order they were asked.

title: Minimum Time to Transport All Individuals
explanation_short: You are given the number of people n, the boat capacity k, the length of the environmental cycle m, an array time where time[i] is the solo crossing time of person i in neutral conditions, and an array mul of length m that repeatedly scales the crossing speed for each stage of the cycle. The boat can carry up to k people at once, and each trip’s duration equals the slowest passenger’s neutral time multiplied by the current stage’s multiplier, with the cycle advancing after every crossing (including returns). Your task is to determine the smallest possible total time needed to move every individual from the start to the destination, or report -1 if the constraints make it impossible. The answer should be printed as a floating‑point number (or -1) representing that minimum total time.

title: Count Prime-Gap Balanced Subarrays
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a number `k`.  
A subarray of `nums` is considered “prime‑gap balanced” if the pattern of prime numbers inside it meets the given gap condition involving `k`.  
Your task is to examine all possible contiguous subarrays and count how many satisfy this prime‑gap balance.  
Return that total count as a single integer.

title: Check if Any Element Has Prime Frequency
explanation_short: You receive an array of integers called nums. For each distinct value in the array, count how many times it occurs. Determine whether at least one of those counts is a prime number (greater than 1 and divisible only by 1 and itself). Return true if such a count exists; otherwise return false.

title: Inverse Coin Change
explanation_short: You are given a 1‑indexed integer array `numWays` where `numWays[i]` tells how many different ways there are to reach the total amount `i` using an unlimited supply of some unknown coin denominations (each denomination is a positive integer not larger than the array length). Your task is to infer which distinct coin values could have produced exactly those counts. Return those possible denominations as a sorted list of unique integers; if no set of denominations can generate the given `numWays` values, return an empty array.

title: Minimum Increments to Equalize Leaf Paths
explanation_short: You are given an integer n, a list of n‑1 undirected edges that define a tree rooted at node 0, and an array cost where cost[i] is the traversal cost of node i. Each root‑to‑leaf path has a score equal to the sum of the costs of the nodes on that path. You may increase the cost of any nodes by any non‑negative amount, and you need to choose the smallest possible number of nodes to adjust so that every root‑to‑leaf path ends up with the same score. Return that minimum number of nodes whose cost must be increased.

title: Partition String
explanation_short:
You are given a single string `s`.  
Starting from the first character, you repeatedly create new substrings, each time extending the current piece until adding another character would make the substring repeat a previously seen segment.  
Whenever that would happen, you close the current segment and begin a new one from the next character.  
Return the list of all segments in the order they were created.

title: Longest Common Prefix Between Adjacent Strings After Removals
explanation_short: You receive an array `words` containing several strings. For each position `i`, imagine deleting the string at that index and then looking at every pair of neighboring strings that remain. Among those neighboring pairs, determine the greatest length of a prefix that the two strings share. The result array `answer` stores that maximum length for each `i`, using 0 when no pair has a common prefix.

title: Maximize Spanning Tree Stability with Upgrades
explanation_short: You are given n nodes numbered 0 to n‑1 and a list of edges, each described by its two endpoints, its strength s, and a flag must (1 means the edge cannot be upgraded). You may choose up to k different edges with must = 0 and double their strength, but each such edge can be upgraded at most once. Your task is to pick a set of n‑1 edges that connects all nodes without cycles (a spanning tree) and makes the smallest strength among the chosen edges as large as possible. Return that largest possible minimum strength, or ‑1 if no spanning tree can be formed.

title: Partition Array to Minimize XOR
explanation_short:
You receive an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`.  
You must split the array into exactly `k` contiguous, non‑empty parts.  
For each part compute the bitwise XOR of its elements, then look at the largest XOR value among the `k` parts.  
Return the smallest possible value that this largest XOR can take over all valid partitions.

title: Minimum Cost Path with Alternating Directions II
explanation_short: You are given the grid dimensions m and n and a matrix waitCost where waitCost[i][j] is the cost of waiting on cell (i, j). Entering any cell also costs (i + 1) × (j + 1). Starting from cell (0, 0) on the first move, you must travel to cell (m − 1, n − 1) while following the required alternating‑direction pattern. Compute the smallest possible sum of all entrance costs and waiting costs needed to reach the destination. Output that minimum total cost as a single integer.

title: Hexadecimal and Hexatrigesimal Conversion
explanation_short: You receive a single integer n. Compute n², write it in base‑16 using digits 0‑9 and uppercase A‑F, then compute n³ and write it in base‑36 using digits 0‑9 and uppercase A‑Z. Finally, join the two resulting strings and return the combined result.

title: Minimum Time to Reach Destination in Directed Graph
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and a list of directed edges; each edge is described by its start node, end node, and a time interval [start, end] during which the edge can be traversed at any integer moment. Starting at node 0 at time 0, you may move along an edge only when the current time lies inside its allowed interval, and each move takes exactly one unit of time. Your task is to determine the earliest possible time at which you can reach node n − 1. Output that minimum arrival time, or -1 if the destination cannot be reached.

title: Coupon Code Validator
explanation_short: You are given three equal‑length arrays: `code`, `businessLine`, and `isActive`, where the i‑th elements describe one coupon. A coupon is considered valid only if it satisfies all the required conditions (such as a non‑empty, properly formatted code and an active status). Collect the codes of all valid coupons and sort them first by their business line following the order electronics → grocery → pharmacy → restaurant, and then alphabetically within each group. Return the resulting list of codes.

title: Minimum Stability Factor of Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a limit `maxC` on how many elements you may replace with arbitrary integers. A subarray is called stable when the greatest common divisor of all its numbers is at least 2, and the stability factor of the whole array is the length of its longest stable subarray. After changing at most `maxC` elements, you must make this longest stable subarray as short as possible. Return that minimum length, or 0 if no stable subarray can remain.

title: Minimum Time for K Connected Components
explanation_short: You receive an integer n, a list of edges where each entry gives two node indices and the time at which that edge disappears, and an integer k. Starting from the full graph, edges whose removal time is ≤ t are deleted, and the remaining edges determine the connected components. Your goal is to find the smallest time t for which the graph is split into at least k separate components. Output that minimum t (or indicate impossibility if no such t exists).

title: Minimum Moves to Reach Target in Grid
explanation_short: You are given four integers sx, sy, tx, ty that describe the starting point (sx, sy) and the target point (tx, ty) on an unbounded 2‑D grid. From any position (x, y) you may make a move that depends on m = max(x, y) according to the problem’s rule. Your task is to determine the smallest number of such moves that can bring you exactly to (tx, ty), or report ‑1 if the target cannot be reached. The answer should be a single integer representing that minimum count (or ‑1).

title: Power Grid Maintenance
explanation_short: You are given the number of power stations c, a list of bidirectional cables connecting pairs of stations, and a sequence of queries. Each query is either “1 x”, which asks for the smallest‑numbered station that is still online and lies in the same connected grid as x (including x itself), or “2 x”, which permanently takes station x offline. Offline stations remain part of their original grid, but they are ignored when answering type‑1 queries. Return an array containing the answers for all type‑1 queries in the order they appear, using ‑1 when no online station exists in x’s grid.

title: Process String with Special Operations I
explanation_short: You receive a single string `s` that contains lowercase letters together with the symbols `*`, `#`, and `%`. While scanning the characters from left to right you must apply the prescribed effects of each special symbol to the characters that have been seen so far. After the entire input has been processed, the characters that remain form the final string. Print that resulting string (it may be empty).

title: Process String with Special Operations II
explanation_short: You receive a string `s` that contains lowercase letters together with the symbols `*`, `#`, and `%`, and an integer `k`. While scanning `s` from left to right you must apply the given special operations to build a new string `result`. After the whole input has been processed, you need to report the character that appears at position `k` in `result`. If `k` is larger than the length of `result`, the answer is the period character `'.'`.

title: Minimize Maximum Component Cost
explanation_short: You are given the number of vertices n, a list of undirected edges where each edge is described by its two endpoints and its weight, and an integer k. You may delete any edges you like, as long as the remaining graph splits into at most k connected components. For each component, its cost is the largest weight among the edges that stay inside it (or 0 if the component has no edges). Your task is to choose which edges to remove so that the highest component cost is as small as possible. Return that minimum possible maximum cost.

title: Longest Palindromic Path in Graph
explanation_short:
You are given the number of nodes n, a list of undirected edges connecting those nodes, and a string where the i‑th character is the label of node i.  
You may begin at any node and walk along edges, never revisiting a node, forming a path of distinct vertices.  
From the labels of the visited nodes you must be able to arrange them into a palindrome, and you need to find the greatest possible length of such a palindrome.  
Return that maximum length as an integer.

title: Count Islands With Total Value Divisible by K
explanation_short: You receive an m × n grid of integers and a positive integer k. An island consists of all cells with a value > 0 that are connected horizontally or vertically. For each island you must add up its cell values and check whether that total is a multiple of k. Return the number of islands whose summed value is divisible by k.

title: Network Recovery Pathways
explanation_short: You receive a directed acyclic graph given as a list of edges, where each edge specifies its start node, end node, and recovery cost.
