A boolean array indicates which nodes are online (nodes 0 and n‑1 are always online), and only paths that stay on online nodes and have a total cost not exceeding the given limit k are considered valid. For every valid path compute the minimum edge‑cost along that path, and output the largest of these minima, or ‑1 if no such path exists.

title: Number of Integers With Popcount-Depth Equal to K I
explanation_short: You are given two integers n and k. For each integer x between 1 and n inclusive, repeatedly replace x by the number of 1‑bits in its binary representation until the value becomes 1; the smallest number of steps required is the popcount‑depth of x. Your task is to count how many numbers in the interval [1, n] have a popcount‑depth exactly equal to k. Output that count as a single integer.

title: Check Divisibility by Digit Sum and Product
explanation_short: You receive a single positive integer n. First compute the sum of its digits and the product of its digits, then add those two results together. Check whether n is evenly divisible by that combined value. Return “true” if it divides evenly, otherwise return “false”.

title: Split Array by Prime Indices
explanation_short: You’re given an integer array `nums`. Separate its elements into two groups: one consisting of the numbers whose positions are prime indices (using 0‑based indexing) and the other containing the rest. Compute each group’s sum (treat an empty group as sum 0) and output the absolute difference between the two sums.

title: Count Number of Trapezoids I
explanation_short: You receive a list of points, each given as an integer (x, y) coordinate. From these points you must choose any four distinct ones that form a convex quadrilateral with at least one pair of sides parallel to the x‑axis (a horizontal trapezoid). Count every different set of four points that meets this condition, and output the total number of such sets modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Number of Integers With Popcount-Depth Equal to K II
explanation_short: You are given an initial array `nums` of non‑negative integers and a sequence of queries. Each query is either of type 1 `[1, l, r, k]`, which asks for the number of positions `i` with `l ≤ i ≤ r` whose popcount‑depth equals `k`, or of type 2 `[2, idx, val]`, which replaces `nums[idx]` with `val`. Process the queries in order, updating the array when a type‑2 query occurs and counting for every type‑1 query. The output is a list containing the answers of all type‑1 queries in the same order they were asked.

title: Count Number of Trapezoids II
explanation_short: You are given a list of points, each represented by its integer (x, y) coordinates. From these points you must choose any four distinct ones that form a convex quadrilateral and have at least one pair of opposite sides with the same slope (i.e., a trapezoid). Two quadrilaterals that use the same four points in a different order count as the same trapezoid. The task is to return the total number of such distinct trapezoids that can be created.

title: Maximum Median Sum of Subsequences of Size 3
explanation_short: You are given an integer array whose length is a multiple of 3. In each step you may choose any three elements, take the median (the middle value after sorting those three), and remove the three chosen numbers from the array. After repeating this until the array is empty, you need to maximize the sum of all medians you obtained, and return that maximum possible sum.

title: Maximum Number of Subsequences After One Inserting
explanation_short: You are given a string `s` made of uppercase English letters. You may insert one additional uppercase letter at any position (including the ends) and then count how many subsequences of the form “L C T” appear in the new string. Return the largest possible number of such “LCT” subsequences that can be achieved with at most one insertion.

title: Minimum Jumps to Reach End via Prime Teleportation
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` of length `n`. Starting from index 0, you may move to adjacent positions or “teleport” according to a rule that involves prime numbers (for example, jumping to indices whose values share a prime factor with the current value). Your task is to determine the smallest number of such moves needed to reach index `n - 1`. The answer should be returned as a single integer representing that minimum jump count.

title: Partition Array for Maximum XOR and AND
explanation_short:
You are given an array of integers `nums`.  
You must divide all the elements into three (possibly empty) groups A, B, and C, each element belonging to exactly one group.  
For the chosen partition compute the bitwise XOR of the numbers in A, the bitwise AND of the numbers in B, and the bitwise XOR of the numbers in C, then add these three results together.  
Return the largest possible sum that can be achieved by any such partition.

title: Minimum Removals to Balance Array
explanation_short:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`.  
You may delete any elements you like, but the array must stay non‑empty.  
Find the smallest possible number of deletions that makes the remaining elements satisfy “maximum ≤ k × minimum”.  
Return that minimum deletion count.

title: Earliest Finish Time for Land and Water Rides II
explanation_short: You are given four arrays: the start times and durations of all land rides, and the start times and durations of all water rides. You must pick exactly one land ride and one water ride, and you may take them in either order, but each ride can only begin at or after its own start time and must run for its full duration. The goal is to schedule the two rides so that the time when the second ride ends is as early as possible. Return that minimum possible finishing time as a single integer.

title: Earliest Finish Time for Land and Water Rides I
explanation_short: You are given four arrays: the start times and durations of all land rides, and the start times and durations of all water rides. The tourist must choose exactly one land ride and one water ride, and can take them in either order, but each ride can only begin at or after its own start time and takes its given duration to finish. Your task is to determine the smallest possible time at which both chosen rides can be completed. Return that minimum finishing time as a single integer.

title: Trionic Array I
explanation_short: You receive an integer array `nums`. Your task is to decide whether you can pick two indices `p` and `q` (with `0 ≤ p < q < n‑1`) that split the array into three consecutive, non‑empty segments that each meet the given condition. If such a pair of indices exists, the answer is `true`; otherwise it is `false`. The output is a single Boolean value.

title: Threshold Majority Queries
explanation_short: You are given an integer array `nums` and a list of queries, each query containing three numbers `li`, `ri`, and `thresholdi`. For every query you must look at the segment of `nums` from index `li` to `ri` (inclusive) and determine whether any value occurs at least `thresholdi` times. If such values exist, return the one with the greatest occurrence count, breaking ties by choosing the smallest value; otherwise return `-1`. The result is an array where the i‑th entry is the answer for the i‑th query.

title: Trionic Array II
explanation_short: The problem asks you to choose four indices l < p < q < r in the given array and take the sum of the whole contiguous segment from l to r; you must find the maximum possible value of that sum (it’s guaranteed that at least one such choice exists). The key is to turn the subarray sum into differences of prefix sums and then, while scanning the array, keep track of the best prefix value before the first cut and the best suffix value after the second cut so you can combine them in linear time rather than trying every quadruple.

title: Minimum Time to Activate String
explanation_short: You are given a string s, a permutation order that tells which position is turned into ‘*’ at each time step t (starting from t = 0), and an integer k. As time progresses, more positions become ‘*’, and a substring counts as valid if it includes at least one ‘*’; the string is considered active once the total number of valid substrings reaches k. Return the smallest t that makes the string active, or -1 if that never happens.

title: Maximum Balanced Shipments
explanation_short: You receive an array weight containing the weights of parcels lined up in order. A shipment is any contiguous block of parcels, and it is “balanced” when the last parcel’s weight is strictly smaller than the maximum weight inside that block. You may choose several shipments that do not overlap, leaving some parcels unused, and you want to maximize how many balanced shipments you can select. Return the largest possible count of such non‑overlapping balanced shipments.

title: Maximum Total from Optimal Activation Order
explanation_short: You are given an integer N and a list of N numbers. You may activate the positions one after another in any order; when a position is activated you earn its own value plus the values of any of its immediate neighbours that have already been activated. Choose the activation sequence that makes the sum of all earned points as large as possible and output that maximum total.

title: Flip Square Submatrix Vertically
explanation_short: You are given an N × N grid of numbers and an integer K that defines a K × K square block. The grid is partitioned into non‑overlapping K × K blocks (the last rows/columns may be ignored if N isn’t a multiple of K). For each block you must reverse the order of its rows – the top row becomes the bottom row, the second row becomes the second‑last, and so on. After performing this vertical flip on every block, print the entire N × N matrix, row by row.

title: Maximum K to Sort a Permutation
explanation_short:
You are given the size N of a permutation and the permutation itself (a list of the numbers 1…N in some order).  
You may only swap elements that are at positions i and i xor K (using 0‑based indices) any number of times.  
Your task is to choose the largest possible integer K that still makes it possible to rearrange the array into the sorted order 1,2,…,N.  
Print that maximum K.

title: Minimum Sensors to Cover Grid
explanation_short: You are given an N × M grid where some cells are marked as needing monitoring and others are blocked. You must choose positions for sensors so that every marked cell lies in the same row or column as at least one sensor, and sensors can only be placed on unblocked cells. The task is to determine the smallest possible number of sensors that achieve this full coverage. Output that minimum count as a single integer.

title: Next Special Palindrome Number
explanation_short: You are given a positive integer N. Your task is to locate the smallest integer that is strictly larger than N and whose binary representation reads the same forwards and backwards. In other words, you must find the next “binary palindrome” after N. Output that integer as a decimal number.

title: Minimum Cost Path with Teleportations
explanation_short: You are given an N × M grid where each cell contains a non‑negative cost to step on. From any cell you may move to the right or down neighbor, paying the cost of the destination cell, and you may also use a limited number of teleportation portals that instantly move you to a specified other cell for a given portal cost. Your task is to determine the smallest total cost required to travel from the top‑left corner to the bottom‑right corner, possibly using some of the teleportations. The output is a single integer representing that minimum cost.

title: Number of Perfect Pairs
explanation_short:
You are given an integer n and a list of n numbers.  
Your task is to count how many unordered pairs of distinct indices (i, j) (i < j) have the property that the sum of the two corresponding numbers is a perfect square.  
The output is a single integer – the total number of such “perfect” pairs.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock using Strategy
explanation_short: You are given an array where each element represents the price of a stock on a successive day. Your task is to determine the greatest possible profit you could earn by buying the stock on one day and selling it on a later day (you may also choose not to trade). The answer is a single integer: the maximum profit, or 0 if the prices never rise enough to make a profit.

title: Minimum Cost Path with Edge Reversals
explanation_short: You are given a directed graph with N vertices and M edges, plus a start vertex S and a target vertex T. Each edge can be used in its original direction for free, but you may also travel against its direction by “reversing” the edge, which incurs a cost of 1. Your task is to determine the smallest total cost (i.e., the fewest edge reversals) needed to form a path from S to T. Output that minimum number, or -1 if no such path exists even after any number of reversals.

title: XOR After Range Multiplication Queries II
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers. Then you receive Q queries; each query provides three numbers L, R and X, meaning that every element whose index lies between L and R (inclusive) must be multiplied by X. After each query is applied to the current array, you must compute the bitwise XOR of all N elements. Output the resulting XOR value for each query on its own line, in the order the queries are processed.

title: Minimum Sum After Divisible Sum Deletions
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers and a divisor k. You may repeatedly remove any contiguous sub‑array whose total sum is a multiple of k, and the deletions can be performed in any order. After all possible deletions, the remaining elements form a new sum. Your task is to compute the smallest sum that can be left after applying an optimal sequence of such deletions. Output that minimum possible sum.

title: XOR After Range Multiplication Queries I
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers and Q queries. Each query provides three numbers l, r, x and asks you to multiply every element whose index lies between l and r (inclusive) by x. After performing each query you must report the XOR of all N elements in their current state. The output consists of Q lines, each containing the XOR value that follows the corresponding query.

title: GCD of Odd and Even Sums
explanation_short: You receive one or more test cases; each case gives the length of a sequence followed by the sequence’s integers. Separate the numbers into two groups: those in odd‑positioned places and those in even‑positioned places (positions are counted from 1). Compute the sum of each group, then find the greatest common divisor of the two sums. Print that GCD for every test case.

title: Jump Game IX
explanation_short: You are given an array of non‑negative integers. Starting from any position, you may move to the index i + arr[i] or i − arr[i] as long as the destination stays inside the array. The task is to decide whether there exists a sequence of such jumps that lands on an element whose value is 0. Return “true” if reaching a zero is possible, otherwise return “false”.

title: Maximum Walls Destroyed by Robots
explanation_short: You are given N walls, each with a strength value, and M robots, each having a power limit. A robot can start at any wall and destroy a contiguous block of walls as long as the sum of their strengths does not exceed the robot’s power. You may assign each robot at most once and choose the order of assignments to maximize the total number of walls destroyed. The output is a single integer: the greatest possible count of walls that can be eliminated.

title: Twisted Mirror Path Count
explanation_short: You are given an N × N grid (each cell is either free or blocked). Starting from the top‑left corner you may move only right or down, and you must finish at the bottom‑right corner. A valid route is one whose sequence of moves reads the same when reflected across the main diagonal (the “twisted mirror” condition). Your task is to determine how many such routes exist, reporting the answer modulo 1 000 000 007. The output is a single integer representing that count.

title: Partition Array Into K-Distinct Groups
explanation_short:
You are given an array of N integers and a number K.  
Your task is to rearrange the elements into groups of exactly K items each, making sure that no group contains the same value twice.  
If such a partition exists, output “YES”; otherwise output “NO”.

title: Two-Letter Card Game
explanation_short: You are given N cards, each described by a two‑letter string (e.g., “AB”). Your task is to decide whether the cards can be ordered so that the second letter of every card matches the first letter of the next card, forming a continuous chain that uses every card exactly once. The input consists of N followed by the N two‑letter strings. Print “YES” if such an ordering exists, otherwise print “NO”.

title: Find The Least Frequent Digit
explanation_short: You are given a non‑negative integer (or a string of digits) as the input. Count how many times each digit from 0 to 9 appears in that number. Identify the digit whose occurrence count is the smallest among all digits that actually appear. Output that least‑frequent digit (if several digits tie, follow the rule stated in the problem, e.g., choose the smallest such digit).

title: Minimum Operations to Equalize Binary String
explanation_short: You are given a binary string S consisting only of ‘0’ and ‘1’. An operation is defined by the problem statement (you may change bits according to certain rules). Your task is to determine the smallest number of such operations required to transform S into a string where every character is identical (all 0’s or all 1’s). Output that minimum number as a single integer.

title: Maximum Product of Two Integers With No Common Bits
explanation_short: You are given a list of positive integers. From this list you must pick two different numbers that share no set bits-that is, their bitwise AND equals zero. Among all such pairs, find the one whose product is the largest. Output that maximum product (or indicate that no valid pair exists).

title: Sum of Beautiful Subsequences
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n positive integers. A subsequence is called beautiful when the greatest common divisor of all its elements equals the length of the subsequence. For each beautiful subsequence, compute the sum of its elements and add all those sums together. Output the final total modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Restore Finishing Order
explanation_short: You are given the number of participants, then a list of all their names, and finally a list of the names of those who finished (which is one short). Exactly one name appears in the first list but not in the second. Output that missing name.

title: Balanced K-Factor Decomposition
explanation_short: You receive two integers N and K. Your task is to break N into exactly K positive integers whose product equals N, arranging the factors so they are as balanced as possible (i.e., the largest factor is as small as it can be). Output the K factors (in any order) or, if specified, just the minimal possible value of the largest factor.

title: Count Bowl Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array a of n numbers. A subarray is considered a “bowl” if you can pick a position inside it so that everything to the left of that position never increases (it’s non‑increasing) and everything to the right never decreases (it’s non‑decreasing), forming a valley shape. Your task is to count how many contiguous subarrays of a satisfy this bowl condition. Output that total count as a single integer.

title: Smallest Absent Positive Greater Than Average
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. First compute the average of all the numbers, then look for the smallest positive integer that is larger than this average and does not occur anywhere in the list. That missing integer is what you must output. If every positive integer above the average appears in the list, output the next larger positive integer.

title: Minimum Operations to Transform String
explanation_short: You are given two strings of the same length, each made of lowercase letters. In one operation you may pick a character that appears in the first string and change **all** of its occurrences to any single character that is alphabetically later. Your task is to determine the smallest number of such operations required to turn the first string into the second (or report that it cannot be done). The output is that minimum count, or ‑1 if the transformation is impossible.

title: Minimum Operations to Equalize Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n integers. In one operation you may increase or decrease any single element by 1. Your goal is to determine the smallest possible number of such operations needed to make every element in the array have the same value. Output that minimum count as a single integer.

title: Count Binary Palindromic Numbers
explanation_short: You receive two integers L and R that define a closed interval. For every integer inside that interval you must check whether its binary representation reads the same forwards and backwards. Count how many of those numbers are binary palindromes. Output the total count.

title: Maximum XOR of Subsequences
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by n non‑negative numbers. From these numbers you may pick any subset (order doesn’t matter) and compute the bitwise XOR of the chosen elements. Your task is to determine the largest possible XOR value that can be achieved by some subset. Output that maximum value as a single integer.

title: Subsequence Sum After Capping Elements
explanation_short: You receive an array of integers and a number K. First you may pick a cap C; any element larger than C is reduced to C, while smaller elements stay unchanged. After capping, choose any subsequence of exactly K elements and compute its sum, and output the greatest possible sum you can obtain by selecting the best cap and subsequence.

title: Minimum Discards to Balance Inventory
explanation_short: You are given N items in order, each identified by an integer type. You may discard items from the front and/or the back, leaving a single contiguous segment of the original list. The goal is to make the remaining segment “balanced” – every distinct type that appears in it must occur the same number of times. Compute the smallest possible number of discarded items, i.e., N minus the length of the longest balanced segment. The output is that minimum discard count.

title: Generate Schedule
explanation_short: You are given a single integer n (the number of teams, n is even). You must arrange a round‑robin tournament so that every pair of teams meets exactly once, and each team plays one match in every round. Print n − 1 lines; each line lists n⁄2 pairs of team numbers (1‑based) that play in that round. If no such arrangement exists, output -1.

title: Earliest Time to Finish One Task
explanation_short: You are given n tasks; each task i is described by two integers sᵢ (the time it becomes available) and dᵢ (the time it takes to complete). Starting a task exactly at its availability time, its finishing moment is sᵢ + dᵢ. Your job is to determine the smallest finishing moment among all tasks. Print that earliest possible finish time as a single integer.

title: Maximum Total Subarray Value I
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N numbers forming an array. For any non‑empty contiguous segment (subarray) its “value” is defined as the sum of the elements in that segment plus the largest element inside the same segment. Your task is to determine the maximum possible value over all subarrays and output that single number.

title: Maximize Sum of At Most K Distinct Elements
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers and an integer K. From the list you may pick any number of elements, but you are allowed to use at most K different values among those picks. Your task is to choose the values so that the total sum of the selected elements is as large as possible. Output that maximum achievable sum.

title: Split and Merge Array Transformation
explanation_short: You are given two sequences of positive integers - the initial array and a target array. You may repeatedly perform two kinds of operations: replace an element by two positive numbers that add up to it (split), or replace two neighboring elements by their sum (merge). Your task is to decide whether a series of such splits and merges can turn the initial array exactly into the target array. Output a single word indicating whether the transformation is possible (for example, “YES” or “NO”).

title: Number of Stable Subsequences
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers. A subsequence is called stable when the difference between its maximum and minimum values is at most 1. Count all non‑empty stable subsequences and output the total modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Majority Frequency Characters
explanation_short: You are given a single line containing a string. Count how many times each character appears and determine which characters occur more often than half the length of the string. Output all such characters (in any order), or output a word like “None” if no character meets the condition.

title: Bitwise OR of Even Numbers in an Array
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. From that list you must consider only the numbers that are even (divisible by 2). Compute the bitwise OR of all those even values, combining their binary representations with the OR operation. Print the resulting integer; if there are no even numbers, the answer is 0.

title: Distinct Points Reachable After Substring Removal
explanation_short: You are given a string S of length n that describes moves on a 2‑D grid (for example ‘L’, ‘R’, ‘U’, ‘D’). For every possible choice of a contiguous substring to delete, you start at the origin (0,0) and follow the remaining moves in order, ending at some grid point. Your task is to count how many different end points can be obtained by deleting any one substring (including the option of deleting nothing). Output a single integer – the number of distinct reachable points.

title: Maximize Alternating Sum Using Swaps
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers and m pairs of positions; each pair indicates that the two elements can be swapped any number of times, and swaps can be chained through overlapping pairs. Within each connected component formed by these swap relations you may reorder the elements arbitrarily. Arrange the numbers in each component so that the overall alternating sum (elements at odd indices minus elements at even indices) is as large as possible. Output that maximum achievable alternating sum as a single integer.

title: Compute Decimal Representation
explanation_short: You are given two integers \(a\) and \(b\) (\(b\neq0\)). Your task is to write the decimal form of the fraction \(a/b\). If the fractional part terminates, just show the digits after the decimal point; if it repeats, enclose the repeating block in parentheses. Output the resulting decimal string.

title: Climbing Stairs II
explanation_short: You are given a positive integer n representing the height of a staircase and an array of allowed step sizes. Each move you can climb any number of steps that appears in the array, and you may use steps repeatedly. Your task is to count how many different ordered sequences of allowed steps add up exactly to n. Output that total count as an integer.

title: Maximum Total Subarray Value II
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers and a number k. You must repeatedly pick a subarray, add the sum of its elements to a running total, and then forbid any element of that subarray from being used again. The task is to choose k pairwise‑disjoint subarrays so that the total sum of their values is as large as possible. Output the maximum total you can achieve (or the cumulative totals after each of the k picks, as required).

title: Compute Alternating Sum
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and then n numbers. Starting with the first number, you add it, subtract the second, add the third, and continue alternating addition and subtraction through the entire list. The final alternating sum is the single value you must output.

title: Split Array With Minimum Difference
explanation_short: You receive an integer n followed by n numbers forming an array. Choose a position to cut the array into a non‑empty left part and a non‑empty right part, and compute the absolute difference between the sums of the two parts. Output the smallest possible difference achievable by any such split.

title: Number of ZigZag Arrays I
explanation_short:
You are given two integers n and m.  
Consider all arrays of length n where each element is an integer between 1 and m (inclusive).  
An array is “zigzag” if for every interior position i (2 ≤ i ≤ n‑1) the element at i is either strictly larger than both neighbors or strictly smaller than both neighbors.  
Your task is to determine how many such zigzag arrays exist.  
Print this number modulo 998 244 353.

title: Longest Subsequence With Non-Zero Bitwise XOR
explanation_short: You receive an integer n followed by n numbers forming an array. From this array you must pick a subsequence-keeping the original order-so that the bitwise XOR of all selected elements is not zero. Your goal is to find the greatest possible number of elements you can include while satisfying that condition. Output that maximum length.

title: Number of ZigZag Arrays II
explanation_short: You are given three integers n, m and k. An array of length n is called a zig‑zag array if the comparisons between consecutive elements alternate between “<” and “>” (the first comparison can be either direction). You must count how many arrays whose entries are chosen from 1 … m satisfy this alternating condition and contain exactly k positions where the comparison is “<”. Output the total number of such arrays modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Count No-Zero Pairs That Sum to N
explanation_short: You are given an integer N. Find how many ordered pairs of positive integers (a, b) satisfy a + b = N while neither a nor b contains the digit 0 in its decimal representation. The input is a single line containing N, and the output is one integer – the total number of such pairs. The result can be large, so use a 64‑bit type.

title: Design Exam Scores Tracker
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of commands, each of which either adds a student’s exam score, removes a previously added score, or asks a question about the current set of scores (for example, how many scores are at least a given value or the sum of the top K scores). Process the commands in the order they appear, updating the collection of scores as you go. For every query command you must compute the requested statistic based on the scores that exist at that moment and output the answer. The output consists of the answers to all queries, printed in the same order they were asked.

title: Remove K-Balanced Substrings
explanation_short: You are given a string and an integer K. Whenever K identical characters appear next to each other, that whole block can be removed, and the remaining parts of the string are concatenated. This removal is repeated until no such K‑character block exists anywhere in the string. The required output is the final string after all possible deletions have been performed.

title: Longest Balanced Substring I
explanation_short: You are given a single string S. Your task is to locate a contiguous part of S in which every character that occurs does so the same number of times – that is, the substring is “balanced.” Among all such substrings, you must determine the one with the greatest length. Print that maximum length (or zero if no balanced substring exists).

title: Equal Score Substrings
explanation_short: You receive a string S of length N that contains only two different symbols (for example, ‘0’ and ‘1’ or ‘a’ and ‘b’). A substring is any consecutive segment of S. Your task is to count how many substrings have the same number of the first symbol as the second symbol. Output that count as a single integer.

title: Longest Fibonacci Subarray
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of integers. Your task is to locate the longest contiguous segment where, starting from the third element, each number equals the sum of the two preceding numbers (a Fibonacci‑type pattern). If no such pattern longer than two elements exists, the answer is simply 2. Report the length of that longest segment.

title: Sum of Elements With Frequency Divisible by K
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers and a positive integer K. For each distinct value in the array, count how many times it occurs. Identify the values whose occurrence count is a multiple of K and add those values together (each value contributes only once to the sum). Print the resulting total; if no value meets the condition, output 0.

title: Sum of Perfect Square Ancestors
explanation_short: The input describes a rooted tree: first the number of nodes, then an integer value for each node, followed by the edges that connect the nodes. For each node you must look at all of its ancestors (the nodes on the path from the root to its parent) and add together the values that are perfect squares. Output the resulting sum for every node in order of their indices (or a single total if the statement asks for the overall sum).

title: Maximum Partition Factor
explanation_short: You are given the length of an array n and the n integer values themselves. Your task is to split the array into one or more contiguous groups so that the sum of every group is divisible by the same integer d, and you want the largest possible d. The output is just that maximum integer d.

title: Smallest Missing Multiple of K
explanation_short: You are given an integer K and a list of N numbers. From the list we consider only the values that are multiples of K. Your task is to determine the smallest positive multiple of K that does **not** appear in the list. Output that missing multiple as a single integer.

title: Lexicographically Smallest Permutation Greater Than Target
explanation_short: You receive two strings of equal length: the first supplies a multiset of characters, and the second is a target string. Your task is to reorder the characters from the first string to create a new string that is lexicographically larger than the target, while being the earliest possible in dictionary order among all such rearrangements. If no ordering can surpass the target, output a designated indicator such as “-1”.

title: Longest Balanced Substring II
explanation_short: You receive a single binary string S. Your task is to determine the greatest possible length of a contiguous part of S in which the number of ‘0’ characters equals the number of ‘1’ characters. Print that maximum length (or 0 if no such segment exists).

title: Maximize Sum of Squares of Digits
explanation_short: You are given a single integer N that represents the total sum you may distribute among the digits of a number (each digit can be 0‑9). Choose any multiset of digits whose values add up exactly to N so that the sum of their squares is as large as possible. The answer is that maximal sum of squares; you should output this single integer.

title: Longest Balanced Subarray I
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N numbers forming an array. A subarray is called balanced when the sum of its elements is zero. Your task is to determine the maximum possible length of a contiguous balanced subarray. Print that length as a single integer.

title: Count Ways to Choose Coprime Integers from Rows
explanation_short: You are given a matrix where each row contains several positive integers. You must pick exactly one number from each row so that every pair of chosen numbers is coprime (their greatest common divisor is 1). Compute how many different selections satisfy this condition and output the total count (typically modulo 10⁹ + 7).

title: Remove Zeros in Decimal Representation
explanation_short: You are given a single integer expressed in base‑10. Delete every digit that equals zero from its decimal representation, keeping the other digits in their original order. The remaining digits form a new integer, which you must output (if no digits remain, output 0).

title: Maximum Alternating Sum of Squares
explanation_short: You are given n integers. You may reorder these numbers arbitrarily and then form the expression a₁² − a₂² + a₃² − a₄² + … where the signs alternate starting with a plus. Your task is to determine the greatest possible value of that alternating sum of squares. Print that maximum value as a single integer.

title: Longest Balanced Subarray II
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N integers forming an array. A subarray is called balanced if the sum of its elements equals 0. Your task is to identify the longest contiguous segment of the array that satisfies this condition. Output the length of that longest balanced subarray (or 0 if none exists).

title: Lexicographically Smallest String After Reverse
explanation_short: You are given a single line containing a string `s` of lowercase letters. You may choose any contiguous segment of `s` and reverse the characters in that segment exactly once (or choose not to reverse anything). Your task is to determine the lexicographically smallest string that can result from such an operation. Output that minimal string.

title: Minimum Operations to Transform Array
explanation_short: You are given the length of an array followed by its n integer elements. Your task is to figure out the smallest number of positions you must change (you may replace an element with any value you like) so that the whole sequence becomes strictly increasing. The answer is a single integer – the minimum number of such replacements required.

title: Stable Subarrays With Equal Boundary and Interior Sum
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n integers. For each contiguous subarray that contains at least two elements, compare the sum of its first and last element with the sum of all the elements in between. You need to count how many subarrays have these two sums equal. Output that count as a single integer.

title: Count Distinct Subarrays Divisible by K in Sorted Array
explanation_short: You are given a sorted array of N integers and an integer K. Your task is to consider every possible contiguous subarray, treat two subarrays as the same only if their sequences of values are identical, and count how many of those distinct subarrays have a sum that is a multiple of K. The input consists of N, K, and the N array elements. Output a single integer: the number of distinct subarrays whose sum is divisible by K.

title: Find Missing Elements
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers that should contain every number from a consecutive range (for example 1 to n), but some values are absent. Your task is to identify which numbers from that full range do not appear in the given list. The input consists of the array (and possibly the range limits), and the output should be the missing numbers, typically printed in increasing order.

title: Maximum Product of Three Elements After One Replacement
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n numbers. You may change exactly one element of the array to any integer value you like. After this single replacement, pick any three distinct positions and compute their product. Output the greatest product that can be obtained in this way.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements III
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. You may repeatedly add 1 or subtract 1 from any element, counting each addition or subtraction as one move. The task is to determine the smallest possible total number of moves needed to make every element in the list have the same value. Output that minimum total move count as a single integer.

title: Lexicographically Smallest Palindromic Permutation Greater Than Target
explanation_short: You are given a string of letters and a target string of the same length. Rearrange the letters of the first string to form a palindrome that is lexicographically larger than the target. Output the lexicographically smallest such palindrome, or “-1” if none exists.

title: Count Subarrays With Majority Element I
explanation_short: You receive an integer n and an array a of n integers. For every contiguous segment of the array, we check whether some value appears strictly more than half the length of that segment (i.e., is a majority element). Your task is to count how many of these subarrays satisfy that majority‑element condition. Output the total number of such subarrays as a single integer.

title: Minimum Time to Complete All Deliveries
explanation_short: You are given the number of deliveries N, the number of available couriers M, and a list of the time each individual delivery requires. The goal is to determine the smallest possible overall time by assigning deliveries to couriers so that each courier works on at most one delivery at a time. You must decide how to distribute the deliveries among the couriers to finish all of them as early as possible. Output that minimum total time.

title: Count Subarrays With Majority Element II
explanation_short: You receive an array of integers. For each contiguous subarray, you must determine whether there is an element that occurs strictly more than half of the positions in that subarray (i.e., a majority element). Your goal is to count how many subarrays satisfy this condition. Output the total count as a 64‑bit integer.

title: Maximize Cyclic Partition Score
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of n integers arranged in a circle. You may cut the circle at several points, creating a collection of contiguous blocks that together cover every element exactly once. Each block contributes a value defined by a specific scoring rule (for example, the maximum element, the sum, or a function of its endpoints), and the total score is the sum of the block scores. Your task is to choose the cut positions so that this total score is as large as possible, and output that maximum score.

title: Longest Non-Decreasing Subarray After Replacing at Most One Element
explanation_short: You are given an array of integers. You may change the value of at most one element anywhere in the array. Your task is to determine the maximum possible length of a contiguous segment that can be made non‑decreasing after that single replacement (or none). Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Minimum Distance Between Three Equal Elements II
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers. For any value that appears at least three times, consider the three positions of that value and compute the distance as the difference between the largest and smallest index among them. Your task is to determine the smallest such distance over all possible triples of equal elements. Print that minimum distance, or -1 if no value occurs three times.

title: Minimum Distance Between Three Equal Elements I
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by a list of n numbers. Among all values that appear at least three times, consider the positions of any three occurrences of the same value; the distance is the length of the segment from the first to the third occurrence (inclusive). Your task is to determine the smallest such distance over the whole array. If no number occurs three times, output -1; otherwise output the minimal distance found.

title: Maximum Path Score in a Grid
explanation_short: You are given an n × m grid of integers. Starting from the top‑left cell, you may move only right or down until you reach the bottom‑right cell. The score of a path is the sum of the numbers in the visited cells, and you must output the maximum possible score among all such paths.

title: Minimum String Length After Balanced Removals
explanation_short: You are given a string made only of the characters ‘(’ and ‘)’. You may repeatedly delete any substring that forms a balanced parentheses pair (for example “()”, “(())”, etc.). After no more deletions are possible, you must report how many characters remain. The output is a single integer – the length of the final string.

title: Count Stable Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n numbers. A subarray is considered stable if the largest value inside it and the smallest value differ by at most 1. Your task is to count how many contiguous subarrays of the given array are stable and output that total.

title: Count Distinct Integers After Removing Zeros
explanation_short: You are given a positive integer N (provided as a decimal string). Starting from N, you may repeatedly pick any digit ‘0’ that appears in the current number and delete it; after each deletion any leading zeros are dropped, so the result is again a valid integer. All numbers that can appear at any step-including the original N-are collected, and you must determine how many different integers are reachable this way. Output that count (usually as a plain integer, possibly modulo a given prime).

title: Maximize Expression of Three Elements
explanation_short: You are given an integer N and a list of N numbers. Choose three positions i < j < k and compute the value a[i] − a[j] + a[k]. Your task is to find the largest possible result among all such triples. Print that maximum value as a single integer.

title: Find Maximum Balanced XOR Subarray Length
explanation_short:
You are given an integer N followed by N integers that form an array.  
Your task is to locate a contiguous segment of this array whose elements XOR to zero and that has the greatest possible size.  
Among all such segments, you must determine the length of the longest one.  
Print that length as a single integer; if no subarray has XOR zero, output 0.

title: Minimum Number of Flips to Reverse Binary String
explanation_short: You are given a string consisting only of ‘0’ and ‘1’. Your task is to change as few characters as possible (each change flips a ‘0’ to ‘1’ or vice‑versa) so that the resulting string reads the same forward and backward. Count the minimum number of flips required and output that number as an integer.

title: Lexicographically Smallest Negated Permutation that Sums to Target
explanation_short: You receive an integer n and a target sum T. For each number 1…n you may either keep it positive or flip it to its negative, and you must pick signs so that the overall sum equals T. Among all sign choices that achieve the target, output the sequence that is lexicographically smallest (the first position where two sequences differ should contain the smaller value). If no such assignment exists, output a designated “impossible” indicator.

title: Total Waviness of Numbers in Range I
explanation_short: You are given two integers L and R that define a closed interval [L, R]. For any integer, look at its decimal digits; a digit is counted as a “wave” if it is strictly larger than both its immediate neighbours or strictly smaller than both. The waviness of a number is the total count of such wave‑positions, and you must add up the waviness of every number from L to R. Output this total (usually modulo 1 000 000 007).

title: Concatenate Non-Zero Digits and Multiply by Sum I
explanation_short: You receive three integers. First, delete every ‘0’ digit from each number, keep the remaining digits in their original order, and write the three resulting strings one after another to form a new integer. Then add the three original integers together and multiply that sum by the newly formed integer. Output the resulting product.

title: Total Waviness of Numbers in Range II
explanation_short: You are given two non‑negative integers L and R (often as decimal strings because they can be up to 10^18). For any integer, its “waviness” is the count of interior digit positions where the digit is either strictly larger than both neighbours or strictly smaller than both neighbours. Your task is to add up the waviness of every number from L through R inclusive. The program should output that total (usually modulo 1 000 000 007).

title: Number of Effective Subsequences
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n non‑negative integers. Your task is to count how many non‑empty subsequences of the array have a bitwise AND that is greater than 0 (i.e., there is at least one bit set in every element of the chosen subsequence). Print the total number of such subsequences, usually modulo 10⁹+7.

title: Count Elements With at Least K Greater Values
explanation_short: You are given an array of numbers and an integer k. For each element you must determine whether there are at least k other elements that are strictly larger than it. Count how many elements satisfy this condition. Output that count as a single integer.

title: Minimum Absolute Distance Between Mirror Pairs
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers. For each index i, consider its “mirror” element at position N‑1‑i (the element that is symmetric to i around the centre of the array). Compute the absolute difference between every such pair and report the smallest of those differences. The output is a single integer – the minimum absolute distance among all mirror pairs.

title: Concatenate Non-Zero Digits and Multiply by Sum II
explanation_short: You are given \(T\) test cases; each case provides a decimal integer as a string. From the string, form a new number by writing all non‑zero digits in their original order (ignoring any zeros). Also compute the sum of **all** digits of the original integer. For each test case output the product of the concatenated‑non‑zero number and the digit‑sum.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Binary Palindrome
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of bits (0 and 1). An operation consists of changing a single bit to the opposite value, and you may apply as many operations as needed. Your task is to determine the smallest number of such flips required so that the whole sequence reads the same forward and backward. Output that minimum count as an integer.

title: Maximum Substrings With Distinct Start
explanation_short: You are given a single string S. You must cut S into several non‑overlapping substrings so that the first character of each chosen substring is unique-no two substrings may begin with the same letter. Determine the greatest possible number of substrings you can obtain under this rule. Output that maximum count as an integer.

title: Minimum Operations to Equalize Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n numbers. In one operation you may add the same integer to every element of any contiguous subarray. Your task is to determine the smallest possible number of such operations that makes all array elements identical. Output that minimum count.

title: Complete Prime Number
explanation_short: You are given a single integer N. A “complete prime” is a prime number whose every decimal digit is itself a prime digit (2, 3, 5, 7). Your task is to locate the smallest complete prime that is greater than or equal to N. Print that number as the answer.

title: Minimum Inversion Count in Subarrays of Fixed Length
explanation_short: You’re given an array of n integers and a length k (1 ≤ k ≤ n). For each contiguous subarray of exactly k elements, count the number of inversions-pairs of indices inside the subarray where the earlier element is larger than the later one. Your goal is to find the smallest inversion count among all such subarrays. Output that minimum value.

title: Total Score of Dungeon Runs
explanation_short: You are given the number of dungeon runs N followed by N integers that represent the score earned in each run, and then Q queries each containing a target score X. For every query you must determine the smallest count of consecutive runs (starting from the first) whose cumulative score is at least X. If the total score of all runs is still less than X, report that it is impossible. The answer for each query is a single integer – the required run count or ‑1.

title: Sort Integers by Binary Reflection
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of integers. For each number, write its binary form, reverse the order of the bits, and treat that reversed string as a new binary value. Sort the original integers according to the size of these reversed‑binary values, from smallest to largest. Output the integers in this new order, preserving their original values.

title: Maximum Subgraph Score in a Tree
explanation_short: You are given a tree with N vertices, each vertex i having an integer value aᵢ. The input lists N, the aᵢ values, and the N‑1 edges that connect the vertices. Your task is to choose any connected set of vertices (a subgraph) so that the sum of the values of the chosen vertices is as large as possible. Print that maximum achievable sum.

title: Maximize Points After Choosing K Tasks
explanation_short: You are given n tasks, each described by two numbers: the points you must have to start the task (its requirement) and the points you gain after completing it (its profit). You also receive an initial amount of points W and may perform at most k tasks, but you can only pick a task whose requirement does not exceed your current points. Choose the tasks in any order to make your total points as large as possible after up to k selections. Output the maximum points you can achieve.

title: Largest Prime from Consecutive Prime Sum
explanation_short: You are given a single integer N. From all prime numbers that are less than or equal to N, you must identify those that can be written as the sum of one or more consecutive prime numbers (for example, 5 = 2 + 3). Among these candidates, select the greatest prime value. Output that prime; if none exist, output ‑1.

title: Reverse Words With Same Vowel Count
explanation_short: You are given a single line of text containing words separated by spaces. For each word, count how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) it contains, then look at all other words that have the same count. Within each such group, reverse the order of the words while keeping the groups themselves in their original left‑to‑right positions. Finally, output the resulting sentence as a space‑separated string.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Have Distinct Elements
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by n integers that may contain duplicates. In one operation you may increase any element by 1, and you may repeat this as many times as needed. Your goal is to make all the numbers pairwise distinct while using the fewest possible operations. Output the minimum total number of increments required.

title: Absolute Difference Between Maximum and Minimum K Elements
explanation_short: You are given a list of N integers and an integer K. From the list you must pick exactly K numbers (any K of them, not necessarily adjacent). Compute the absolute difference between the largest and the smallest of the chosen K numbers, and report the smallest possible such difference over all choices. The output is a single integer representing that minimum difference.

title: Minimum Moves to Balance Circular Array
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers that forms a circle, meaning the first and last positions are also neighbors. In one move you may transfer a single unit from any element to one of its two adjacent positions. The goal is to make every element contain the same value (the total sum divided equally) using the fewest possible moves. The input consists of n followed by the n array values, and the output is a single integer: the minimum number of moves required to achieve a balanced circular array.

title: Minimum Deletions to Make Alternating Substring
explanation_short: You are given a string S of length n (usually consisting of ‘0’ and ‘1’) and a number of queries, each specifying a segment [l, r] of the string. For each query you must determine the smallest number of characters that can be removed from the chosen segment so that the remaining characters form an alternating pattern (no two adjacent characters are the same). The answer for a query is the minimum deletions required for that particular substring. Output one integer per query, each on its own line.

title: Mirror Distance of an Integer
explanation_short: You are given one or more integers, each representing a number written in decimal. For each integer you must form its “mirror” by writing its digits in reverse order, then compute how far apart the original and its mirror are. The required result is the absolute difference between the original number and its reversed‑digit counterpart. Output that distance for every input number, each on its own line.

title: Minimum Deletion Cost to Make All Characters Equal
explanation_short: You are given a string `s` and an integer array `cost` of the same length, where `cost[i]` is the price to delete the character `s[i]`. The task is to remove some characters (paying their costs) so that every character left in the string is the same letter. You must choose which letter to keep and delete all characters that are different from it, minimizing the total amount spent. The output is a single integer: the smallest possible sum of deletion costs that achieves this.

title: Minimum Swaps to Avoid Forbidden Values
explanation_short: You receive an array of n integers and, for each index i, a single forbidden value that must not appear at that position. You may swap any two elements any number of times. Find the smallest number of swaps needed so that after the swaps no index contains its forbidden value (or output -1 if it cannot be achieved).

title: Maximum Score After Binary Swaps
explanation_short: You are given an integer n, a limit k, and a binary string s of length n. Each swap of two adjacent characters costs 1, and you may perform at most k such swaps. The score of a configuration is the sum of the positions (1‑based) of all ‘1’ characters in the final string. Your task is to rearrange the bits using no more than k swaps so that this score becomes as large as possible. Output the maximum achievable score.

title: Last Remaining Integer After Alternating Deletion Operations
explanation_short: You are given a single integer n, representing the list [1, 2, …, n]. Starting from the left, you repeatedly remove every second element; the next pass goes from the right, again deleting every second remaining element, and you keep alternating directions until only one number is left. Your task is to determine which integer survives this process. Output that final remaining integer.

title: Maximum Sum of Three Numbers Divisible by Three
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. From this list you must pick exactly three distinct numbers whose total is as large as possible while being a multiple of three. If no such triple exists, the answer should indicate that (for example, by outputting -1). The output is a single integer: the maximum achievable sum that satisfies the divisibility condition.

title: Smallest All-Ones Multiple
explanation_short: You are given a single positive integer N. Your task is to find the smallest positive number that contains only the digit 1 (for example 1, 11, 111, …) and is exactly divisible by N. The input consists of one line with the integer N, and the output should be that all‑ones multiple (usually printed as a string because it can be very long). If there is no such number, output -1.

title: Minimum Cost to Acquire Required Items
explanation_short: You are given the quantities you must obtain for each of several item types, plus a list of purchase options where each option has a price and tells you how many of each item it supplies (you can also buy items one‑by‑one at their unit prices). Your task is to choose a combination of these options so that for every item type you end up with at least the required amount. The goal is to make that combination cost as little as possible. Output the minimum total cost needed to satisfy all requirements.

title: Total Sum of Interaction Cost in Tree Groups
explanation_short: You are given a tree with N vertices, described by N‑1 edges each connecting two vertices and possibly having a length. After the tree, there are G groups; each group lists some vertices that belong to it. For every group you must consider all unordered pairs of its vertices and add the length of the unique path between the two vertices – this is the group’s interaction cost. Finally, output the sum of the interaction costs of all G groups.

title: Number of Balanced Integers in a Range
explanation_short: You are given two integers L and R that define a closed interval. An integer is considered balanced if, when its decimal representation is split into two equal‑length halves (adding a leading zero if necessary), the sum of the digits in the first half equals the sum of the digits in the second half. Your task is to determine how many numbers within the interval [L, R] satisfy this property. Output a single integer representing that count.

title: Maximum Score of a Split
explanation_short: You receive an array of integers. For every possible way to cut the array into a non‑empty left part and a non‑empty right part, compare the largest value in the left side with the largest value in the right side. Count a split whenever the left‑side maximum is less than or equal to the right‑side maximum, and output the total number of such splits.

title: Count Routes to Climb a Rectangular Grid
explanation_short: You are given an n × m grid where each cell is either free or blocked. Starting from the top‑left corner you may move any positive number of steps right or down, but you must stay on free cells and never cross a blocked one. Your task is to count how many different routes can reach the bottom‑right corner. Output the total number of such routes modulo 10⁹+7.

title: Reverse String Prefix
explanation_short:
You receive a word `s` and an integer `k`.  
Your task is to reverse only the first `k` characters of the word while leaving the rest unchanged.  
After performing this operation, you must produce the new string.  
The output is that modified string.

title: Minimum Subarray Length With Distinct Sum At Least K
explanation_short: You are given an array of positive integers and a target value K. From the array you may choose any contiguous segment (subarray). Your task is to determine the smallest possible length of such a segment whose elements add up to at least K. Output that minimum length, or 0 if no subarray reaches the required sum.

title: Find Maximum Value in a Constrained Sequence
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by n numbers that act as upper limits for the positions of a sequence. You must imagine a sequence where each element is non‑negative, never exceeds its own limit, and any two neighboring values differ by at most one. Among all such feasible sequences, determine the greatest value that can appear at any position. Output that single maximum value.

title: Minimum Cost to Merge Sorted Lists
explanation_short: You are given \(k\) sorted arrays, each described by its length and the sequence of numbers it contains. When you combine any two lists into one, the operation costs the total number of elements in the two original lists, and the resulting list remains sorted. Your task is to choose the order of pairwise merges so that, after repeatedly merging until only a single sorted list remains, the sum of all incurred costs is as small as possible. Output that minimum total cost as a single integer.

title: Minimum Cost to Make Two Binary Strings Equal
explanation_short: You are given two binary strings of equal length n and two integers x and y. Each position where the strings differ can be fixed either by flipping one of the bits (cost x) or by swapping two mismatched bits (cost y). Your task is to choose a combination of flips and swaps that turns the first string into the second with the smallest possible total cost. Output that minimum cost, or -1 if it cannot be achieved.

title: Count Residue Prefixes
explanation_short: You are given an integer n, a modulus m, and a sequence of n numbers. For each position i (0 ≤ i ≤ n) compute the sum of the first i numbers and look at its remainder when divided by m. Count how many unordered pairs of positions have the same remainder. Output that total count as a single integer.

title: Largest Even Number
explanation_short: You are given a string of decimal digits. Rearrange its characters to form the greatest possible integer that is even (its last digit must be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8). If no rearrangement can produce an even number, output -1. The result should be printed as a string representing the number.

title: Word Squares II
explanation_short:
You are given an array of words, all having the same length \(n\).  
Your task is to arrange some of these words into an \(n \times n\) grid so that every row forms a word from the list and the words read down each column are exactly the same as the rows (i.e., the grid is a word square).  
Return all distinct word squares that can be built from the given words.  
The output is a list of grids, each represented as an array of \(n\) strings.

title: Count Caesar Cipher Pairs
explanation_short: You are given n words, each consisting of lowercase letters. Two words form a Caesar‑cipher pair if they have the same length and every character of one word can be shifted by the same amount (mod 26) to obtain the other word. Your task is to count how many unordered pairs of the given words satisfy this condition. Output a single integer – the total number of such pairs.

title: Number of Centered Subarrays
explanation_short: You receive an array of integers. A subarray is considered centered when it has a middle element and the count of that middle value on the left side of the subarray equals the count of the same value on the right side. Your task is to determine how many subarrays of the given array meet this condition. Output the total number as a single integer.

title: Maximum Bitwise AND After Increment Operations
explanation_short: You are given an integer N, a limit K, and a list of N non‑negative integers. You may add 1 to any element any number of times, but the total number of additions across all elements cannot exceed K. After performing at most K increments, compute the bitwise AND of the entire modified array. Your task is to determine the largest possible value of that AND. Output this maximum value as a single integer.

title: Number of Alternating XOR Partitions
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n non‑negative numbers. You must count how many ways you can split the array into consecutive segments so that the XOR of each segment is either 0 or 1 and these XOR values strictly alternate (0, 1, 0, 1, … or 1, 0, 1, 0, …). The answer is the total number of such partitions, reported modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Minimum Operations to Reach Target Array
explanation_short: You are given an array of positive integers representing the desired final values of a list that initially contains all zeros. In one operation you may choose any contiguous segment of the list and increase every element in that segment by exactly one. Your task is to determine the smallest number of such operations required to transform the all‑zero list into the given target array. Output that minimum count as a single integer.

title: Minimum Edge Toggles on a Tree
explanation_short: You are given a tree with N vertices, each vertex labeled with a 0 or 1 representing its current state, and a second label indicating the desired final state. One operation consists of picking an edge and “toggling” it, which flips the states of the two vertices it connects. Your task is to determine the smallest number of edge‑toggles required to turn the initial labeling into the target labeling (or report that it’s impossible). Output that minimum count as a single integer.

title: Maximum Capacity Within Budget
explanation_short: You are given N items, each described by a capacity value and a price, together with a total budget B. Your task is to determine the greatest capacity that can be attained without spending more than B by selecting any subset of the items (each item at most once). The answer is a single number – the maximum achievable capacity, or 0 if no selection fits the budget.

title: Best Reachable Tower
explanation_short: You are given N and an array of N integers, where each integer is the height of a tower placed in a line. Starting from any tower you may walk left or right, but you can only step onto a tower whose height is not higher than the tower you are currently on. For each possible starting tower count how many towers (including the start) you can reach following that rule, and pick the tower that reaches the most. Output the 1‑based index of that tower; if several towers reach the same maximum, output the smallest index.

title: Vowel-Consonant Score
explanation_short: You are given a single word made up of lowercase English letters. Count how many letters are vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and how many are consonants, then compute the difference between the two counts. Output that integer value.

title: Rotate Non Negative Elements
explanation_short: You are given a list of N integers. All numbers that are zero or positive must be shifted cyclically by one position among themselves, while any negative numbers stay exactly where they are. In other words, the first non‑negative element becomes the second, the second becomes the third, …, and the last non‑negative element moves to the position of the first non‑negative element. Print the resulting sequence after this rotation.

title: Lexicographically Smallest String After Deleting Duplicate Characters
explanation_short: You are given a single string consisting of lowercase English letters. From this string you may delete any number of characters, but the remaining characters must keep their original relative order and each letter may appear at most once. Among all possible results that satisfy those conditions, you need to produce the one that is smallest in lexicographic (dictionary) order. Output that resulting string.

title: Design Auction System
explanation_short: You receive a sequence of commands that model an online auction, where each command either adds a new item, records a bid for an existing item, removes an item, or asks for information about bids. The system must keep track of all bids so that it can answer queries such as “what is the current highest bid for this item?” or “which item has the overall highest bid?”. Process the commands in order, updating the stored data as needed, and output the answer for every query command while producing no output for the other operations.

title: Pythagorean Distance Nodes in a Tree
explanation_short: You are given a tree with N nodes (numbered 1…N) and N‑1 edges, each edge having an integer length. Starting from node 1 (the root), compute the total distance along the unique path to every other node. A node is “Pythagorean” if its distance from the root can be the hypotenuse of a Pythagorean triple-that is, the squared distance can be expressed as a² + b² for some positive integers a and b. Output the number of Pythagorean nodes in the tree.

title: Minimum Prefix Removal to Make Array Strictly Increasing
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers. You may delete a contiguous block starting at the first element (a prefix) and keep the rest of the array unchanged. The goal is to make the remaining sequence strictly increasing, where each element is larger than the one before it. Output the smallest possible size of the prefix that must be removed to achieve this.

title: Minimum Partition Score
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers and an integer K. The array must be divided into exactly K non‑empty contiguous groups. Each group has a score defined by the problem’s formula (based on the numbers inside the group), and the total score is the sum of the scores of all groups. Your task is to choose the partition that yields the smallest possible total score and output that minimum value.

title: Longest Strictly Increasing Subsequence With Non-Zero Bitwise AND
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of n positive integers. From this sequence you must select a subsequence that is strictly increasing, and for each pair of consecutive elements in the chosen subsequence the bitwise AND of the two numbers must be non‑zero. Your goal is to find the greatest possible length of a subsequence that satisfies both conditions. Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Find Nth Smallest Integer With K One Bits
explanation_short: You are given two integers N and K. Consider all positive integers whose binary representation contains exactly K bits set to 1, arrange them in increasing order, and identify the Nᵗʰ element in this sequence. Output that integer.

title: Reverse Letters Then Special Characters in a String
explanation_short: You are given a single line of text that may contain alphabetic letters and non‑letter symbols (such as punctuation or digits). Your task is to rearrange the characters so that all the letters appear in reverse order, and independently all the non‑letter symbols also appear in reverse order, while each type stays in the positions originally occupied by that type. The resulting string, with the same length as the input, should be printed as the output.

title: Minimum K to Reduce Array Within Limit
explanation_short: You are given the length n of an array, the n positive integers themselves, and a limit L. You may lower each element by any amount up to a common value K (but not below zero). Your task is to find the smallest K that makes the sum of the adjusted array ≤ L. Output that minimum K.

title: Count Monobit Integers
explanation_short: You are given two integers L and R that define a closed interval. We need to determine how many numbers inside that interval have a binary representation containing exactly one ‘1’ bit (i.e., they are powers of two). The answer is a single integer representing that count.

title: Final Element After Subarray Deletions
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by a sequence of N numbers. You may repeatedly choose any contiguous subarray of length ≥ 2, delete it, and join the remaining parts together. After performing deletions until only one number remains, output that final element.

title: Design Ride Sharing System
explanation_short: You receive a sequence of operations that either add a driver, move a driver, or request a ride. Each driver has an ID and a location on a 2‑D grid; each ride request provides a passenger location and a maximum distance. For every request you must return the ID of the closest driver whose distance is within the limit, breaking ties by the smallest ID, or –1 if no such driver exists. The output is the list of IDs produced by the ride‑request operations.

title: Maximum Score Using Exactly K Pairs
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers and an integer K. From the array you must choose exactly K disjoint pairs of indices (each element can belong to at most one pair). Each chosen pair contributes a score that depends on the two numbers in the pair, and the total score is the sum of those contributions. Compute and output the largest possible total score achievable with exactly K pairs.

title: Longest Alternating Subarray After Removing At Most One Element
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by a sequence of n numbers. You may delete zero or one element from the sequence, then look at any contiguous segment of the remaining numbers. The segment must be alternating: each pair of neighboring values must switch between “greater than” and “less than” (or vice‑versa). Output the greatest possible length of such a segment.

title: House Robber V
explanation_short: You are given the root of a binary tree where each node contains a certain amount of money. If you choose to rob a house represented by a node, you cannot also rob its direct children. Your task is to compute the largest total amount of money you can obtain while respecting this restriction. Return that maximum sum as an integer.

title: Merge Adjacent Equal Elements
explanation_short: You are given a list of N integers. Whenever two neighboring numbers are equal, they are combined into a single element whose value is the sum of those two numbers, and the list shrinks by one position; this merging can be repeated as long as adjacent equal values exist. Your task is to perform all possible merges and report the resulting sequence. Output the final list of numbers after no more adjacent equal elements remain.

title: Count Dominant Indices
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N numbers. An index i is called dominant if the value at position i is strictly larger than every element to its left **and** strictly larger than every element to its right. Your task is to determine how many such dominant indices exist in the array. Output a single integer – the count of dominant indices.

title: Count Subarrays With Cost Less Than or Equal to K
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers and a number K. The cost of a contiguous subarray is defined as the difference between its maximum and minimum elements. Your task is to count how many subarrays have a cost that does not exceed K. Output that total count.

title: Toggle Light Bulbs
explanation_short: You are given a single integer N representing the number of light bulbs numbered 1 to N, all initially off. Starting with the first round, you toggle (turn on if off, turn off if on) every i‑th bulb on the i‑th round for i = 1 to N. After completing all N rounds, determine how many bulbs remain on. Output that count as a single integer.

title: First Element with Unique Frequency
explanation_short: You are given an array of integers. For each distinct value, count how many times it appears in the array. Find the element whose frequency is unique-that is, no other value has the same count-and, if there are several, pick the one that occurs first in the original order. Output that element, or output -1 if no element has a unique frequency.

title: Longest Almost-Palindromic Substring
explanation_short:
You are given a single string S.  
Your task is to locate the longest contiguous part of S that is either already a palindrome or can become a palindrome after changing at most one character.  
Only the length of that substring (or the substring itself, depending on the specification) is required as the answer.  
Return that length (or the substring) as the output.

title: Weighted Word Mapping
explanation_short:
You are given a list of 26 integers that assign a weight to each letter of the alphabet (the first number is the weight of ‘a’, the second of ‘b’, and so on).  
A single word follows, consisting only of lowercase letters.
