Your task is to add up the weights of all the letters that appear in the word.  
Print the resulting sum as a single integer.

title: Number of Prefix Connected Groups
explanation_short: You are given \(n\) words (or strings). Two words belong to the same group if one can be reached from the other by repeatedly moving to a word that is a prefix of the current one (or vice‑versa), so groups are formed by the transitive closure of the prefix relation. Your task is to determine how many such distinct groups exist among the \(n\) words. Output a single integer: the total number of prefix‑connected groups.

title: Check Digitorial Permutation
explanation_short: You are given a single positive integer N. First compute the sum of the factorials of each digit of N. Then check whether any rearrangement of N’s digits can produce a number exactly equal to that sum. Print “YES” if such a permutation exists, otherwise print “NO”.

title: Palindromic Path Queries in a Tree
explanation_short: You are given a rooted tree with n vertices, each vertex labeled by a lowercase letter. For each of q queries you receive a vertex v and a depth h; you must look at all vertices that lie in the subtree of v and have depth exactly h, collect their letters, and decide whether those letters can be rearranged into a palindrome. The answer for each query is a single word: “Yes” if a palindrome arrangement exists, otherwise “No”. The output consists of the answers to the q queries in order.

title: Find the Score Difference in a Game
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by n numbers that represent the points arranged in a line. Two players take turns removing either the leftmost or rightmost number, adding its value to their own total. Assuming both players play optimally, determine how much more (or less) the first player’s final score will be compared to the second player’s. Output a single integer equal to the first player’s score minus the second player’s score.

title: Maximum Subarray XOR with Bounded Range
explanation_short: You are given an array of n integers and two integers L and R that define a length window. For every subarray whose length lies between L and R (inclusive) you must consider the XOR of all its elements. Among all those subarrays, determine the largest possible XOR value. Output that maximum XOR as a single integer.

title: Merge Close Characters
explanation_short: You are given a string of lowercase letters. Two adjacent letters are considered “close” if their positions in the alphabet differ by at most 1, and you may repeatedly merge any such pair into a single character (choosing the smaller letter). Your task is to apply any sequence of these merges so that the resulting string is as short as possible. Output the minimum possible length of the string after all allowed merges.

title: Sum of K-Digit Numbers in a Range
explanation_short: You are given three integers L, R and K. Among all numbers between L and R (inclusive) you must consider only those that contain exactly K digits. Compute the total sum of those qualifying numbers. Output that sum as a single integer (often required modulo 10⁹+⁷ if the sum can be very large).

title: Count Sequences to K
explanation_short: You are given an integer K and an array of N positive numbers. From the array you may pick any number of elements (repetitions allowed) and arrange them in an order to form a sequence. Your task is to count how many different ordered sequences have a product that equals exactly K. The answer should be printed modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: Maximum Bitwise XOR After Rearrangement
explanation_short: You receive an integer n followed by a binary string S of length n. You may permute the characters of S in any order, then split the reordered string into two binary numbers (the two halves, with the longer half getting the extra bit if n is odd). Your task is to choose a rearrangement that makes the bitwise XOR of those two numbers as large as possible. Output the maximum XOR value achievable, expressed as a decimal integer.

title: Count Subarrays With K Distinct Integers
explanation_short: You are given an integer array and a positive integer K. Your task is to determine how many contiguous subarrays contain exactly K different values. Output that total count as a single integer.

title: Smallest Pair With Different Frequencies
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. First count how many times each distinct number occurs. Then consider every pair of two different numbers whose occurrence counts are not the same, and pick the pair with the smallest possible combined value. Output the sum of that pair (or the two numbers themselves, as specified).

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Parity Alternating
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n integers. You may change any element to any other integer, counting each change as one operation. The task is to make the array’s parity alternate (odd, even, odd, … or even, odd, even, …). Compute the smallest number of operations needed and output that minimum.

title: Minimum Capacity Box
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N positive numbers that describe the size (or weight) of each item. The task is to determine the smallest possible capacity a single box must have so that every item can fit inside it. Because the box must be large enough for the biggest item, the answer is simply the maximum value among the given numbers. Output that maximum as a single integer.

title: Trim Trailing Vowels
explanation_short: You are given a single line of text containing only alphabetic characters. Your task is to delete every vowel (a, e, i, o, u, case‑insensitive) that appears at the very end of the string, stopping as soon as a consonant is reached. The resulting string-possibly unchanged if it ends with a consonant-should be printed as the output.

title: Find the Smallest Balanced Index
explanation_short: You are given an array of integers. Your task is to locate the first position where the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it (the element at the position itself is not counted). The index should be reported using the array’s natural zero‑based numbering. If no such position exists, output –1.

title: Minimum Cost to Split into Ones
explanation_short:
You are given a single integer n greater than 1.  
You may repeatedly pick any number x > 1 that you currently have, break it into two positive parts a and b with a + b = x, and you must pay a cost equal to a × b for that split.  
Continue splitting until every remaining number equals 1.  
Your task is to compute the smallest possible total cost achievable by an optimal sequence of splits.  
Print that minimum cost as a single integer.

title: Minimum Bitwise OR From Grid
explanation_short: You are given an n × m matrix of non‑negative integers. From each row you must choose exactly one cell (the column can be different for each row). Compute the bitwise OR of the chosen numbers and output the smallest possible value that can be achieved by any selection. The result is a single integer.

title: First Unique Even Element
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. From this list you must identify the even numbers that occur only once. Among those, pick the one that appears earliest in the original order. Output that value, or indicate that no such element exists (for example, by printing -1).

title: Sum of GCD of Formed Pairs
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N positive integers. For every unordered pair of distinct indices you must compute the greatest common divisor of the two numbers and add all those values together. Output a single integer equal to this total (usually taken modulo 1 000 000 007).

title: Count Fancy Numbers in a Range
explanation_short: You are given two integers L and R defining a closed interval. A “fancy” number is any integer whose decimal representation satisfies the special digit rule described in the statement. Your task is to count how many numbers x with L ≤ x ≤ R are fancy. Output the total count as a single integer.

title: Minimum Operations to Sort a String
explanation_short: You are given a single string S as input. The task is to determine the smallest number of allowed operations needed to rearrange the characters so that the whole string becomes sorted in non‑decreasing (lexicographic) order. An operation consists of swapping two neighboring characters. Output the minimum count of such swaps as an integer.

title: Minimum Cost to Partition a Binary String
explanation_short: You are given a binary string `s`. You may repeatedly split any current substring into two non‑empty parts; the cost of a split equals the number of ‘0’s in the left part plus the number of ‘1’s in the right part. The goal is to keep splitting until every character stands alone, while minimizing the sum of all split costs. Output the smallest possible total cost as an integer.

title: Longest Arithmetic Sequence After Changing At Most One Element
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. You may modify at most one element to any value you like. Determine the maximum possible length of a contiguous segment that can become an arithmetic progression after this single change. Output that length as a single integer.

title: Maximum Points Activated with One Addition
explanation_short: You are given an N × N grid containing only 0s and 1s. A cell with value 1 is considered “activated” and cells are linked together when they are orthogonally adjacent (up, down, left, right). You may change exactly one 0 to 1; after this single addition, find the largest possible number of activated cells that belong to the same connected group. Output that maximum size.

title: Minimum Cost to Equalize Arrays Using Swaps
explanation_short: You are given two arrays of the same length containing integers. First check whether the two arrays can be rearranged to become identical (they must have the same multiset of values). If they can, determine the smallest total cost required to make them equal by swapping elements between the arrays, where each swap’s cost depends on the values being exchanged. Output that minimum cost, or output -1 if it’s impossible to equalize the arrays.

title: Count Commas in Range
explanation_short: You are given two integers L and R ( L ≤ R ). Imagine writing every number from L to R in the usual decimal form that inserts a comma after every three digits counting from the right (e.g., 1 234 567). Your task is to determine how many commas would appear in total across all those written numbers. Output that single integer count.

title: Count Good Subarrays
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers. A subarray is called “good” when the bitwise OR of all its elements is exactly the same as the largest element inside that subarray. Your task is to determine how many subarrays of the given array satisfy this condition. Output a single integer – the total count of good subarrays.

title: Count Commas in Range II
explanation_short: You are given two integers \(L\) and \(R\) (with \(L \le R\)). Write every number from \(L\) through \(R\) in the usual decimal form that inserts a comma after each group of three digits (e.g., 1,234,567). Count how many commas appear in total across all of those written numbers. Output that total as a single integer.

title: Direction Assignments with Exactly K Visible People
explanation_short: You are given two integers N and K. Each of the N people standing in a line must be assigned a direction-either left or right. A person is considered “visible” if, in the direction they face, there is at least one other person standing somewhere ahead of them. Your task is to count how many different direction assignments result in exactly K people being visible. Output that count (usually modulo 10⁹+⁷).

title: Construct Uniform Parity Array I
explanation_short: You are given a single integer n. Your task is to output any sequence of n positive integers such that every element has the same parity – either all of them are even or all of them are odd. Print the n numbers separated by spaces.

title: Construct Uniform Parity Array II
explanation_short:
You are given a single integer n, the length of the array you must build.  
Your task is to output any sequence of n positive integers such that every element shares the same parity (all even or all odd) and the overall sum of the sequence has that same parity as well.  
Print the n numbers separated by spaces.

title: Minimum Removals to Achieve Target XOR
explanation_short: You are given an array of n non‑negative integers and a target value T. By deleting any subset of the elements (possibly none), the XOR of the remaining numbers should become exactly T. Your task is to determine the smallest possible number of deletions that makes this happen, or report that it cannot be achieved. Output that minimum count (or -1 if no such subset exists).

title: Design Event Manager
explanation_short: You receive a list of commands that either add an event with a unique name and a timestamp, delete an existing event, or ask for the event that occurs immediately after or before a given event in chronological order. Your task is to keep the events organized so that each query can be answered correctly at the moment it appears. For every “next” or “previous” query you must output the name of the appropriate event, or a sentinel value (e.g., -1) if no such event exists. All other commands produce no output.

title: Sum of Sortable Integers
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by a list of N numbers. Consider every permutation of the list that ends up sorted in non‑decreasing order; for each such sorted arrangement compute the sum of its elements, and then add all those sums together. Print the final total (typically modulo 10⁹+7).

title: Minimum Absolute Difference Between Two Values
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. From all possible pairs of different elements, you must determine the smallest absolute difference between the two numbers in any pair. The input consists of the number of elements followed by the elements themselves. Output that minimum absolute difference as a single integer.

title: Minimum XOR Path in a Grid
explanation_short: You are given a rectangular grid where each cell contains a non‑negative integer. Starting from the top‑left corner, you may move only right or down until you reach the bottom‑right corner, and you must compute the XOR of all numbers visited along a chosen path. Your task is to determine the smallest possible XOR value achievable by any such path. Output that minimum XOR as a single integer.

title: Mirror Frequency Distance
explanation_short: You are given a single string (usually of even length) containing only letters. Split the string into its left half and its right half, which are mirror images of each other. Count how many times each distinct letter appears in each half and sum the absolute differences of those counts across all letters. The required output is that total sum, a single integer.

title: Count Non Decreasing Arrays With Given Digit Sums
explanation_short: You are given two integers n and S. You must count how many length‑n sequences of digits (0‑9) are non‑decreasing-each element is at least as large as the one before it-and whose total digit sum equals S. Print the count modulo 1 000 000 007.

title: First Matching Character From Both Ends
explanation_short: You are given a single string as input. Starting from the leftmost and rightmost positions, move inward one step at a time, comparing the characters at the two ends. Find the first character that appears in the same position from both sides (i.e., the first matching pair). Output that character; if no such pair exists, output “-1”.

title: Integers With Multiple Sum of Two Cubes
explanation_short: You receive one integer N. Your task is to find every number x ≤ N that can be expressed as a sum of two positive cubes in at least two distinct ways (ignoring the order of the two cubes). List those numbers in increasing order. The output consists only of these integers, one per line (or space‑separated).

title: Incremental Even-Weighted Cycle Queries
explanation_short: You are given N vertices with no edges at the start, followed by Q operations. Each operation either adds an undirected edge between two vertices together with an integer weight, or asks whether the graph built so far already contains a cycle whose total weight is even. For every query you must output “YES” if an even‑weighted cycle exists in the current graph, otherwise “NO”.

title: Minimum Operations to Achieve At Least K Peaks
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers and a target number K. By adding 1 to any element (each addition counts as one operation) you may turn positions into peaks-places where the value is strictly larger than its immediate neighbors. Your task is to perform the fewest total additions so that at least K indices become peaks. Output that minimum number of operations.

title: Count Digit Appearances
explanation_short:
You are given two integers \(n\) and \(d\) (where \(0\le d\le9\)).  
Your task is to determine how many times the digit \(d\) shows up when writing all numbers from 1 through \(n\) in decimal notation.  
The answer is a single integer representing that total count.

title: Minimum Operations to Transform Array into Alternating Prime
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array of n positive numbers. You may increase or decrease any element by 1 as a single operation. Your task is to change the array so that prime and non‑prime numbers appear in alternating positions (for example, all even indices are prime and all odd indices are composite, or vice‑versa). Compute the smallest total number of +1/‑1 operations required to achieve either alternating pattern, and output that minimum count.

title: Minimum Increase to Maximize Special Indices
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by n numbers forming an array. An index i is called special if the value at i is strictly larger than the sum of all elements before it. You may increase any elements by any non‑negative amount; the task is to make the number of special indices as large as possible while adding as little total value as necessary. Output the minimum total increase required to achieve that maximum count.

title: Good Subsequence Queries
explanation_short: You are given an array of n positive integers and q queries, each query specifying a segment [l, r]. A “good” subsequence is any non‑empty selection of elements from that segment whose product is a perfect square. For every query you must determine how many good subsequences exist inside the indicated range. Print the answer for each query, usually modulo 10⁹ + 7.

title: Traffic Signal Color
explanation_short: You receive two values: a word that tells the current traffic‑signal colour (green, yellow or red) and an integer n indicating how many seconds will pass. The signal follows a fixed repeating cycle (green → yellow → red → green …) with known durations for each colour. Determine which colour the signal will show after those n seconds and print that colour.

title: Maximum Value of Concatenated Binary Segments
explanation_short: You are given N binary strings (or numbers written in base 2). By choosing an order and concatenating the strings one after another you form one long binary number. Your task is to find the ordering that makes this final binary value as large as possible. Print that maximum value (usually as a decimal integer).

title: Find the Degree of Each Vertex
explanation_short: You receive a graph with n vertices, given as an adjacency matrix (or an equivalent list of edges). For every vertex you must count how many edges touch it-that is, its degree. The degrees are then output as n integers in order, one for each vertex. Each edge in an undirected graph contributes to the degree of both of its endpoints.

title: Angles of a Triangle
explanation_short: You receive three integer values that represent angles in degrees. You must decide whether these three angles can be the interior angles of a single triangle. Print “YES” if each angle is positive and their sum equals 180; otherwise print “NO”.

title: Longest Balanced Substring After One Swap
explanation_short: You receive a single line containing a string of only '(' and ')' characters. You may optionally swap any two positions in the string at most once, or leave it unchanged. Your task is to determine the greatest possible length of a contiguous substring that forms a correctly balanced parentheses sequence after this operation. Output that maximum length as an integer.

title: Multi Source Flood Fill
explanation_short: You are given a grid of R × C cells containing some starting points (often marked with a special value) and empty cells. For every empty cell you must determine how many steps are required to reach the nearest starting point, moving only up, down, left, or right through adjacent cells. The input consists of the dimensions followed by the grid values, and the output is a grid of the same size where each cell holds its minimum distance to any starting point (the starting points themselves typically have distance 0). If a cell cannot reach any starting point, its distance is left as a designated sentinel (e.g., -1).

title: Smallest Stable Index I
explanation_short: You are given an integer N followed by N numbers. We need to locate the first position (using 1‑based indexing) where the sum of all elements before that position equals the sum of all elements after it. If such a position exists, output its index; otherwise output -1.

title: Smallest Stable Index II
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and a sequence of n numbers. A “stable index” is an position i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) where the sum of all elements before i is exactly the same as the sum of all elements after i. Your task is to locate the smallest such i in the array. If no position satisfies the condition, output -1; otherwise output the index (using 1‑based numbering).

title: Count Connected Subgraphs with Even Node Sum
explanation_short: You are given an undirected graph with N vertices, each vertex assigned an integer value, and a list of the M edges connecting them. Your task is to count how many different non‑empty subsets of vertices form a connected subgraph whose total sum of assigned values is an even number. The answer should be printed as a single integer (often modulo 10⁹+7). The input consists of N, the N values, M, and the M edge pairs; the output is just that count.

title: Count Good Integers on a Grid Path
explanation_short: You are given an N × M grid of integers. A path starts at the top‑left cell, ends at the bottom‑right cell, and may move only right or down at each step. An integer is considered “good” if there exists at least one such monotone path that visits a cell containing that value. Output the total number of distinct good integers.

title: K-th Smallest Remaining Even Integer in Subarray Queries
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers. Each of the Q queries provides three numbers L, R and K, defining a subarray from position L to R (inclusive). Within that subarray you look only at the even numbers that remain, sort them, and report the K‑th smallest one. If fewer than K even numbers exist in the range, output -1. Print the answer for each query on a separate line.

title: Valid Elements in an Array
explanation_short: You are given the length of an array N followed by N integers. For each position we consider the elements to its left and to its right; an element is “valid” if it is not smaller than any element on its left and not larger than any element on its right. Your task is to count how many such valid elements exist in the array. Print that count as a single integer.

title: Valid Digit Number
explanation_short: You are given a single integer N. We need to decide whether every decimal digit of N is either 0 or 1. If that condition holds, the answer is “YES”; otherwise it is “NO”. The output is just this single word.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Non Decreasing
explanation_short: You are given the length of an array \(n\) and the \(n\) integer values in order. You may increase any element any number of times, and each unit increase counts as one operation. Your task is to determine the smallest total number of operations required so that the entire array becomes non‑decreasing (each element is at least as large as the one before it). Output that minimum number.

title: Compare Sums of Bitonic Parts
explanation_short: You are given the length \(n\) of an array followed by the \(n\) integer elements. The array first rises (or stays equal) and then falls, forming a single bitonic shape; the peak separates the left and right parts. Compute the total of the numbers on the left side of the peak and the total on the right side, then report which sum is larger (or that they are equal). The output is a single word such as “LEFT”, “RIGHT” or “EQUAL”.

title: Count Indices With Opposite Parity
explanation_short: You receive an integer n and then n numbers. For each position i (0‑based), check whether the element’s parity is different from the index’s parity – i.e., an odd number at an even index or an even number at an odd index. Count how many positions meet this opposite‑parity condition. Output that count.

title: Maximum Sum of Alternating Subsequence With Distance at Least K
explanation_short: You are given an integer N, an integer K, and a sequence of N numbers. You must pick a subsequence whose indices are at least K apart and whose signs alternate (the first chosen element adds, the next subtracts, then adds, etc.). The aim is to maximize the total sum of the selected elements. Output the largest possible sum.

title: Sort Vowels by Frequency
explanation_short: You are given a single line of text containing letters, spaces, and punctuation. Your task is to rearrange only the vowel characters (a, e, i, o, u, case‑insensitive) so that they appear in order of how many times each vowel occurs in the original string. Vowels that occur more often should come before those that occur less often, and vowels with the same count should keep their original relative order. All non‑vowel characters must stay in their original positions, and the resulting string is printed as the output.

title: Sum of Primes Between Number and Its Reverse
explanation_short: You receive a single positive integer N. By writing its digits in reverse order you obtain another number R. Look at every integer that lies strictly between the smaller of N and R and the larger of them, and add up those that are prime. Output the total sum (or 0 if no such primes exist).

title: Minimum Flips to Make Binary String Coherent
explanation_short: You are given a binary string S consisting only of ‘0’ and ‘1’. You may change any character to the opposite value, and each change counts as one flip. Your task is to determine the smallest number of flips required so that the entire string becomes alternating (no two neighboring characters are the same). The answer should be a single integer representing that minimum number.

title: Minimum Cost to Move Between Indices
explanation_short: You are given an array where the i‑th element tells the cost of moving between index i and i+1. Afterwards a list of queries follows, each containing a start index s and a target index t. For every query you must report the smallest total cost required to travel from s to t. Because you can only move along the line, the cheapest route is the direct segment, so the answer is the sum of the costs on that segment. Output one number per query.

title: Score Validator
explanation_short: You are given the number of recorded moments `N` followed by `N` integers that represent the cumulative score after each moment in a game. We have to decide whether that list could arise from a game where, at each step, at most one point is added to the total score (so the score can stay the same or increase by exactly 1). Print “YES” if the sequence obeys those rules, otherwise print “NO”.

title: Maximize Fixed Points After Deletions
explanation_short: You are given an array a of length n. A position i is a fixed point if, after removing some elements (keeping the remaining order), the element at that position equals its new index. You must choose deletions so that the number of fixed points is as large as possible. Output that maximum possible count. (Think of the condition a[i] – i forming a non‑increasing sequence.)

title: Minimum Generations to Target Point
explanation_short: You are given a target point (x, y) and a list of allowed move vectors. Starting from the origin (0, 0), you may apply any of the given vectors in each generation, and you may reuse vectors as many times as you like. Your task is to determine the smallest number of generations (i.e., moves) required to land exactly on the target point, or report that it is impossible. The output is that minimum count, or –1 if no sequence of moves can reach (x, y).

title: Count Valid Word Occurrences
explanation_short: You are given a text string that may contain letters, spaces and punctuation, and a list of words. Your task is to determine how many of the listed words actually occur in the text as whole words (not as parts of longer words), ignoring differences in case and any surrounding punctuation. The result you must output is a single integer representing that count.

title: Minimum Threshold Path With Limited Heavy Edges
explanation_short: You receive a graph with N vertices and M edges, each edge having a numeric weight, plus a start node S, a target node T, and an integer K. The task is to pick the smallest possible threshold X so that there exists a path from S to T containing at most K edges whose weight exceeds X. In other words, you may traverse at most K “heavy” edges, and you want the maximum allowed weight X to be as low as possible. Output that minimal X (or indicate impossibility, e.g., with -1).

title: Minimize Array Sum Using Divisible Replacements
explanation_short: You are given the length n of an array and the n integers it contains. You may repeatedly choose any element and replace it with any positive integer that divides the current value (including 1). Your task is to determine the smallest possible total sum of the array after performing any number of such replacements. Output that minimum sum as a single integer.

title: Concatenate Array With Reverse
explanation_short: You receive an integer n followed by n integers. Create a new list that first contains the given numbers in their original order and then the same numbers in reverse order. Output the resulting 2 × n numbers separated by spaces.

title: Minimum Cost to Buy Apples II
explanation_short: You are given a target number N of apples you want to obtain and M different pack types, each described by its size Aᵢ (how many apples it contains) and its price Cᵢ. Starting with zero apples, you may purchase any number of packs in any order, possibly buying the same type multiple times. Your task is to determine the smallest total amount of money needed to end up with at least N apples. Output that minimum cost, or indicate that it is impossible if no combination reaches the target.

title: Check Adjacent Digit Differences
explanation_short: You are given a single line containing a string of decimal digits. Your task is to verify whether every pair of neighboring digits differs by exactly 1 (the absolute difference of the two digits must be 1). If the whole string satisfies this condition, output a positive response (e.g., “YES”); otherwise output the negative response (e.g., “NO”).

title: Count K-th Roots in a Range
explanation_short: You are given three integers A, B and K. A and B define a closed interval [A, B] on the number line, and K specifies the exponent. Your task is to determine how many integer values x satisfy x^K lying inside that interval. Output a single integer representing that count.

title: Smallest Unique Subarray
explanation_short: You are given an array of N integers. Your task is to determine the minimum length of a contiguous segment (subarray) whose exact sequence of values occurs only once anywhere in the whole array. If no such subarray exists, you should report that it is impossible. The output is a single integer: the smallest length that satisfies the uniqueness condition, or ‑1 if every possible subarray repeats.

title: Count Non Adjacent Subsets in a Rooted Tree
explanation_short: You are given a rooted tree with N vertices, described by the list of edges (the root is usually vertex 1). A subset of vertices is called “non‑adjacent” if no two vertices in the subset share an edge of the tree. Your task is to determine how many different non‑adjacent subsets exist for the whole tree. Print that count (often modulo 10⁹+7) as a single integer.

title: Maximum Path Intersection Sum in a Grid
explanation_short: You are given an N × M grid of integers. Choose two monotonic paths that both start at the top‑left corner and end at the bottom‑right corner, moving only right or down, and require that the paths intersect at exactly one cell. The score is the sum of all numbers visited by either path, counting the intersecting cell only once. Output the maximum achievable total score.

title: Largest Local Values in a Matrix II
explanation_short: You are given an n × n grid of integers. For every possible 3 × 3 block inside the grid, you must determine the greatest number that appears in that block. Collect those maxima into a new (n‑2) × (n‑2) matrix, preserving the relative positions of the blocks. The input consists of n followed by n lines of n integers each, and the output is the resulting matrix, printed row by row.

title: Minimum Swaps to Move Zeros to End
explanation_short: You are given a list of n integers that may contain zeros and non‑zero values. Your task is to compute the smallest number of swaps needed to push every zero to the end of the list while keeping the relative order of the non‑zero elements unchanged. Output that minimum swap count as a single integer.

title: Number of Pairs After Increment
explanation_short: You are given an integer n followed by n numbers. For any pair of positions (i, j) you may optionally add 1 to each of the two numbers (at most once per element). We need to count how many unordered pairs can become equal after these optional increments. Print that total count as a single integer.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Modulo Alternating I
explanation_short: You are given an integer k and an array a of length n. For each position you may repeatedly add 1 to the element (each addition counts as one operation). Choose two different residues r₀ and r₁ (0 ≤ r < k) and make every even‑indexed element congruent to r₀ mod k and every odd‑indexed element congruent to r₁ mod k, using the fewest total additions. Output the minimum number of operations required.

title: Limit Occurrences in Sorted Array
explanation_short:
You are given a non‑decreasing array of integers.  
Your task is to discard any extra copies of a value so that each distinct number appears no more than twice.  
The removal must be done in‑place, and you should report the length of the shortened array.  
The first part of the original array will then contain all the kept elements in their original order.

title: Minimum Operations to Sort a Permutation
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and a list of n distinct numbers that form a permutation of 1…n. The task is to determine the fewest swaps of any two positions that will reorder the list into ascending order 1, 2, …, n. The answer is a single integer representing that minimum number of swap operations.

title: Password Strength
explanation_short: You receive an integer n and a string representing a password of that length. A strong password must contain at least one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter, one digit, one special character, and be at least six characters long. Determine the fewest characters you need to add so the password meets all these requirements. Output that minimum number.

title: Maximum Number of Items From Sale I
explanation_short: You are given n item prices and a budget p. You may purchase items individually, paying their listed price, or you can buy any two items together and only pay the higher price of the pair (the cheaper one becomes free). Your task is to choose purchases so that the total spent does not exceed p while obtaining as many items as possible. Output the maximum number of items you can acquire.

title: Pattern Printing 1
explanation_short: You are given a single integer N. Print N lines where the first line contains one ‘*’, the second line contains two ‘*’, and so on, with the i‑th line having i asterisks. The output should form a left‑aligned triangle of stars.

title: Digit Frequency Score
explanation_short: You are given a single integer (or a string of digits) as the input. First count how many times each digit 0‑9 appears in that number. Then compute the “digit frequency score” by multiplying each digit by its own count and adding up all those products. Output the final sum as a single integer.

title: Maximum Number of Items From Sale II
explanation_short: You are given a list of item prices, one price for each day, and a total amount of money you can spend. You may buy at most one item per day, and you can apply a one‑time discount that halves the price (rounded down) on any single day you choose. Your task is to decide which items to purchase and where to use the discount so that the total spending does not exceed the given budget. The answer you must output is the greatest possible number of items you can buy.

title: Check Palindrome (Number)
explanation_short:
You receive a single integer N as input.  
Your task is to decide whether the sequence of its decimal digits reads the same forward and backward.  
If it does, you should output a word indicating success (for example, “YES”); otherwise output the opposite word (for example, “NO”).  
Only the result matters-no extra text or formatting is required.

title: Lexicographically Maximum MEX Array
explanation_short: You are given an integer n and an array a of length n containing numbers between 0 and n. In one move you may pick any position i and replace a[i] by the MEX (minimum excluded value) of the whole current array; you may repeat this operation arbitrarily many times. Your task is to transform the array into the lexicographically largest possible sequence of numbers. Print the resulting array after all optimal moves have been applied.

title: Count Digits
explanation_short: You are given an integer n (or several such numbers, one per test case). For each n you must look at every decimal digit it contains, ignoring any zeros. Count how many of those digits divide n evenly (i.e., n mod digit = 0). Output that count for each input number on its own line.

title: Pattern Printing 2
explanation_short: You receive one integer N. From it you must produce N lines of output. The first line should contain N asterisks (separated by a space), the second line N‑1 asterisks, and so on until the last line has a single asterisk. The result is a left‑aligned triangle that shrinks by one star each row.

title: Count all Divisors
explanation_short: You receive one integer n. Your task is to figure out how many positive integers divide n exactly, i.e., leave no remainder. The result is the total count of those divisors. Output that count as a single number.

title: Reverse a Number
explanation_short:
You are given an integer N as input.  
Your task is to rearrange its decimal digits so that they appear in the opposite order.  
If N is negative, keep the minus sign in front of the reversed digits.  
Print the resulting number, discarding any leading zeros that appear after the reversal.

title: Check Prime
explanation_short: You receive one integer n as input. Your task is to decide whether n is a prime number – that is, whether it has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. If n is prime, output the word “YES”; otherwise output “NO”. The answer must be a single line containing only that word.

title: Largest Element in Array
explanation_short: You are given a list of numbers representing an array. Your task is to determine which number in the array is the greatest. Scan through the elements to identify the maximum value. The result you output should be that single largest number.

title: Check if Array is Sorted
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of N numbers. Your task is to decide whether the whole sequence appears in non‑decreasing order from left to right. If every element is at least as large as the one before it, the array is considered sorted; otherwise it is not. Output a single word such as “YES” when the array is sorted and “NO” when it isn’t.

title: GCD / HCF
explanation_short: You receive two positive integers as input. Your task is to determine the largest integer that divides both numbers without leaving a remainder. Print that greatest common divisor as the only output.

title: Check Armstrong Number
explanation_short:
You are given a single integer \(n\).  
You must decide whether the sum of each of its decimal digits raised to the power of the number of digits equals \(n\) itself.  
If the condition holds, output a positive answer (for example, “YES”); otherwise output a negative answer (for example, “NO”).

title: Linear Search
explanation_short: You are given a list of numbers and a single target value. Your task is to scan the list from the beginning until you either locate the target or reach the end. If the target appears, report the position of its first occurrence (using zero‑based indexing); otherwise output a sentinel such as –1. The output is just that single integer.

title: Union of Two Sorted Arrays
explanation_short:
You are given two arrays that are already sorted in non‑decreasing order.  
Your task is to combine them into a single collection that contains every element that appears in either array, but without repeating any value.  
The resulting list must also be sorted.  
Print the elements of this union, typically separated by spaces or on one line.

title: Second Largest Element
explanation_short: You are given a list of numbers, typically supplied as an integer N followed by N integers. Your task is to identify the element that is smaller than the maximum value but larger than every other element in the list. The required output is that second‑largest value (or an appropriate indication if it does not exist).

title: Maximum Consecutive Ones
explanation_short: You are given an array that contains only 0s and 1s. Your task is to determine how many 1s appear consecutively at most in any part of the array. Scan the array and keep track of the longest run of 1s you encounter. Output that maximum length as a single integer.

title: Move Zeros to End
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers. Rearrange the list so that all zeros appear after every non‑zero element, while keeping the original order of the non‑zero numbers unchanged. The output is the same list with the zeros moved to the end. Print or return this reordered list.

title: Longest Subarray with Sum K (Positives)
explanation_short: You are given an array of positive integers and a target value K. Your task is to determine the maximum length of a contiguous segment of the array whose elements add up exactly to K. Consider all possible subarrays, but only those whose sum equals K are relevant. Output the length of the longest such subarray, or 0 if no subarray meets the requirement.

title: Find Missing Number
explanation_short: You are given an array that contains n distinct integers ranging from 0 to n (or 1 to n + 1), with exactly one value missing from the sequence. Your task is to identify which number from that range does not appear in the array. The input provides the size of the array followed by the n numbers, and the output should be the single missing integer.

title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's)
explanation_short: You receive a list of integers, which can include both positive and negative values. Your task is to identify a contiguous portion of the list whose elements add up to the greatest possible total. The output should be that maximum sum, and the chosen segment must contain at least one element.

title: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag)
explanation_short: You are given an array that contains only the values 0, 1, and 2, each representing a different color. The task is to rearrange the elements so that all 0s appear first, followed by all 1s, and finally all 2s. This reordering must be done in place, without using extra storage for another array. After processing, the array itself is the required output.

title: Majority Element (>n/2)
explanation_short: You are given a list of n integers. Your task is to identify the value that occurs strictly more than ⌊n/2⌋ times in the list. If such a value exists, output that integer; otherwise indicate that no majority element is present (for example, by printing -1). The result should be a single number representing the majority element or the chosen “not found” marker.

title: Anagram Check
explanation_short:
You are given two strings as input.  
Your task is to decide whether the two strings contain exactly the same letters in any order, ignoring differences such as case or spacing if the specification requires.  
If they are anagrams, output a positive response (e.g., “YES”); otherwise output a negative response (e.g., “NO”).

title: Reverse a Linked List
explanation_short: You are given a singly linked list where each node points to the next element in the sequence. Your task is to reorder the list so that the direction of all the links is reversed, making the former tail become the new head. The input consists of the original list’s head node, and you must produce a reference to the head of the reversed list. The output should be a linked list that contains exactly the same values as the input, but in opposite order.

title: Middle of Linked List
explanation_short: You are given the head of a singly linked list. Your task is to locate the node that lies in the middle of the sequence. If the list has an even number of nodes, you should return the node that starts the second half. Output that middle node (or its value).

title: Linked List Cycle Detection
explanation_short: You are given the head node of a singly‑linked list. The list may contain a loop where a node’s next pointer points back to an earlier node, creating an infinite cycle. Your task is to decide whether such a cycle exists anywhere in the structure. Return a boolean value (or equivalent “true/false” answer) indicating the presence or absence of a cycle.

title: Remove Nth Node from End
explanation_short: You are given the head of a singly‑linked list and an integer n. Count from the tail of the list toward the front until you reach the n‑th node. That node must be removed, reconnecting its neighbors so the list remains intact. Return the head of the resulting list (which may change if the first node was removed).

title: Two Sum (Hashing)
explanation_short: You are given a list of integers and a single target integer. Your task is to locate two distinct elements in the list whose sum equals the target value. You must identify the positions (indices) of those two elements. The result should be those two indices, typically returned in any order.

title: Pow(x, n)
explanation_short: You are given a real number x and an integer n. The task is to calculate the value of x raised to the power n (equivalent to multiplying x by itself n times, handling negative exponents as reciprocals). Return the computed result as a floating‑point number.

title: Kth Smallest Element in Sorted Matrix
explanation_short: You are given an n × n matrix where each row and each column is sorted in non‑decreasing order, together with an integer k. Your task is to determine the value that would appear in position k if all the matrix elements were listed in a single sorted sequence. Print that k‑th smallest value.

title: Preorder Traversal
explanation_short: You receive a binary tree defined by its node values and left/right child connections. Beginning at the root, you must visit each node before its children, following the order: node, then left subtree, then right subtree. Produce the sequence of visited node values in that order. Output the sequence as a space‑separated list (or equivalent format).

title: Kth Smallest in BST
explanation_short: You are given a binary search tree and an integer k. The task is to determine which node’s value is the k‑th smallest when all the tree’s values are ordered from smallest to largest. Return that value as the answer.

title: Inorder Traversal
explanation_short: You are given a binary tree, described by its root node and the connections to each node’s left and right children. Your task is to visit the nodes in “inorder” order – first everything in the left subtree, then the current node, and finally everything in the right subtree. Collect the values of the nodes as you visit them. The output should be a sequence (or list) of those values in the exact order they were visited.

title: Implement Trie
explanation_short: You are given a sequence of commands that either add a word to a data structure or ask whether a word or a prefix exists in it. Each command consists of an operation name (such as insert, search, or startsWith) followed by a string argument. Your task is to build a Trie that supports these operations and to report the result of every search or startsWith query as “true” or “false”. The output should list the answers in the order the queries appear.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of BST
explanation_short: You are given a binary search tree and two distinct node values that are guaranteed to exist in the tree. Your task is to identify the node that is the deepest (i.e., farthest from the root) while still being an ancestor of both given nodes. The output should be the value stored in that lowest common ancestor node.

title: Validate BST
explanation_short: You are given the root of a binary tree where each node stores an integer value. Your task is to decide whether the tree satisfies the binary search‑tree property: every node’s left descendants must contain only smaller values and every node’s right descendants only larger values, with this rule holding recursively for all subtrees. The input consists of the tree structure (typically as node references or an array representation). Return a single boolean answer-true if the tree is a valid BST, otherwise false.

title: Kth Largest Element in Array
explanation_short: You are given an unsorted array of integers and a positive integer k. Your task is to identify the element that would appear in the k‑th position if the array were sorted in descending order. In other words, you need to find the k‑th largest value among all the numbers. The program should output that single integer.

title: Number of Connected Components
explanation_short: You are given an integer n representing vertices numbered 0 to n‑1, and a list of undirected edges connecting pairs of these vertices. Your task is to determine how many separate groups of vertices exist where each vertex can reach any other vertex in the same group via the given edges. The result should be a single integer indicating the total number of such connected components.

title: Range Sum Query (Segment Tree)
explanation_short: You are given an initial array of numbers. Afterwards you will receive a sequence of operations, each either changing the value at a single position or asking for the sum of all elements between two given indices (inclusive). For every sum‑query you must output the computed total. The updates affect all subsequent queries. The task is to process all operations efficiently.

title: Best Time to Buy/Sell Stock with Cooldown
explanation_short: You are given an array where each element represents the price of a stock on a particular day. You may complete as many buy‑sell transactions as you like, but after you sell you must wait one full day before buying again. Your task is to choose the days to buy and sell so that the total profit is as large as possible. Return that maximum achievable profit as an integer.

title: Find Indices of Stable Mountains
explanation_short: We are given a list of mountain heights and a threshold value. Our task is to identify the mountains that are considered stable, which happens when the previous mountain is significantly taller than the threshold. We need to find the positions of these stable mountains in the list. The result will be a list of indices corresponding to the stable mountains.

title: Count the Number of Houses at a Certain Distance I
explanation_short: We are given the number of houses in a city, and the minimum and maximum distances between them. Our task is to find the number of pairs of houses that are at a certain distance from each other, for each possible distance from the minimum to the maximum. The output will be a list of counts, where each count represents the number of pairs at a specific distance.

title: Divide an Array Into Subarrays With Minimum Cost I
explanation_short: We are given an array of integers and need to divide it into 3 separate subarrays. The goal is to find the minimum possible sum of the costs of these subarrays, where the cost of each subarray is the value of its first element. The input is the array of integers, and the output is the minimum sum of the costs of the 3 subarrays. We need to determine how to split the array to achieve the lowest total cost.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make Array XOR Equal to K
explanation_short: We are given an array of integers and a target number. Our goal is to find the minimum number of operations required to make the bitwise XOR of all elements in the array equal to the target number. The operation involves flipping bits in the binary representation of the array elements. The output will be the minimum number of operations needed to achieve the desired XOR result.

title: Maximum Good Subarray Sum
explanation_short: We are given an array of numbers and a target difference. Our task is to find the maximum sum of a subarray where the difference between the first and last elements is exactly equal to the target difference. The output will be the maximum sum of such a subarray, or 0 if no such subarray exists. We need to examine all possible subarrays to determine which ones meet the condition and have the largest sum.

title: Count the Number of Powerful Integers
explanation_short: We are given a range of numbers from start to finish, a limit for each digit, and a string s. Our task is to find all the numbers within this range that end with the string s and have each digit less than or equal to the given limit. The output will be the total count of such numbers, known as powerful integers.

title: Minimum Number of Pushes to Type Word I
explanation_short: We are given a string of distinct lowercase English letters. Our goal is to find the minimum number of times keys on a telephone keypad need to be pushed to type this string, considering that the keys can be remapped to any set of letters. The output will be the total minimum number of pushes required to type the entire string. We need to determine the optimal mapping of letters to keys to achieve this minimum number of pushes.

title: Find Beautiful Indices in the Given Array I
explanation_short: We are given a string and two specific substrings, along with a distance limit. Our task is to find all indices in the string where the first substring is found and there is also an occurrence of the second substring within the given distance limit. The output will be a sorted list of these indices, ordered from smallest to largest.

title: Maximum Size of a Set After Removals
explanation_short: We are given two integer arrays, nums1 and nums2, of the same even length. Our task is to remove half of the elements from each array and then combine the remaining elements into a set. The goal is to find the maximum possible number of unique elements in this set after the removals. The output will be the size of this set, which contains the unique elements from both arrays after removals.

title: Divide an Array Into Subarrays With Minimum Cost II
explanation_short: We are given an array of integers and two numbers, k and dist. Our task is to divide the array into k non-overlapping subarrays such that the distance between the start of the second subarray and the start of the last subarray is within a certain limit, dist. The goal is to find the minimum total cost, where the cost of each subarray is the value of its first element, and the total cost is the sum of these individual costs. The output will be the minimum total cost to divide the array into k subarrays under the given conditions.

title: Minimum Amount of Damage Dealt to Bob
explanation_short: We are given Bob's power and two lists: one for the damage each enemy deals to Bob per second, and one for each enemy's health. We need to figure out the minimum total damage Bob will take before killing all his enemies, considering he can attack one enemy each second. The output will be the total minimum damage dealt to Bob. Bob's goal is to minimize the damage he takes by strategically choosing which enemy to attack each second.

title: Find if Array Can Be Sorted
explanation_short: We are given an array of positive integers as input. Our task is to determine if it's possible to sort this array in ascending order by swapping adjacent elements that have the same number of set bits in their binary representation. The output will be a boolean value indicating whether the array can be sorted or not. We need to find out if there's a sequence of such swaps that can arrange the numbers in the correct order.
